I. CUm multa sunt, quæ Pastoris Ecclesiastici curas & ἐπισύσεως commotionem (1.Cor.XI.28.) occupant: tum illud inprimis ad industriam & procurationem Divinitus illi mandatam pertinet, ut ovium sibi commissarum exorbitationes & peccata religiosè observet, & spiritualis Medici adinstar, idoneis remediis curet, ne Divinam temporalem & æternam maledictionem iis inconcilient.
units.tr: I. Although many things occupy the pastor's care and the anxious stirring of conscience [ἐπισύσεως] (1 Cor. 11:28), this above all belongs to the diligence and duty committed to him by God: that he carefully observe the straying and sins of the sheep entrusted to him, and, like a spiritual physician, treat them with suitable remedies, so that he does not bring upon them God's temporal and eternal curse.

units.la: II. Sicut verò, juxta tritum illud, ignoti nulla est curatio morbi: ita ante omnia peccatorum cognitio, & nonnulla etiam inquisitio defectuum & peccatorum populi haud postrema curæ Pastoralis pars est. Licet enim curiosius secreta omnium rimari, hunc in finem, ut fama, fortuna vel vita proximi per malevolentiam in discrimen præsens adducatur, charitati, quam Deo, & propter Deum proximo debemus, è diametro repugnet; ἀλλοτριεπισκοπησις, συκοφαντια & ψιθυρισμὸς crimen incurrat; & plerunque alienæ vitæ rigidi exactores, propriæ incuriosi sint; hominum genus, uti Augustinus Confess. lib. X. 11. loquitur, curiosum, ad cognoscendam vitam alienam, desidiosum ad corrigendum suam; tamen in universum cognoscere & scrutari aliorum ἁμαρτήματα, haud equidem nefas est, si ita fiat, ex conscientia pura & charitate ἀνωτ. ἐλέγχτων, ad Dei gloriam, & salutem proximi peccantis, vel ex alieno peccato periclitantis; atque insuper scrutator ejusmodi, juxta S.Pauli Gal.VI 4. regulam, proprium opus suum prius exploraverit. Charitas enim à se incipit, & quisque secum habitare, salutem suam cum timore & tremore operari; ac demum conversus fratres confirmare, & transgressores vias Domini docere (Psal.LI.15. Luc.XXII.32.) tenetur.
units.tr: II. Yet, as the common saying has it, there is no cure for a disease that is unknown; so before all else, the knowledge of sins, and some inquiry into the failings and sins of the people, is no small part of pastoral care. For although to pry curiously into the secrets of all men, for the purpose of bringing another's reputation, fortune or life into present danger through malice, is wholly contrary to the love we owe to God and, for God's sake, to our neighbour; and incurs the crimes of meddling in others' affairs [ἀλλοτριεπισκοπησις], of false accusation [συκοφαντια] and of whispering [ψιθυρισμὸς]; and although those who are strict judges of another's life are often careless of their own; a kind of men who, as Augustine says in Confessions Book X, chapter 11, are curious to know the lives of others, but idle in correcting their own; nevertheless, to know and examine the sins of others in general is by no means wrong, provided it is done with a pure conscience and out of love, in order to rebuke [ἀνωτ. ἐλέγχτων], for the glory of God and the salvation of the sinning neighbour, or of one endangered by another's sin. Moreover, such an examiner, according to the rule of St. Paul in Gal. 6:4, should first have examined his own work. For charity begins at home: each man must dwell with himself, work out his own salvation with fear and trembling, and then, once converted, is bound to strengthen his brothers and to teach transgressors the ways of the Lord (Ps. 51:15; Luke 22:32).

units.la: III. Præ cæteris autem omnibus cognitio & inquisitio moderata, & generalis saltem, nec in conscientiam & perniciem errantis peccatoris grassans (qualem in Ecclesia Romana Inquisitorum Fidei & Confessionis tribunalia crudeliter sibi tribuunt) curatorem animarum decet. Horum enim præcipuum munus est, contra hæreses & peccata populi sibi commissi vigilanter excubare, & correctionibus ac correptionibus paternis atque fraternis delinquentes in orbitam fidei & pietatis revocare. Fili hominis, צופה speculatorem dedi te domui Israelis. Audies igitur de ore meo verbum, & admonebis eos nomine meo.
units.tr: III. Above all others, however, a moderate and at least general inquiry, one that does not rage against the conscience and ruin of the erring sinner (such as the tribunals of the Inquisitors of the Faith and Confession, which the Roman Church cruelly claims for itself), befits the shepherd of souls. For his chief task is to keep watch vigilantly against the heresies and sins of the people committed to him, and by paternal and brotherly corrections and admonitions to recall the offenders to the path of faith and piety. Son of man, I have made you a watchman [צופה] for the house of Israel. You shall hear a word from my mouth, and warn them in my name.

units.la: Cūm Cùm dixero ego impio: Moriendo morieris, & non admonueris eum, nec locutus fueris, ut caveat impius ut recedat à via sua impia; ipse in iniquitate sua morietur; sanguinem autem ejus de manu tua requiram, Ezech. III. 17-18. Obedite ductoribus vestris & subjacete. Ipsi enim vigilant pro animabus vestris, quasi rationem reddituři, ut cum gaudio id faciant, & non ingemiscentes. Hoc enim inutile vobis esset, Heb. XIII. 17.
units.tr: When I say to the wicked, "You shall surely die," and you do not warn him, nor speak to warn the wicked to turn from his wicked way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand (Ezek. 3:17-18). Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they watch for your souls, as those who must give account, that they may do so with joy and not with groaning; for that would be unprofitable for you (Heb. 13:17).

units.la: IV. Sunt ergo Pastores Ecclesiæ םיפֹצ Speculatores, Ἐπίσκοποι Episcopi. Attendite vobis ipsis & toti gregi, cui vos Spiritus S. præfecit Ἐπισκόπους, ut pascatis Ecclesiam, quam proprio sanguine suo acquisivit, Actor. XX. 28. Notat porrò vox Ἐπίσκοπ& Episcopus tum speculatorem, vigilem, inspectorem: tum visitatorem. Et Speculator talis, & visitator Pastor Ecclesiæ est. Sicut enim speculatores Romani huc illuc amandati occulta quæque investigarunt: ita quodammodo Ecclesiæ Ministris id ipsum incumbit. Sol quippe mundi, elogio Salvatoris, Matth. V. 14. cluent. Sol, radiosus ille mundi oculus, inferiora omnia aspicit & penetrat. Pari ratione Ecclesiæ Ministri, Ecclesiarum suarum oculi emissitii, circumspiciunt, & ἐπισκοπῶν attendunt, quæ hujus vel illius oviculæ, familiæ, societatis facies & constitutio sit; locum ne apud eas religio habeat, an ab iis exulet; an ἀξίως τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ condignè Evangelio ambulent, Phil. I. 27. dicta factis adæquent, Divinis & humanis legibus obsequantur, nec ne. Huc facit munus visitandi Ecclesias & familias iisdem injunctum; exemplo S. Pauli Barnabam ita alloquentis: Ἐπισχέψαντες δὴ Βαρναβᾶς ἐπιφανῶς τὰς ἀδελφὰς ἡμῶν κατὰ πᾶσαν πόλιν. Reverti invisamus fratres nostros per omnes civitates, in quibus annunciavimus sermonem Domini, cogniturí, quomodo habeant, Act. XV. 36. Unde nihil eorum, quæ fidelibus conducerent, se subterfugisse, quò minùs ea annuntiaret & doceret δημοσίᾳ καὶ κατ' οἴκους publicè & per singulas domus; idem S. Paulus Act. XX. 20. testatur. Ad Thessalonicenses pariter scribit: Ναΐτις quemadmodum unumquemque vestrum, tanquam pater liberos suos, hortabamur & consolabamur, obtestabamur, ut ambulȧ retis, sicut dignum est Deo, 1. Thess. II. 11. Et S. Johannes piæ cuipiam matronæ gaudium suum testatur, quòd ex domesticis & filiis ipsius invenerit, qui incederent ἐν ἀληθείᾳ in veritate, 2. Joh. 4. Ita quilibet Ecclesiæ Minister quodammodo ἀποστολῆς est, licet munus isthoc Episcoporum vicariis Jura Canonica eximium fecerint.
units.tr: IV. Therefore the ministers of the Church are watchmen [צֹפִים] and overseers [Ἐπίσκοποι, Episcopi]. Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers [Ἐπισκόπους], to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The word overseer [Ἐπίσκοπος, Episcopus] signifies a watchman, a vigilant inspector, and also a visitor. Such a watchman and visitor is the minister of the Church. For just as Roman scouts, sent here and there, searched out whatever was hidden, so something similar falls to the ministers of the Church. The sun of the world, as the Saviour calls it (Matt. 5:14), shines: that radiant eye of the world looks upon and penetrates all lower things. In the same way, the ministers of the Church, the eyes of their churches, look round and attend with care [ἐπισκοπῶν] to what is the face and condition of this or that little sheep, family or society; whether religion has a place among them or is banished from them; whether they walk worthily of the Gospel [ἀξίως τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ] (Phil. 1:27), whether their words match their deeds, and whether they obey the divine and human laws or not. To this belongs the duty of visiting the churches and families entrusted to them, following the example of St. Paul, who spoke thus to Barnabas: Let us now return and visit our brothers in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, to see how they are (Acts 15:36). Hence St. Paul also testifies (Acts 20:20) that he had shrunk from declaring nothing that would be useful to the faithful, nor from teaching it publicly and from house to house [δημοσίᾳ καὶ κατ' οἴκους]. Likewise he writes to the Thessalonians: As you know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father does his own children, that you walk worthy of God (1 Thess. 2:11). And St. John testifies to a pious matron his joy that he had found some of her children walking in truth [ἐν ἀληθείᾳ] (2 John 4). Thus every minister of the Church is in some measure an apostle [ἀποστολῆς], although canon law has made this office a special privilege of the vicars of the bishops.

units.la: V. Neque enim Pastor Ecclesiæ pulchrè satis rerum suarum sategit una atque altera concione & declamatione ad populum hebdomadatim defunctus, quæ quorundam, ventri suo potiùs, quàm Deo inservientium, stulta persuasio est. Sume tibi vas כְּלֵי רֹעֶה אִוִּיל Pastoris stulti. Nam ecce, suscito Pastorem in terra, qui oves succisas non visitabit, quod parvum est, non quaeret, & quod contritum est, non sanabit, quod consistit, non portabit, sed carnes pinguium comedet, & ungulas earum confringet. הוֹי רֹעִי הָאֱלִיל Va, Pastor idolum, qui derelinquet gregem, gladius erit super brachium ejus, &c. Zach. XI. 15. 16. 17. Quin potius, sicut Mithridatem, Ponti Regem, duarum & viginti gentium, quae ejus imperium suspiciebant, linguas didicisse ferunt, ut sine interprete suos audire & coram alloqui posset; & de Cyro Persarum proditum literis est, quod in numerosissimo exercitu suo omnia singulorum nomina noverit, gnarus etiam sine monitore quosvis salutare, & ad fortitudinem atque officium strenue peragendum stimulare: ita Pastoris Ecclesiastici est, auditores suos omnes, quos in curam & fidem suam publica & solenni stipulatione coram Sanctae Trinitatis facie recepit, & de quibus tremendo illo Jesu Christi tribunali coram respondere eum oportet, in numerato eos habere, & exacte novisse, non de facie duntaxat, sed inprimis de animo; hoc est, ut illorum in doctrina prosectum, ingenium, mores, conversationem, naevos, quibus in doctrina vel vita laborant, fortunam externam, aliaque id genus ad curam ejus pertinentia, probe cognita & explorata habeat, atque noverit, quando vel doctrina, vel redargutione, vel institutione, vel correctione, vel consolatione apud illos non publice duntaxat, sed privatim etiam defungendum sit. Boni enim Pastoris officium est oves suas ad laeta, & pinguia Verbi Divini pascua ducere, perditas requirere, abjectas reducere, confractas obligare, aegrotas consolidare: pingues contra & fortes, seu petulantes coërcere, & in judicio pascere, Ezech. XXXIV. 15. nonaginta novem oves in deserto relinquere & ad unam perditam, usque dum eam repererit, proficisci, Luc. XV. 4. Quem scopum nisi cognita omnium indole, ingenio, conversatione, virtute, & a virtutum tramite aberratione, assequi nunquam poterit.
units.tr: V. For the pastor of the Church does not discharge his duty sufficiently well by a single sermon and declamation to the people each week; that is the foolish notion of some who serve their belly rather than God. Take for yourself the instruments of a foolish shepherd [כְּלֵי רֹעֶה אִוִּיל]. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit those that are cut off, nor seek the young, nor heal the broken, nor feed what stands; but he will eat the flesh of the fat and tear their hooves in pieces [הוֹי רֹעִי הָאֱלִיל]. Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword shall be on his arm, etc. (Zech. 11:15-17). Indeed, just as they say Mithridates, King of Pontus, learned the languages of the twenty-two peoples who were subject to his rule, so that he could hear and address his own people without an interpreter; and just as it is recorded in writing of Cyrus, King of the Persians, that in his very numerous army he knew the names of all his soldiers, and without a prompter could greet any of them and stir him to courage and to vigorous performance of his duty: so it is the duty of the ecclesiastical pastor to have his hearers, all those whom he has received into his care and trust by public and solemn stipulation before the face of the Holy Trinity, and for whom he must answer before the dreadful tribunal of Jesus Christ, at his fingertips and to know them exactly, not merely by sight but above all by their hearts. That is to say, he should have well known and carefully examined their progress in doctrine, their disposition, morals, conduct, faults by which they labour in doctrine or life, external fortune, and other such matters pertaining to his care; and should know when he must deal with them, not only publicly but also privately, whether by teaching, rebuke, instruction, correction or consolation. For it is the duty of a good pastor to lead his sheep to the joyful and rich pastures of the divine Word: to seek the lost, to bring back the scattered, to bind up the broken, to heal the sick; but the fat and the strong, or the wanton, he is to restrain, and to feed them with judgement (Ezek. 34:15-16); to leave the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it (Luke 15:4). This aim he can never attain unless he knows the disposition, character, conduct and virtue of all, and their straying from the path of virtue.

units.la: VI. Cum vero in scrutinio, cognitione & cura peccatorum, eorum inprimis, quae occulta dicuntur, creber usus sit delationum, per quas peccata ad Pastores, & ab iisdem ad Ecclesiam, ac quandoque etiam ad Magistratum civilem deferuntur, de his solis & universis in praesentiarum, ob dubios circa easdem incidentes casus, quorum enodatio, a paucis equidem, & de industria a nemine hactenus, quod sciam, tentata, & utilis, & propemodum necessaria nobis videtur, in praesentiarum edisserere nobis animus est. Quo quidem in explicando & excutiendo argumento hunc ordinem tenebimus, ut primò de Delatione delinquentium in universum dicturi: inde explicaturi sumus, quæ delatio tum quorumvis, tum Pastorum Ecclesiæ inprimis in foro sive Divino, sive Ecclesiastico, sive Politico, sive privato etiam locum habere possit.
units.tr: VI. Since the search for, knowledge of, and care of sins, especially those called hidden, often make use of denunciations, by which sins are reported to the ministers, from them to the Church, and sometimes even to the civil magistrate, I intend to set out here, for the present, these matters alone and in general, together with the doubtful cases that arise about them. Their solution has, as far as I know, been attempted by few and deliberately by no one so far, and it seems to us useful and nearly necessary. In explaining and examining this subject we will follow this order: first we will speak of the denunciation of offenders in general, and then explain what denunciation may have a place for anyone, and especially for the ministers of the Church, in the divine forum, the ecclesiastical forum, the political forum, or even the private forum.

units.la: VII. Delatio indicium rei occultæ est. Græci μήνυμα & μήνυσιν[?], delatorem vero μηνύτωρ[?] appellant. Perperam vero Macrobius Saturnal. l. VII. 3. Ἀλαβολὴν[?] delationem reddit, cùm hæc potiùs sit criminatio, quæ in vitio semper est, & Sathanæ, non sancto ulli convenit. Delationis verò vox media cùm sit, quædam pia & honesta esse potest. Quamobrē perperam etiam Herodianus delatorem συκοφάντην insignit, cùm & hæc vox delatorem non quemvis, sed calumniosum significet. Neque rectius quadruplatorem alii appellant, quia quadruplator non quivis olim delator fuit, sed is demum, qui rem ad fiscum pertinentem ei præmii, puta quadrupli, causa (cùm priùs Lex Papia dimidiam bonorum portionem delatori vindicasset) denuntiare suevit. velut qui crimina publica, bona caduca, vacantia, commissa, tacita fidei commissa, vaga mancipia, thesauri inventionem nuntiavit. Hebræis quoque הולך רכיל vel רכיל (Levit. XIX. 16. Prov. XI. 13. XX. 19. &c.) non quivis delator est, sed is demum, qui famam proximi nundinatur, domatim mercatoris vel aromatarii (Speci-krämer) instar, ambulando & rumores conquirendo existimationem & famam proximi in commercio habet; mercede sola animi livori, levitati & malevolentiæ suæ satisfacientis, ut qui proprio, quo innotescat, bono caret, ex alienis malis se commendet, uti nundinatores, seu delatores ejusmodi non tam mercium, quàm verborum, quæ ab uno empta alteri vendunt, Maximus Serm. 53. describit. Latinis verò in universum deferre idem est, quod indicare: sicut delator index. Hinc deferre vocem alicujus est indicare quid dixerit. Quomodo Clodio dicente, Milonem triduo, vel ad summum quatriduo periturum, Cicero pro Milone dixit: Quam vocem ejus ad M. Catonem statim Favonius detulit. Unde etiam Germanis deferre idem est, quod anzeigen / anmelden / vel Leiden / quod veteres leiten dixerunt. Quæ vox huic argumento propria, & usitata inprimis est, quia per delationis delinquentis peccatum ad judicem dirigitur (geleitet wird.) Fatendum enim, vocem Latinam delatoris & delationis, mediam licet, usu tamen δύσφημον esse, quia plerunque delatores ad deferendum non charitas erga delinquentem, vel Rempublicam, sed odium, livor, criminandi libido, atque subinde etiam lucrum impellere suevit, ne dicam,à delatoribus haud raro innocentes falsorum criminum arcessi, ut horum fama, fortuna & vita in præsens discrimen veniat. Unde delationem maximum malum Imperator dixit. Adeóque turpe factum est usu delatoris nomen, ut l. 3. C.de injur. injuriarum teneatur, qui alium delatorem appellat. Nos verò non tam vocis usum aliena vi, & apud quosdam receptum, quàm rem ipsam spectamus.
units.tr: VII. Delatio is the indication of a hidden matter. The Greeks call it μήνυμα and μήνυσις, and the informer μηνύτωρ. Macrobius (Saturnalia VII.3) wrongly renders [Ἀλαβολή] as delatio, since that is rather a criminal accusation, which is always evil and belongs to Satan, not to any holy person. Since the word delatio is neutral, however, it can be pious and honourable. For this reason Herodian also wrongly labels the informer συκοφάντης, since that word means not any informer but a slanderous one. Nor do others more rightly call him a quadruplator, because a quadruplator was not just any informer in former times, but only the one who used to report matters belonging to the treasury for the sake of a reward, namely a fourfold share (since the Lex Papia had earlier granted the informer half of the goods). Such a man reported public crimes, forfeited, vacant and confiscated goods, secret trusts, vagrant slaves, and the discovery of treasure. Among the Hebrews too, הולך רכיל or רכיל (Lev. 19:16; Prov. 11:13; 20:19, etc.) does not mean any informer, but only the one who trades in his neighbour's reputation, like a peddler or spice-seller going from house to house. Walking about and gathering rumours, he deals in his neighbour's good name and honour; his only wage is the satisfaction of his own envy, levity and malice, since he who lacks a good by which he may become known commends himself by other people's evils. Maximus (Sermon 53) describes such informers as merchants, not so much of goods as of words, which they buy from one person and sell to another. In Latin, deferre generally means the same as indicare, just as the informer is an index. Hence deferre of someone's word means to report what he said. So when Clodius said that Milo would perish within three days, or four at the most, Cicero in his speech for Milo said: Favonius at once reported this remark of his to Marcus Cato. Hence also among the Germans deferre means the same as anzeigen / anmelden, or what the older writers called leiten. This word is especially proper and usual for this subject, because through the denunciation the sin of the offender is directed (geleitet wird) to the judge. For it must be admitted that the Latin words delator and delatio, though neutral, have in usage an ill sound, since informers are usually driven to inform not by love for the offender or concern for the commonwealth, but by hatred, envy, a lust for accusing, and sometimes also by gain. Not to mention that innocent people are not seldom brought in by informers with false charges, so that their reputation, fortune and life are put in present danger. Hence an emperor called denunciation a very great evil. And the name of informer has become so shameful in use that by l. 3 C. de injuriis whoever calls another a delator is liable to an action for insult. We, however, look not so much at the usage of the word, which rests on an alien force and is accepted among some people, as at the thing itself.

units.la: VIII. Est igitur Delatio seu Denuntiatio indicium delicti occulti factum ei, qui delinquentem emendandi vel puniendi jus habet. Jurisconsulti quidem accusationem, inquisitionem & denuntiationem ita distinguunt; quòd Accusatio sit rei alicujus per libellum ad judicem delatio, ad quam requiruntur tres personae, accusator, accusatus & judex: Inquisitio, qua judex non existente accusatore seu actore ex officio suo de crimine aliquo inquirit: Denuntiatio, seu vulgò dicta delatio, quando per denuntiatorem, clam eo, qui denuntiatur, crimen ad judicem defertur, quæ postrema potissimum in foro Ecclesiastico obtinet. Aliam enim significationem denuntiatio in Romanis legibus habet, uti copiosè Alciatus in l. Detestatio. de Verb. significat. demonstrat. Juxta Canonistas verò accusatio non sine accusatore; inquisitio non sine infamia inquirendi; & denuntiatio non sine correptione privata procedit, quod postremum cum grano salis accipiendum esse, infra dicemus. Tum Denuntiatio seu delatio versatur circa secreta, tanquam materiam propriam. Sicut enim prudens taciturnitas secretorum premendorum, non propalandorum directrix virtus, & annulus ille signatorius, quem Hephæstionis ori Alexander M. admovit, est: ita delatio honesta circa secreta aperienda occupatur. Euripides, quòd secretorum tenax esset, multa arcana in ore suo computruisse, ideóque malè se olere, jocatus est. Contra delator secreta aperit, & foras, quò vult, eliminat. Unde in universum Delatio definiri potest, quòd sit indicatio clam, seu absente accusatore, dicta vel facta alterius patefaciens. quæ si recto animo & instituto, puta corrigendi peccatorem, & humanæ societati ac gloriæ Dei consulendi suscipiatur, honesta: sin impellente odio, invidia, lucro, calumniandi pruritu, infamis merito & vitiosa censetur.
units.tr: VIII. Denuntiatio, or delatio, is therefore the indication of a hidden offence made to the one who has the right to correct or punish the offender. The jurists distinguish accusation, inquisition and denuntiation as follows. Accusation is the bringing of a matter before a judge by a written charge, and it requires three persons: accuser, accused and judge. Inquisition is when the judge, with no accuser or plaintiff present, inquires into some crime on his own authority. Denuntiatio, or what is commonly called delatio, is when a crime is reported to the judge by a denouncer, secretly from the one denounced; this last form holds chiefly in the ecclesiastical forum. For denuntiatio has another meaning in Roman law, as Alciatus fully shows (on l. Detestatio, de verborum significatione). According to the canonists, accusation does not proceed without an accuser, inquisition does not proceed without the infamy of the one inquired into, and denuntiation does not proceed without private correction; we shall say below that this last must be taken with a grain of salt. Further, denuntiation or delatio is concerned with secrets as its proper matter. For just as prudent silence, which keeps secrets and does not spread them, is the guiding virtue, and that signet ring which Alexander the Great pressed to the mouth of Hephaestion is its symbol, so honest delatio is concerned with disclosing secrets. Euripides joked that a man who held his secrets too tightly had many mysteries rotting in his mouth, and so smelled bad. The informer, on the contrary, opens up secrets and drives them out wherever he likes. Hence delatio in general may be defined as an indication made in secret, without an accuser present, that discloses what another has said or done. If it is undertaken with an upright mind and purpose, such as correcting a sinner and caring for human society and the glory of God, it is honourable; but if it is driven by hatred, envy, gain or an itch for slander, it is rightly judged infamous and vicious.

units.la: IX. Esse porro delationem quandam honestam & legitimam, nullo negotio comprobari potest. Ipsa enim vox deferendi nativa sua vi media est, adeóque in bona & mala cadit. Deferri enim aliquid ex officio, rectóque consilio ad alium, velut parentem, magi-stratum, stratum, Pastorem potest. Ergo vi conjugatorum, delatio quædam bona & honesta esse potest. Quomodo etiam Græca vox μήνυσις, & Germanica Läidung quævis patefactio certo quodam indicio & argumento esse potest. velut in illo Aristotelis: [illegible, ~12 letters] δοκεῖ μηνύειν ἀρετήν, excellentia indicat virtutem. Potest autem patefactio, indicatio quædam carere vitio omni, adeóque recta censeri. Tum cognatæ species idem probant. Exploratio enim, bellum, accusatio, censura de moribus & vita quædam justa, honesta, necessaria esse potest: adeóque etiam delatio. Sicut enim bello flagrante exploratores hostium consilia explorant, ut suis ad victoriam legitimis mediis aditum patefaciant: ita delatores pace vigente, civium mores observant, ut in vita humana honestati & tranquillitati locus detur. Prætera Lex Divina Levit. V.1. sic sonat: Cum anima peccaverit, וְנִשְׁבְּעָה[?] קוֹל אָלָה itaut audiverit vocem juramenti (vel adjurationis) & ipse sit testis, qui vidit, vel scivit; אִם לֹא יַגִּיד si non indicaverit, feret pœnam iniquitatis suæ. Fateor equidem, sensum Legis illius simpliciorem videri, quòd à judice in delictum inquirente adjuratus, ut testimonium veritati reddat, si delictum viderit, vel certò cognoverit, neque tamen ita adjuratus illud indicaverit, denuntiaverit, iniquitatis suæ pœnam laturus, imò criminis ita celati reatum ipse subiturus sit. Nihilominus si judici licet adjurare testem, ut sibi visa vel nota denuntiet, etiam sine adjuratione ejusmodi denuntiationem non omnino vitiosam esse consequitur. Non enim judex ausit juramento imponere delationem criminis, si delatio omnis vitiosa est. In eandem verò rem sic Solomon loquitur חוֹלֵק עִם גַּנָּב שׂוֹנֵא נַפְשׁוֹ אָלָה יִשְׁמַע וְלֹא יַגִּיד Qui participat cum fure, odit animam suam: Maledictionem audit, & non indicat, Prov. XXIX. 24. Quorum etiam verborum sensus proprius non is est, ne perjuria, diras, blasphemias, omnemque nominis Divini abusum dissimulemus (quamvis sensus ille non omnino alienus, & omnino verum sit, redarguendum esse proximum, juxta illud Levit. XIX. 17. Non habebis odio fratrem tuum; sed corripiendo corripies proximum tuum, ne propter illum peccatum feramus, hoc est, cum peccato ejus communicemus) sed hic potius, quòd qui ab homine, puta judice, adjuratus, annon hoc vel illud viderit, vel cognoverit, non indicat visa vel cognita, perinde faciat, atque si cum fure partiretur, & animam suam odio haberet. Alludit igitur Solomon ad legem Divinam, & delationem quandam licitam esse eadem ratione, quam in Lege Divina ipsa ostendimus, haud obscurè innuit. Sed & Christus ipse delationem quandam mandavit his verbis: Si non audiverit (correptores) εἰπὲ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ[?], Dic Ecclesiæ, Matth. XVIII.17. Et S.Paulus
units.tr: IX. That there is a certain honourable and lawful delatio can be proved without difficulty. The word deferre is neutral in its own force, and so it can fall into good or bad use. For something may be reported to another out of duty and with right counsel, for example to a parent, a magistrate or a minister. Therefore, by force of these considerations, a certain good and honourable delatio can exist. In the same way the Greek word μήνυσις and the German Läidung can be any disclosure by a certain sign or proof, as in the saying of Aristotle: [illegible] excellence indicates virtue. And a disclosure or indication of this kind can be free of all vice and so be judged right. Moreover, related kinds prove the same point. Investigation, war, accusation, and censure of morals and life can be some just, honourable and necessary things, and so too can delatio. For just as, when war is blazing, spies explore the enemy's plans so that they may open the way for their own side to victory by lawful means, so in time of peace informers watch the conduct of citizens so that room is given for honesty and tranquillity in human life. Besides, the divine law at Lev. 5:1 reads: When a soul has sinned, and has heard the voice of an oath [וְשָׁמַע קוֹל אָלָה] and is himself a witness who has seen or known, [אִם לֹא יַגִּיד] if he does not report it, he shall bear the punishment of his iniquity. I admit that the simpler sense of that law seems to be that one who is put under oath by the judge inquiring into a crime, to give true testimony, if he has seen or certainly known the crime, and yet does not report it when so sworn, shall bear the punishment of his iniquity, indeed shall himself be liable for the guilt of a crime so concealed. Nevertheless, if a judge may put a witness under oath to report what he has seen or known, then it follows that such a denunciation is not altogether vicious even without such an oath. For a judge would not dare to impose by oath the reporting of a crime if all delatio were vicious. Solomon speaks to the same effect: [חוֹלֵק עִם גַּנָּב שׂוֹנֵא נַפְשׁוֹ אָלָה יִשְׁמַע וְלֹא יַגִּיד] Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul; he hears the curse and does not report it, Prov. 29:24. The proper sense of these words is not that we should overlook perjuries, curses, blasphemies and every abuse of the divine name (although that sense is not wholly foreign, and it is entirely true that a neighbour must be rebuked, according to Lev. 19:17: You shall not hate your brother, but you shall surely rebuke your neighbour, lest you bear sin because of him, that is, lest we share in his sin). Rather, the point is that one who, adjured by a man, a judge for instance, is asked whether he has seen or known this or that, and does not report what he has seen or known, acts just as if he shared with a thief and hated his own soul. Solomon therefore alludes to the divine law, and quite plainly hints that a certain delatio is lawful, for the same reason that we have shown in the divine law itself. But Christ himself also commanded a certain delatio in these words: If he will not hear them (the correctors), tell it to the Church [εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ], Matt. 18:17. And St Paul, at 1 Tim. 5:19, forbidding Timothy to receive an accusation [κατηγορία] against an elder except at the mouth of two or three witnesses, implies that a certain delatio is lawful even before the ministers of the Church or evangelists (for that is what Timothy was). For delatio is a species…

units.la: 1. Tim. V. 19. vetans, ne Timotheus contra Presbyterum κατηγορίαν[?] accusationem suscipiat, nisi duobus vel tribus testibus contra illum se sistentibus, delationem quandam etiam apud Ecclesiæ Pastores vel Evangelistas (talis enim Timotheus erat) licitam esse innuit. Est enim delatio species accusationis, proportionem, & justum ordinem ad defensionem & conservationem Societatis publicæ habens. Insuper etiam actus est virtutis justitiæ, quatenus est vindicatio injuriarum atrocium ex authoritate publica. Cùm enim Magistratus sit Dei Minister, vindex ad iram ei, qui malum patrat, (Rom. XIII. 4.) quomodo ministerio hoc fungetur, si desint indices & denuntiatores eorum, qui mala patrant? Licet enim ex jure naturali & Divino ad sententiam judicialem ferendam tantùm sufficiens facti testificatio, quæ sine accusatore & delatore quandoque haberi potest, requiratur; tamen non adeò manifesta semper facti evidentia est, ut delatorum vel accusatorum usus omnino nullus sit. Quin potiùs juxta illud Apuleji,oportet Imperatori esse aures Regias, & oculos quosdam,quorum officiis discat, quicquid ubique geratur. In aliis etiam vitæ generibus exploratoribus locus est. Nam & paterfamilias delatoribus utitur ad cognoscendum statum familiæ; & Ludimagister procul omni culpa per corycæos discipulorum sequiora facta cognoscit; & belli dux per exploratores secretiora rimatur. Denique delictorum dissimulatio delationi opposita, communicatio quædam cum alieno peccato est. Hæc fecisti, & tacui; Propterea existimasti me tibi similem esse. Sed arguam te, &c. Psal. L. 21. Unde inter eos, qui cum alienis peccatis communicant, etiam non retegentes culpam numerantur, juxta versus decantatos:
units.tr: 1 Tim. 5:19, where Paul forbids Timothy to receive an accusation (accusationem) against an elder unless two or three witnesses come forward against him, implies that some kind of denunciation is also lawful before the ministers of the Church or the evangelists (for Timothy was such a man). Denunciation is a form of accusation, having a proportion and a just order to the defence and preservation of public society. It is also an act of the virtue of justice, insofar as it is the vindication of grave wrongs by public authority. For since the magistrate is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil (Rom. 13:4), how will he fulfil this ministry if there are no informers and reporters of those who do evil? For although, by natural and divine law, a sufficient attestation of the fact is required to pronounce a judicial sentence, and this can sometimes be had without an accuser or informer, nevertheless the evidence of the fact is not always so manifest that the use of informers and accusers is altogether nil. Indeed, rather, according to the saying of Apuleius, the emperor should have royal ears and certain eyes, by whose services he may learn whatever is done everywhere. In other walks of life too there is a place for spies. For the father of a household uses informers to learn the state of his household; the schoolmaster, free of all blame, learns the lesser faults of his pupils through informers; and a general searches out the secret plans of the enemy through scouts. Finally, the concealment of wrongdoing, which is opposed to denunciation, is a kind of communion with another's sin. You did these things, and I was silent; therefore you thought I was like you. But I will rebuke you, etc. (Ps. 50:21). Hence, according to the well-known verses, among those who share in others' sins are counted also those who do not expose the fault:

units.la: Consulo, præcipio, consentio, provoco, laudo, Non retego culpam, non punio, non reprehendo, Non obsto, sed præcipio & defendo alienâ.
units.tr: I advise, I command, I consent, I provoke, I praise; I do not expose the fault, I do not punish, I do not rebuke, I do not hinder, but I command and defend another's.

units.la: X. Honestæ delationis exempla etiam sacræ paginæ suppeditant. Ita enim Josephus יבא דבת רעה[?] detulit (ψόγον πονηρόν) malum crimen, vel infamiam fratrum suorum ad parentem, Genef. XXXVII.
units.tr: X. Scripture also supplies examples of honourable denunciation. Thus Joseph brought (ψόγον πονηρόν) an evil report, or the infamy of his brothers, to their father (Gen. 37).

units.la: 2. Quod cùm & optimo consilio & apud benevolentem filiis suis patrem, & modo debito fecerit, culpa omni vacavit. Nam nec Jacobi parentis, nec boni ullius reprehensionem eo nomine incurrit. Cùm enim ipse fratres suos corrigendi authoritate & potestate non polleret, recte & ordine ab eo factum, quod ad eum mala facinora detulit, qui corrigendi fine corporali & spirituali detrimento, jus & potestatem habuit. David quoque à facie Absolonis fugiens, Hierosolymis Tzadokum, & alios exploratores Chuzai, Tzadokum, Abiatharem reliquit, מגידים indicatores, delatores, qui nuntiarent sibi consilia hostium, 2. Sam. XV. 28. 35. 36. Similiter Jonathan Davidi יגיד indicavit consilia sanguinaria patris, 1.Sam.XIX.2. & nepos Pauli conjurationem Judaeorum ad ipsum Paulum, & mox ad Tribunum militum detulit, Act. XXIII.16. Chloe quoque Corinthiorum lites ad S.Paulum detulit: Manifestum est mihi de vobis, fratres, à Chloe, quod lites inter vos sint, 1.Cor.I.11. Denique experientia testis est, delationi honestae Regna & Respublicas conservationem suam quandoque acceptam retulisse. Nam & in Anglia delatio & indicium amico factum, & à Rege Jacobo sagacissimè evolutum, à sacris capitibus interitum, quem iis immanes & Cerberei πυρσοβόλοι[?] machinabantur, Thuano, Casaubono, aliisque narrantibus, avertit: & Tigurina Respublica à turbatoribus Reipublicae, noviter à civibus patriae amantibus erectae, vexata delatione pueri unius incolumitatem ad haec usque tempora feliciter productam debet.
units.tr: 2. He did this with the best intention, to a father who was kindly disposed towards his sons, and in a proper manner, so he was free of all blame. For he incurred no reproach from Jacob his father, nor from any good man on that account. Since he himself had no authority or power to correct his brothers, it was rightly and orderly done that he reported their evil deeds to the one who had the right and power to correct them, for the sake of correction and without bodily or spiritual harm. David too, fleeing from the face of Absalom, left at Jerusalem Zadok and others, Hushai, Zadok and Abiathar, informers, reporters (מגידים), who were to tell him the plans of the enemy (2 Sam. 15:28, 35, 36). Likewise Jonathan told (יגיד) David the bloody plans of his father (1 Sam. 19:2). And Paul's nephew reported the plot of the Jews to Paul himself, and soon to the tribune of the soldiers (Acts 23:16). Chloe also reported the quarrels of the Corinthians to St Paul: It has been made clear to me, brethren, by Chloe's people, that there are quarrels among you (1 Cor. 1:11). Finally, experience bears witness that kingdoms and commonwealths have sometimes owed their preservation to honourable denunciation. For in England a denunciation and information given to a friend, and skilfully unravelled by King James, turned away the destruction of the sacred heads which savage and Cerberus-like fire-raisers were plotting against them, as Thuanus, Casaubon and others relate. And the Tigurine Republic, harassed by the disturbers of the commonwealth, newly raised up by citizens who loved their country, owes to the denunciation of one boy the safety it has happily kept down to the present day.

units.la: XI. Neque delationem honestam testimonia quaedam Scripturae allegari à quibusdam solita feriunt, veluti cùm David dicit מלשני בסתר רעהו אצמית Perdam eum, qui clam mihi defert proximum suum, Psalm.CI. ץ. איש לשון vir linguae, seu delator, non prosperabitur in terra, Psal. CXL. 12. Non enim quivis delator est מלשין linguosus & איש לשון vir linguae, sed is demum, qui lingua sua dominatur & grassatur in perniciem proximi, more illorum, qui impotenter ita se efferunt: לשוננו נגבור linguam nostram corroboremus, labia nostra nobiscum, quis dominus nobis? Psal. XII. [?]5.
units.tr: XI. Nor do the testimonies of Scripture which some are wont to cite for honourable denunciation strike the ear: for instance, when David says, I will destroy him who secretly slanders his neighbour (מלשני בסתר רעהו אצמית), Ps. 101:5. And, a man of the tongue (איש לשון), that is a slanderer, shall not prosper in the land, Ps. 140:12. For not every informer is a talebearer (מלשין) and a man of the tongue (איש לשון), but only he who rules and rages with his tongue to the ruin of his neighbour, after the manner of those who so arrogantly boast: with our tongue we will prevail; our lips are our own, who is lord over us? (לשוננו נגביר, Ps. 12:5).

units.la: Solomon quoque passim quidem secretorum revelatores detestatur. הולך רכיל מגלה סוד Qui obtectat, revelat secretum, & qui fidelis est animo, tegit rem, Prov. XI.13. Qui revelat arcanum, obtrectator est, Prov.XX.19. Verùm ei sermo est non de delatione honesta, sed de temeraria & inverecunda propalatione eorum, quae salva conscientia, citra offensam Dei, Reipublicae vel proximi celari possunt & debent. Cujusmodi sunt consilia, facta, vel facienda proximi innoxia, infirmitates humanae, aliaque ejusmodi, uti quidem verbum גלה aliquando revelationem inverecundam notat, veluti cùm revelantur membra verenda, Levit.XVIII 6. XX.11.&c. opes vel thesauri reconditi, Jerem. XLIX.19. fundamenta Urbis,
units.tr: Solomon too indeed everywhere detests the revealers of secrets: He who goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets, but he who is faithful in spirit conceals the matter (הולך רכיל מגלה סוד, Prov. 11:13). He who reveals a secret is a gossip (Prov. 20:19). But his discourse is not about honourable denunciation, but about the rash and shameless divulging of those things which, without harm to conscience and without offence to God, can and should be kept hidden from the commonwealth or from a neighbour. Such are the innocent counsels, deeds or intended deeds of a neighbour, human infirmities, and other things of this kind; for the word גלה sometimes denotes shameless revelation, as when the private parts are uncovered (Lev. 18:6; 20:11, etc.), or hidden riches and treasures (Jer. 49:19), or the foundations of a city

units.la: Mich. I. 6. Habent enim arcana sua Principes, patres-familias, artifices, mercatores, alii, quæ citra ullam noxam silentii supparo involvi, inprimis si fidei alterius credita sint, possunt. Quomodo etiam justo omnium odio laborat Medicus, qui apud ægrotantem visa & audita inverecundo gutture propalat. Nempe juxta Poëtæ[?] illud:
units.tr: (Mic. 1:6). For princes, heads of households, craftsmen, merchants and others have their secrets, which can be wrapped in silence without any harm, especially if they have been entrusted to the faith of another. In the same way a physician, who blabs with a shameless throat what he has seen and heard in a sick patient, labours under the just hatred of all. Indeed, according to the saying of the poet:

units.la: Eximia est virtus præstare silentia rebus: At contra gravis est culpa, tacenda loqui.
units.tr: It is an excellent virtue to keep silence about things; but on the contrary, it is a grave fault to speak of things that should be kept silent.

units.la: Injusta enim secreti revelatio perniciosam fidei, amicitiæ, honestatis violationem haud raro involvit, adeoque inter maxima peccata deputatur, tum communi & tacito consensu hominum; tum Legis Divinæ sententia, Non inimicus probris me affecit; sed tu homo instar mei, dux meus & notus meus, אשר יחדיו נמתיק סוד[?] qui suaviter communicabamus, Psal.LV.13.14 1 s[?]. Quos προδοτῶν[?] proditorum nomine S.Paulus 2.Tim.III.4. perstringit. Qui vero officii sui & salutis proximi habita ratione, non evertendi, sed ædificandi animo, & citra fidei datæ violationem, secreta quædam rupto intempestivo silentio, revelat, & defert ad eos, quorum est pro salute publica excubare, quod honesti delatores faciunt, nullius, nedum sonticæ culpæ rei sunt, sed id instituunt, quod viros bonos, & honestos decet, & quod citra communicationem cum alieno peccato omittere nequeunt. Est etiam, ubi Amyclas silentium perdidit.
units.tr: For the unjust revelation of a secret often involves a grievous violation of faith, friendship and honour, and so it is counted among the greatest sins, both by the common and tacit consent of men and by the sentence of the divine law: It was not an enemy who reproached me, but you, a man like me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together sweetly kept counsel (אשר יחדיו נמתיק סוד, Ps. 55:13–14). These are the men whom St Paul brands with the name of traitors (προδόται, 2 Tim. 3:4). But whoever, having regard to his duty and the welfare of his neighbour, with the intent not to overthrow but to build up, and without violating a trust given, breaks an untimely silence and reveals certain secrets and reports them to those whose duty it is to keep watch for the public good, as honourable informers do, is not guilty of any fault, still less of a guilty one; rather he does what good and honourable men ought to do, and what he cannot leave undone without sharing in another's sin. There is also the case where silence ruined Amyclae.

units.la: XII. Multò minùs honestæ delationi officit, quòd nomen ipsum infamia laborat, & delationibus haud raro pœnæ decretæ sunt. Quomodo Tacitus Annal. IV. 30. 5. delatores genus hominum publico exitio repertum, & pœnis nunquam satis coërcitum; & Hist. II. 53. 2. invisum memoriæ delatorum nomen vocat. Senatus quoque Romanus sic Imperatori Pertinaci, post Commodum, delatorum operâ usum, apud Lampridium in Commodo acclamavit: Nunc fecisti sumus: Delatoribus metum: salvi simus, delatores de senatu; Delatoribus fustem, te salvo: Delatores ad Leonem, te imperante: Delatoribus fustem &c. Mitto authorum veterum adversus delatores συκοφαντικά[?] complura. Quæ tamen ad rem nihil faciunt, quia de delatoribus non quibuslibet, sed illis demum, qui improbæ & tyrannicæ dominationis instrumenta sese gerentes, & insidiosè se occultantes, nil deinceps pensi habebant, quos, qua de causa, quóve modo delatos odiosos redderent, dum Mæcenatibus suis in quavis re, pessima etiam, inservirent, intelligenda omnino sunt. Tali fraude usus Tarquinius superbus, insignitæ nequitiæ Tyrannus, suos, narrante Dionysio Halicarnassæo lib. IV. habuit ναρέ-[?] πῖλας [?] καὶ διερευνητὰς τῶν λεγομένων [?] παρὰ πεπραττομένων, speculatores & exploratores eorum, quae dicerentur & gererentur. qui vulgo ignoti confabulantibus se miscebant, & tyranno obtrectantes, singulorum animos pertentabant, ut quos ei minus propitios reperissent ad Principem deferrent, qui convicti acerbas poenas dederunt. Fuerunt etiam Tyranni, qui delatoribus promiscue omnibus fidem habérent. quomodo de Tiberio dictitare astute solito, jura sul [?] verti, si legum custodes amoverentur, Suetonius in vita ejus scribit: Nemini delatorum fides abrogata. Idem Suetonius in Nerone, Coryczeos ab eo adhibitos in rebus etiam minus seriis testatur. Dispositi, inquit, etiam erant, cum carmen recitaret in theatro, multi & plures occulti, qui vultus alacritatem tristitiamque observarent. Eorum autem indiciis, qui aliqua in re peccassent, aut statim aut mox gravi poena afficiebantur. Hieron quoque Syracusanorum tyrannus eodem modo, Aristotele Polit. lib. V. ii. narrante, submisit ὠτακουστὰς [?], seu Emissarios auritos, quos Syracusani sua lingua Potagogidas (delatores) insigniebant; qui in omnibus conventibus & circulis hominum de se sermones captarent, & loquendi libertatem minuerent. Nam tyrannos per ejusmodi delatores loquendi audiendique commercium ademisse, Tacitus Agric. 2, 3. queritur. Quod perversum eorum institutum a Persarum Regibus Cyro, Dario juniore, Artaxerxe exortum ad Romanos Caesares tyrannos manasse, Arnisæus Politicus insignis, de Repub. lib. II. cap. 3. ariolatur. Atque hi delatores non minus quam tyranni ipsi omnibus bonis merito invisi fuerunt; adeo ut Imperatores boni eos poenis etiam subjecerint. Nam & Vespasianus magna cum laude delatores ejusmodi flagris per aream amphitheatri coesos abegit: & Antoninus Pius, si nihil eorum, quae detulere, probassent, capitali supplicio affecit; sin etiam probassent, infames haberi voluit, jussit; & Trajanus in navibus maris & scopulorum periculo objectos, sine remis & velis, naufragio expositi, uti Dio Cassius, Xiphilinus, Flavius Vopiscus, alii testantur. De Pelopida quoque referunt, quod cum bonus quidam miles apud ipsum deferretur, quasi Imperatori convivium fecisset, responderit: Facta illius aspicio: verba non audivi. Quae prudentia hodieque publicis & privatis rebus necessaria erat, cum id genus hominum, utpote latrones potius quam delatores, ad Garamantas & corvos relegandum, omnia, ipsam etiam Christi Ecclesiam, inprimis sacerdotum quorundam & Inquisitorum, qui a muscis suis innocentes captos nefarie evertunt, tribunalia tyrannica pervaserit. Neque tamen ideo laude sua defraudandus est vir bonus, qui sceleratum nebulonem ad Magistratum defert, dummodo Magistratus caveat, ne quidvis cuivis de quovis referenti credat; & secundum leges in eos, qui hoc munere abutuntur, animadvertat. Nam juxta Domitiani illud, Princeps, qui delatores ejusmodi non punit, irritat. Nihil enim obtrectatione ejusmodi insidiosa magis volucre; nihil facilius emitti, nihil citius excipi, latius dissipari solet.
units.tr: XII. Much less does it detract from honourable denunciation that the very name suffers infamy, and that penalties have often been decreed against informers. Thus Tacitus (Ann. 4.30) calls informers a class of men found for public destruction and never sufficiently restrained by punishments; and (Hist. 2.53) he calls the name of informers hateful to memory. The Roman Senate too, when the Emperor Pertinax, after Commodus, made use of the services of informers, cried out, as Lampridius reports in the Commodus: Now you have made us safe: fear to the informers; let us be safe, informers out of the senate; the rod to the informers, while you are safe; informers to the lion, while you rule; the rod to the informers, etc. I pass over many of the ancient authors' writings against informers (συκοφαντικά). These, however, have no bearing on the matter, because they must be understood as referring not to informers of any kind, but only to those who, acting as instruments of a wicked and tyrannical domination, and concealing themselves insidiously, had no further scruple, and who, for whatever cause or by whatever means they made people hateful when denounced, served their patrons in any matter, even the worst. Tarquin the Proud, a tyrant of notorious wickedness, used this fraud: according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book 4), he had scouts and spies (ναρέπιλας and διερευνητὰς) of what was said and done, who, unknown to the common people, mixed with those who were talking, and, disparaging the tyrant, sounded out the minds of individuals, so that they might report to the prince those they found less well disposed towards him; these, when convicted, were given bitter punishments. There were also tyrants who gave credence to all informers indiscriminately, as Suetonius writes in his life of Tiberius, who was wont to say craftily that the laws would be overturned if the guardians of the laws were removed: No informer's word was ever disregarded. The same Suetonius, in his life of Nero, testifies that informers (coryczeos) were employed by him even in less serious matters: There were, he says, also set in place, when he recited a poem in the theatre, many secret men who watched the cheerfulness and sadness of the face; and by their information those who had offended in any matter were punished with severe penalties, either at once or soon after. Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, did the same: as Aristotle relates (Pol. 5.11), he sent out ear-listeners (ὠτακουστὰς), or emissaries with ears, whom the Syracusans in their own tongue called potagogidas (informers); these caught up talk about themselves in all the gatherings and circles of men, and diminished freedom of speech. For Tacitus (Agr. 2–3) complains that tyrants by such informers took away the commerce of speaking and hearing. The wicked practice, begun by the Persian kings Cyrus, Darius the Younger and Artaxerxes, and passed on to the Roman emperor-tyrants, is, as the distinguished politician Arnisaeus conjectures (De Rep. 2.3), an old story. And such informers, no less than the tyrants themselves, were rightly hated by all good men; so much so that good emperors even subjected them to punishments. For Vespasian, to great acclaim, drove informers of this kind away, having them beaten with whips across the arena of the amphitheatre; and Antoninus Pius, if he found none of the things they had reported to be true, had them put to death, and if he found them true, he ordered that they be held infamous; and Trajan exposed them, without oars and sails, to the danger of the sea and the rocks, to be shipwrecked, as Dio Cassius, Xiphilinus and Flavius Vopiscus attest. They also relate of Pelopidas that when a certain good soldier was denounced to him as having made a banquet as if for the emperor, he replied: I look at his deeds; I have not heard his words. This prudence is necessary even today in public and private affairs, since that class of men, who are robbers rather than informers and should be banished to the Garamantes and the crows, has invaded everything, even the tribunals of Christ's Church itself, especially those of certain priests and inquisitors who, through their flies, wickedly destroy innocent people they have taken. Nor, however, is a good man to be deprived of his praise who denounces a wicked scoundrel to the magistrate, provided the magistrate takes care not to believe anything anyone reports about anyone, and punishes according to the laws those who abuse this office. For according to the saying of Domitian, a prince who does not punish informers of this kind encourages them. For nothing is more winged than insidious slander of this kind; nothing is more easily sent out, nothing more quickly received, nothing more widely scattered.

units.la: XIII. Denique nec illud delationem quamvis illicitam reddit,quòd nemo se & consilia sua prodi ac deferri cupiat. cui mox accommodant illud juris naturalis scitum: Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris. Si enim ratiocinatio talis reciperetur, nemo ob quodcunque crimen plecti amplius posset. Quotusquisque enim in poenas suas libens consentiat? Paratum esset latronibus, parricidis, furibus responsum: Tute plecti nolis; proin nec me plectere jure potes. Videndum hic, non quid reo placeat, sed quid aequitati & justitiae congruat. Etiam Josephi fratres delationem fraternam animo iniquissimo ferebant. Sed non minus justa illa & laudabilis fuit, utpote quam pietatis & honestatis amor extorsit.
units.tr: XIII. Finally, the fact that no one wishes to have his own plans betrayed and reported does not make an accusation unlawful. Some people quickly apply to this the rule of natural law: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another." For if such reasoning were accepted, no one could be punished for any crime whatever. Who, after all, willingly consents to his own punishment? Robbers, murderers and thieves could always reply: "You don't want me punished; therefore you have no right to punish me." Here one must consider not what pleases the accused but what agrees with equity and justice. Even Joseph's brothers resented the accusation made against them by a brother, with the utmost ill will. Yet that accusation was no less just and praiseworthy, since it was wrung from him by love of piety and honour.

units.la: XIV. Ne vero putemus, honestae delationis titulo quidvis concedi posse, quibus conditionibus & legibus illa honesta fieri possit, dispiciendum. Honesta autem illa efficitur hoc generali indicio, si in causa honesta, ex authoritate legitima, finis honesti intuitu, per media honesta progrediatur, atque tanta delationis utilitas sperari possit, ut malo & infamiae proximi, qui delationem patitur, praeponderet. Plane sicut bellum justum & honestum illud reputatur, quod in causa justa, fine justo, per media Divinitus concessa, plus humanae societati profuturum, quam obfuturum praesumitur.
units.tr: XIV. Lest we think that anything at all can be allowed under the title of honourable accusation, we must examine under what conditions and laws such an accusation can be made honourable. It becomes honourable by this general mark: if it proceeds in a just cause, on legitimate authority, with an honourable aim, by honourable means, and if such a great benefit can be expected from the accusation that it outweighs the harm and infamy suffered by the neighbour who is accused. Just as a war is reckoned just and honourable when it is waged in a just cause, with a just aim, by means permitted by God, and is presumed to be more profitable than harmful to human society.

units.la: XV. Honesta igitur & legitima delatio fit Primo, si fiat animo & intentione abrumpendi peccatum, sive id fiat per emendationem peccati, sive per coercitionem & poenam ejusdem infligendam ab eo, qui jus puniendi habet. Ita Christus peccatorem contumacem, ut corrigi possit, ad Ecclesiam deferri jubet, Matth. XVIII. 17. Et S. Paulus lites fidelium ad fideles deferri jubet, ne coram infidelibus disceptandi cum scandalo necessitas incumbat, 1.Cor.VI.1.5. Atque eodem animo Josephus fratres suos apud parentem detulit. Neque hic charitatis regula laeditur. Qui enim clam peccavit, is clam moneri potest. Si non emendetur, pietatis ratio postulat, ut ad superiores deferatur, per quos emendari & coerceri potest. Absque hoc enim est, peccandi cursus sufflaminari nequit, cùm tamen eum sufflaminari & charitas jubeat, & peccatoris interfit; ut ubi peccatum coepit, ibi non commoretur, sed ilico potius commoriatur. Secundò honesta erit, sit fiat causa vitandi ingens periculum, sive universitati illud, sive singulari personæ à malis & insidiatoribus illud imminet. Quomodo nepos S. Pauli in necem ejusdem conjuratos detulit, Act. XXIII. 21. Quod factum non solum consanguinitatis jus, sed studium etiam pietatis, & amor erga proximum innocentem tuebatur. Ita si honestus civis Patriæ salutis studiosus, libertatis & pacis publicæ insidiatores detulerit, laudabile facinus omnes merito deputabunt. Tertiò huc faciunt Jurisconsultorum regulæ, honestam delationem definientium; Si delatio & vera sit, & non spe præmii potiundi, vel consilio proximi lædendi, sed Reipublicæ & proximo inserviendi animo suscipiatur; & sui quandoque defendendi gratiâ instituatur. Veluti si vir bonus & innocens homicidii vel furti crimine arcessatur, atque is homicidii & furti ejusdem authorem compertum habeat, fas ei ad judicium suíque defensionem vocato erit, authorem verum deferre, ut ipse innocens liberetur.
units.tr: XV. An accusation is therefore honourable and lawful, first, if it is made with the purpose and intention of breaking off sin, whether this is done by the correction of the sin or by the coercion and punishment of it, to be inflicted by one who has the right to punish. So Christ orders that an obstinate sinner, so that he may be corrected, be reported to the Church (Matt. 18:17). And St Paul orders that the disputes of believers be brought before believers, so that there is no need for them to be argued before unbelievers, with scandal (1 Cor. 6:1–5). And with the same intention Joseph reported his brothers to their father. Nor is the rule of charity violated here. For one who has sinned in secret can be admonished in secret. If he is not corrected, the duty of piety requires that he be reported to his superiors, through whom he can be corrected and restrained. For without this, the course of sin cannot be checked, although charity itself commands that it be checked, and it is in the sinner's own interest that, where sin has begun, he should not linger there but rather die to it at once. Second, an accusation will be honourable if it is made to avoid a great danger which threatens either the community or a single person from wicked men and plotters. So the nephew of St Paul reported the men who had conspired to kill him (Acts 23:21). This act was supported not only by the right of kinship but also by zeal for piety and love of an innocent neighbour. So if an honest citizen, zealous for the safety of his country, reports the plotters against liberty and public peace, everyone will rightly count it a praiseworthy deed. Third, the rules of the jurists, which define an honourable accusation, apply here: if the accusation is true, and is undertaken not in hope of gaining a reward or with the aim of harming a neighbour, but with the intention of serving the commonwealth and the neighbour, and is sometimes instituted also in defence of oneself. For example, if a good and innocent man is charged with murder or theft, and he knows the true author of that murder or theft, he may rightfully, when summoned to judgement and to his own defence, name the true author, so that he himself may be freed as an innocent man.

units.la: XVI. Ad legitimam insuper delationem requiritur, ut nec quivis delator admittatur, nec temerè fides etiam admisso habeatur, nec semper admittatur, nec in quovis negotio, nec contra quofvis. Danda ergo iis, quorum interest delatores habere, opera est, ut iis demum isthoc munus committant, quorum spectata præ cæteris fides & integritas est. Oculi mei ad fideles terræ, ut sedeant mecum. Ambulans in via perfecta, ipse ministrabit mihi. Psal. CI.6 [?] Sicut enim Præceptor corycæos non ex corruptis, sed integris, probis & diligentibus; atque paterfamilias ex fidissimis deligit: ita ii, quorum interest habere, qui denuncient, delectu utantur oportet, ne munus isthoc iis injungant, qui præ cæteris deferendi ipsi fuerant. Tum nec delationem quamvis suscipere, nec delatos ob solam delatio-nem damnare fas piumque est, cùm delatio remedium quidem sit cognitionis eorum, qui emendandi vel puniendi sunt; sed nec infallibile, nec solum, sed cum aliis certioribus indiciis conjunctum. Sæpe enim per errorem vel malivolentiam pii deferuntur, quos mox certioribus argumentis explorata veritas noxæ eximit. Est etiam, ubi verba & facta in pravum sensum detorquentur, quæ in meliorem partem accipi poterant. Virisanguinarii oderunt integrum, at recti requirunt animam ejus. ejus, Prov. XXIX. 10. Unde Lex Divina diserte prohibet: לא תשא שמע שוא Non accipias famam [?], Exod. XXIII. 1. & duos vel tres testes ad judicium exigit, Num. XXXV. 20. Deut. XVII. 6. XIX. 15. Laudatusque haud immerito veteribus est Domitianus Imperator, qui delatoribus ipsis animadversores ordinavit, ut delatorem alium delator ipse timere haberet. Contra Tiberio tyranni nota vel eo nomine merito inusta est, quòd delatores & quosvis, & semper, & adversus quosvis libenter admisit, quia male factorum conscientia pavescens timuit, ne, qui omnes laesit, jure talionis ab omnibus vicissim laederetur, & male, uti meruit, periret. Sapientissimè Solomon משל מקשיב על רבר שקר כל משרתיו רשעים Qui in potestate est, si attendat ad verbum falsitatis, omnes ejus ministri improbi, seelesti[?] fiunt. Prov. XXIX. 12.
units.tr: XVI. For a lawful accusation, it is further required that not every accuser be admitted, nor that his word be readily believed even when admitted, nor that he always be admitted, nor in every matter, nor against anyone at all. Therefore those whose interest it is to have accusers must take care to entrust this office only to those whose faithfulness and integrity are proven above others. "Mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me; he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall minister unto me" (Ps. 101:6). For just as a schoolmaster does not choose his assistants from the corrupt, but from the upright, honest and diligent, and a householder chooses his most trusted men, so those whose interest it is to have informers ought to exercise discernment, lest they entrust this duty to those who were themselves most deserving of being accused. Then it is neither right nor pious to receive any accusation whatever, or to condemn the accused merely on the basis of the accusation, since an accusation is indeed a means of discovering those who are to be corrected or punished, but it is neither infallible nor sufficient by itself, and must be joined with other, more reliable indications. For often the pious are accused through error or malice, and soon the established truth frees them from harm by more certain arguments. There are also cases where words and deeds are twisted into a bad sense, when they could have been taken in a better one. "Bloodthirsty men hate the upright, but the just seek his soul" (Prov. 29:10). Hence the divine law expressly forbids it: "You shall not take up a false report" [לא תשא שמע שוא] (Exod. 23:1), and it requires two or three witnesses for judgement (Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:15). And the emperor Domitian was rightly praised by the ancients, who appointed punishers of the informers themselves, so that an informer had to fear another informer. On the other hand, Tiberius was rightly marked with the stain of tyranny on this very account: he gladly admitted informers of every sort, always and against anyone, because, trembling from a guilty conscience, he feared that he who had injured everyone would in turn be injured by everyone, by the law of retaliation, and would perish badly, as he deserved. Solomon wisely says: "If a ruler gives heed to a lying word, all his ministers become wicked" [משל מקשיב על דבר שקר כל משרתיו רשעים]. If one who is in power listens to a word of falsehood, all his ministers become wicked. (Prov. 29:12).

units.la: XVII. Se ipsum vero ultro deferre nemo tenetur; ac si nulla ejus infamia praecesserit, ne anquisitus quidem, vel sub juramento etiam interrogatus, an noverit quempiam hujus vel illius delicti reum. Nemo enim in se ipsum animadvertere, vel ad sui punitionem ac interitum directè cooperari tenetur. Neque etiam tum ex intentione judicis, qui secundum juris viam procedit, de se ipso interrogatur, vel, non diffamatus ante, seu gravem in suspicionem patrati facinoris non adductus, interrogari de se ipso potest. Nunquam enim judex vel de iis, quae penitus occulta sunt, vel de homine integrae famae, & ἀνεγκλήτῳ[?] unquam, tanquam reo & authore occulto delicti patentis, interrogare, vel inquirere, secundum juris formam, potest. Adeò vero naturae repugnat, ut quis sui ipsius se proditorem ac delatorem gerat, in gravi praesertim periculo, ut inquisitiones, quibus de se ipso, in causa inprimis criminali, aliquis illibati nominis, etiam sub juramento, quod inquisitorium ex officio vocant, & in Hispanico-Romana Inquisitione usitatum est, interrogatur, vim naturae ipsi adferant, & horrendis perjuriis occasionem praebeant. Aliud est, si quis ob peccatum manu Dei tactus, vel conscientiae urgentis vi compunctus, exemplo Achanis, quem sors Divina pertulit, ipsemet Deo honorem dare, & non ipsi solùm, sed etiam judici & societati, adversus quam deliquit, peccatum ultro confiteri & revelare, satisfactionémque debitam offerre statuerit. Ejusmodi enim sui ipsius spontanea delatio & delinquentis conscientiam multùm sublevat, & justitiae exercendae ansam praebet, & Deo honorifica, & hominibus, quibus offensis jus suum reddit, aprime utilis atque salutaris est.
units.tr: XVII. No one, however, is bound to accuse himself of his own accord. Even if no infamy of his has gone before, he is not bound to answer when investigated, nor when questioned under oath whether he knows of anyone guilty of this or that crime. For no one is bound to pass sentence on himself, or to cooperate directly toward his own punishment and destruction. Nor can a man be questioned about himself, whether by the intention of a judge who proceeds in the ordinary course of law, or if he was not previously defamed, nor brought under grave suspicion of having committed a crime. For a judge can never, according to the form of law, question or investigate someone about things that are wholly hidden, or question a man of unblemished reputation, who is blameless [ἀνεγκλήτῳ], as though he were the accused and secret author of a manifest crime. Indeed it so runs against nature for anyone to play the betrayer and accuser of himself, especially in grave danger, that the inquisitions by which a man of unblemished name is questioned about himself, especially in criminal cases, even under oath (which they call inquisitorium ex officio, a practice used in the Spanish-Roman Inquisition), inflict violence on nature itself and offer occasion for horrible perjuries. It is different if someone, touched by the hand of God for his sin, or pricked by the force of an urgent conscience, has resolved, like Achan, whom the divine lot pointed out (Josh. 7), to give honour to God himself, and to confess and reveal his sin of his own accord, and to offer due satisfaction, not only to God but also to the judge and to the society against which he has offended. For such a spontaneous self-accusation greatly relieves the conscience of the offender, provides an occasion for the exercise of justice, and is most useful and salutary both to God, who is honoured by it, and to the men whom he has offended and to whom he renders what is theirs.

units.la: XVIII. Decantata apud Juris Canonici peritos distinctio est delationis, seu denuntiationis, ut alia sit Evangelica, quæ per Evangelia inducta est, juxta Matth. XVIII.17 alia Canonica, quæ per Canones introducta est, qua proceditur specialiter vel generaliter, ut removeatur aliquis ab officio, dignitate, beneficio; item, ut clerici, vel laici à criminibus arceantur; vel denuntiatur alicujus promovendi indignitas, matrimonii impedimentum, &c. alia Judicialis, qua procedit judex contra maleficos, ut crimina poena publica puniantur: alia Regularis, qua proceditur in Ordinibus regularibus contra ipsos Religiosos, juxta eorum Canones, constitutiones & Regulas. Non desunt tamen, quibus minus accurata distinctio videatur, eò quòd divisionis hujus membra coincidant; cùm Canonica & Regularis etiam Judicialis esse possit. Addo, perperam etiam Evangelicam & Canonicam distingui; atque insuper Regularem tam otiosam esse, quàm otiosæ & frigidæ sunt regulæ ab hominibus otiosis, & non tam religiosis, quàm tristi superstitione pallentibus, inductæ.
units.tr: XVIII. Among the experts in canon law there is a well-known distinction of accusation, or denunciation: one kind is evangelical, introduced by the Gospels, according to Matt. 18:17; another is canonical, introduced by the canons, by which proceedings are carried out specially or generally, so that someone may be removed from office, dignity or benefice; also so that clergy or laity may be restrained from crimes; or the unworthiness of someone to be promoted, or an impediment to marriage, etc., is denounced; another is judicial, by which a judge proceeds against wrongdoers, so that crimes may be punished by public penalty; another is regular, by which proceedings are carried out within the regular orders against the religious themselves, according to their canons, constitutions and rules. Yet there are those who think this distinction is not sufficiently exact, because the members of this division coincide, since the canonical may also be judicial, and the regular as well. I add that the evangelical and the canonical are wrongly distinguished, and moreover that the regular is as idle as the idle and frigid rules introduced by idle men, who are less religious than pale with gloomy superstition.

units.la: XIX. Rectius delatio delinquentium juxta forum, quod delinquentes sortiri possunt, distinguitur. Quadruplex autem peccator forum subire potest; puta Divinum, Politicum, Ecclesiasticum, & Privatum. uti quidem peccator reconciliari debet tum Deo, in quem peccavit: tum Magistratui & Reipublicae, quam & ipsam offendit: tum Ecclesiae, in quam redundavit scandalum & opprobrium inde, quod quidam Ecclesiae civis improbè se gessit: tum denique Privato, si fortè privatum peccato suo laesit, aut injuria affecit. Quod in uno horum agitur, vel transfigitur, alteri non praejudicat, nec facultatem jus suum prosequendi adimit. Ita privatus condonavit injuriam sibi factam, puta caedem fratris vel cognati. Hoc non obstante, integrum est Ecclesiae, & Reipublicae poenam exigere. Quin etsi cum Deo per veram poenitentiam transactum sit, Respublica tamen non tenetur condonare multam sibi debitam, nec Ecclesia satisfactionem Canonicam. Sic absolutus in foro Ecclesiastico nihilominus obligatur ad subeundam poenam à Republica decretam, & viceversa, qui Magistratui Politico satisfacit multa vel carcere, hoc ipso Ecclesiae reconciliatus non est. Cùm verò cuivis foro delicti adversus se commissi, quatenus id aboleri interest, notitia necessaria sit, quousque delatio delinquentium cuivis inservire debeat, facilè intelligitur.
units.tr: XIX. A more accurate division of the reporting of offenders is made according to the forum which the offenders may come before. A sinner may be brought before four forums: the Divine, the Political, the Ecclesiastical, and the Private. A sinner ought to be reconciled to God, against whom he has sinned; to the magistrate and the commonwealth, which he has also offended; to the Church, into which scandal and disgrace have flowed because a member of the Church has behaved badly; and finally to the private person, if perhaps he has harmed him or done him an injury by his sin. What is done or settled in one of these forums does not prejudice another, nor does it take away the right of the others to pursue their claims. Thus a private person may have forgiven an injury done to him, such as the killing of a brother or a kinsman. Even so, it remains open to the Church and the commonwealth to exact punishment. Indeed, even if the matter has been settled with God through true repentance, the commonwealth is not bound to remit the fine owed to it, nor the Church the canonical satisfaction. So one absolved in the ecclesiastical forum is nonetheless bound to undergo the penalty imposed by the commonwealth; and conversely, one who has satisfied the political magistrate by a fine or imprisonment is not for that reason reconciled to the Church. Since knowledge of a wrong committed against each forum is necessary, insofar as it is in that forum's interest to have it annulled, it is easily understood how far the reporting of offenders ought to serve anyone.

units.la: XX. Et DEUS quidem, adversus quem solum proprie peccatur, delatione, ceu medio notitiae peccati, nullatenus indiget, quia coram oculis ejus omnia nuda & refupinata sunt, Heb. IV.13. Nihilominus Satanas hominem defert apud Deum: unde κατήγορος τῶν ἀδελφῶν accusator, delator fratrum vocatur, quia eos die & nocte coram Deo nostro κατηγορεῖ accusat, defert, Apoc.XII.10. non sine mendacio & criminatione manifesta. Quis enim ἐγκαλέσει accusationem intentabit electis Dei? Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν, Deus est, qui justificat, Rom.VIII.33. Etiam λογισμοὶ cogitationes hominis male sibi conscii eum κατηγορῶσι accusant, apud judicem Deum deferunt, Rom. II.15. Moses, seu Lex Mosis, est ὁ κατηγορῶν ὑμᾶς, qui vos accusat, Joh.V.45. Sed & fideles ac electi eorum, à quibus iniquè hac in vita vexantur & occiduntur, apud Deum justum judicem delatores se gerunt. Quomodo Deus ad Cainum fraternæ cædis reum dicit: Vox sanguinum fratris tui [?]דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ clamat ad me è terra, Gen.IV.10. & Electi ad Deum vindicem malorum sibi illatorum clamare die ac nocte dicuntur, Luc.XVIII.7.
units.tr: XX. God, against whom sin is properly committed, has no need at all of a report as a means of knowing the sin, because all things are naked and laid open before his eyes (Heb. 4.13). Nevertheless, Satan brings charges against man before God; hence he is called the κατήγορος τῶν ἀδελφῶν [kategoros tōn adelphōn], the accuser, the informer of the brethren, because he accuses and informs against them day and night before our God (Rev. 12.10), not without lying and manifest calumny. For who will bring an accusation against the elect of God? It is God who justifies (Rom. 8.33), θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν [theos ho dikaiōn]. Also the thoughts (λογισμοί [logismoi]) of a man who is conscious of evil accuse (κατηγορῶσι [katēgorousi]) him and inform against him before God the judge (Rom. 2.15). Moses, or the Law of Moses, is ὁ κατηγορῶν ὑμᾶς [ho katēgorōn hymas], the one who accuses you (John 5.45). But also the faithful and the elect, by whom they are unjustly harassed and killed in this life, act as informers before God the just judge. So God says to Cain, guilty of fratricide: The voice of your brother's blood [Hebrew: demei akhika] cries out to me from the earth (Gen. 4.10). And the elect are said to cry out to God, the avenger of the wrongs done to them, day and night (Luke 18.7).

units.la: XXI. In eodem Divino foro Ministris & Legatis suis Deus utitur, quorum præconio humano generi reconciliari vult. Pro Christo legatione fungimur: tanquam Deo admonente per nos, oramus pro Christo: Reconciliamini Deo, 2.Cor.V.20. Quibus etiam potestatem ligandi & solvendi, remittendi & retinendi peccata Christus impertitus est, Matth.XVI.19. XVIII.18, Joh.XX.13 citra tamen præjudicium potestatis illius judicialis & prætoriæ, quæ soli Deo competit, Esaj. XLIII.25. Psal.XXXII.5. Luc.V.21. Atque hi etiam in peccatorum notitiam veniunt tum per se, singulas gregis oves circumeundo, earumque maculas observando, & verbi Divini ad conscientias applicati præconio, si fieri poterit, curando; sin, iisdem pertinacibus æternam damnationem obnuntiando: tum per ipsos peccatores liberè peccata sua in gremium Pastoris deponentes, & afflictæ conscientiæ fomenta, institutionem & consolationem ex Dei verbo ardenter flagitantes: tum denique per alios, non quidem clam & insidiose à Pastore subornatos, sed liberè, solius charitatis instinctu, & salutis peccantium desiderio, delinquentes, in gravi periculo animæ constitutos ad Pastorem deferentes, non ut delinquentes indicio ejusmodi destruantur, vel famæ etiam & existimationis, siquidem peccata occulta fuerint, naufragium faciant, sed ut idoneis remediis ex Evangelio Christi petitis ad salutem ædificentur. Qua verò cum charitate deferentis, & prudentia ac cautione delationem suscipientis, ne temerè nimis credulus, suspicax peccatorum vulnera exulceret magis, quàm sanet, delatio hæc libera instituì debeat, veræ charitatis & pietatis genius, non aliud dictare potest.
units.tr: XXI. In the same divine forum God makes use of his ministers and envoys, through whose proclamation he wishes the human race to be reconciled. We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us; we beg you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5.20). To them Christ also gave the power of binding and loosing, of forgiving and retaining sins (Matt. 16.19; 18.18; John 20.23), yet without prejudice to that judicial and praetorian power which belongs to God alone (Isa. 43.25; Ps. 32.5; Luke 5.21). And these men come to knowledge of sins in several ways: first, by themselves, going round each of the sheep of the flock and observing their stains, and healing them, if possible, by proclaiming the divine Word applied to the conscience; but if not, by announcing eternal damnation to those who remain obstinate. Second, through the sinners themselves, who freely lay their sins in the bosom of the Shepherd and ardently ask for instruction and consolation from the Word of God as a remedy for a troubled conscience.
