Finally, through others who, not secretly or treacherously prompted by the Pastor, but freely, moved by love alone and by the desire for the salvation of sinners, report to the Pastor those who are involved in grave danger to their souls. They do this not so that the offenders may be destroyed by such an information, or suffer shipwreck of their reputation and good name, even if their sins have been hidden, but so that they may be built up to salvation by suitable remedies drawn from the Gospel of Christ. Indeed, the spirit of true love and piety can dictate nothing other than that such a free report should be made with the charity of the one who reports, and with the prudence and caution of the one who receives the report, lest one who is too quick to believe and too suspicious should irritate the wounds of sinners rather than heal them.

units.la: XXII. In foro Ecclesiastico, in quo peccata, non quatenus Deum offendunt, sed quatenus Ecclesiam gravi scandalo perculsam lædunt, dijudicantur, delationi locum esse, Christus Matth. XVIII. 15.16.17. aperte tradit. Si, inquit, peccaverit in te frater tuus, vade & corripe eum inter te & ipsum solum; si te audiverit, lucratus es fratrem tuum; Si vero non audiverit, assume unum vel duos, ut in ore duorum vel trium omne verbum stabile sit. Si iis non obediverit, εἰπὲ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. Dic Ecclesiæ. Si Ecclesiam non audiverit, esto tibi instar Ethnici & publicani, Matth.XVIII.15-18. Manifestum verò satis est, verba illa, ἐὰν ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου, peccaverit in te frater, non ad illa duntaxat peccata restringenda esse, quibus ab alio quispiam privata injuria læsus fuerit; sed intelligenda potiùs esse de quocunque peccato, quod nobis exploratum est, & cujus cognitione alii nos offendere possunt. Neque enim illis tantùm peccatis, quibus nos privatim lædimur, aut damnum aliquod patimur, offendi nos par est, sed iis etiam omnibus, quæ sub nostra conscientia admittuntur, & quorum certi testes sumus. Pro ea enim, quæ nobis inter nos mutuò atque Ecclesiam, imò ipsum Ecclesiæ caput, Christum intercedit, κοινωνίᾳ & ἑνώσει, in nos etiam peccatum commissum existimare debemus, non tantùm, si ipsi, tanquam privati læsi fuerimus, sed multò magis, si cætera Christi membra, adeòque ipsum Ecclesiæ corpus, omnium verò maximè Christus, Ecclesiæ caput, injuriâ quapiam aut contumelia afficiatur. Imò plus juris in privatis injuriis remittendis, quàm in publicis, Ecclesiam & Christum concernentibus, nobis permissum est. Multum enim de nostro jure nobis remittere licet, cùm in aliis, inprimis illis, quæ Ecclesiæ saluti, & gloriæ Christi detrahunt, rigidos & tenaces exactores nos esse conveniat.
units.tr: XXII. That in the ecclesiastical forum, in which sins are judged not insofar as they offend God but insofar as they wound the Church, struck by grave scandal, there is room for reporting, Christ plainly teaches in Matt. 18.15–17. If, he says, your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear, take with you one or two, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he does not obey them, εἰπὲ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ [eipe tē Ekklēsia]. Tell the Church. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector (Matt. 18.15–18). Indeed it is clear enough that the words ἐὰν ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου [ean hamartēsē eis se ho adelphos sou], if your brother sins against you, are not to be restricted to those sins by which someone has been harmed by a private injury from another; rather they are to be understood of any sin which is known to us and of which others may be made aware. For we ought to feel offended not only by those sins by which we are harmed privately or suffer some loss, but also by all those which are committed in our sight and of which we are certain witnesses. For, because of the fellowship and union (κοινωνίᾳ καὶ ἑνώσει [koinōnia kai henōsei]) which binds us to one another and to the Church, and indeed to the Head of the Church, Christ himself, we ought to think that a sin committed is also committed against us, not only if we ourselves have been harmed as private persons, but much more if the other members of Christ, and so the body of the Church, or above all Christ the Head of the Church, is struck by any injury or insult. Indeed, we are permitted to remit more of our right in private injuries than in public ones which concern the Church and Christ. For we may well relinquish much of our own right, whereas it is fitting that we be strict and unyielding exactors in those matters, above all, which detract from the salvation of the Church and the glory of Christ.

units.la: XXIII. Neque etiam quævis peccata adversus Deum & Ecclesiam commissa Christus celebri illo in loco intelligit. Sunt enim infirmitates & πταίσματά quædam, omnibus fere Christianis communia. Πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαντες. In multis omnes offendimus, Jac. III.2. [illegible, ~8 letters] Errores suos omnes quis intelligit? Ab occultis me munda, Psal. XIX.13. Harum verò singularis curatio & emendatio cùm vel expectari, vel ab iis, qui similibus infirmitatibus obnoxii sunt, exigi non possit, manifestum est, neque illa, ceu vel clam & remotis, vel adscitis etiam nonnullis arbitris, vel à tota Ecclesia, corripienda, à Christo intelligi. Inprimis si constet, eos, qui infirmitatibus ejusmodi laborant, cum iisdem serio luctari, easdem detestari, & quotidiana resipiscentia abstergere. Sunt etiam delicta quædam leviora, non tam Divinis, quàm humanis legibus repugnantia, quæ rectius Potestati civili corrigenda relinquuntur. Correctio enim Ecclesiastica cùm pars sit administrationis Regni Christi, ac proin spiritualem naturam habeat, perfectionem longè majorem, quàm quæ in civili societate obtinet, quærit. Si tamen adsit præfractus erga humanas leges, à Potestate Divinitus ordinata legitimè sancitas, animus, ille tum à Pastore seorsim, tum à tota Ecclesia merito reprehenditur. Proprium verò & adæquatum Ecclesiasticæ censuræ objectum est scandalum ex peccato adversus nos, vel potiùs Deum & Ecclesiam commissò, manans. Scopus enim Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ omnis est scandala tollere per correctionem ejus, qui peccando Deum, Ecclesiam & nos ipsos offendit, quò ita fideles inoffenso pede in cursu pietatis pergant, & alii, offendiculis impedientibus è medio sublatis, ad eandem viam alliciantur.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor does Christ in that famous passage mean any and every sin committed against God and the Church. There are weaknesses and πταίσματα [ptaismata], stumbles, which are common to almost all Christians: Many times we all stumble. In many things we all offend (Jas. 3.2; Πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαντες [polla ptaiomen hapantes]). [illegible, about eight letters] Who understands all his errors? Cleanse me from hidden faults (Ps. 19.13). Since the particular cure and correction of these cannot either be expected, or be required of those who are subject to similar weaknesses, it is clear that Christ does not mean that these should be rebuked either privately and apart, or with a few witnesses taken in, or before the whole Church. This holds especially if it is established that those who labour under such weaknesses struggle seriously against them, detest them, and wipe them away by daily repentance. There are also certain lighter offences, opposed less to divine laws than to human ones, which are more properly left to be corrected by the civil power. For ecclesiastical correction, since it is a part of the administration of Christ's kingdom and therefore has a spiritual nature, seeks a far greater perfection than that which obtains in civil society. If, however, there is a stubborn spirit toward human laws legitimately enacted by the power ordained by God, that spirit is rightly reproved both by the Pastor separately and by the whole Church. The proper and adequate object of ecclesiastical censure, however, is the scandal arising from sin committed against us, or rather against God and the Church. For the whole aim of ecclesiastical discipline is to remove scandals by correcting the one who, by sinning, offends God, the Church and ourselves, so that the faithful may go on along the course of piety without stumbling, and others, with the obstacles that hinder them removed from the middle, may be drawn to the same way.

units.la: XXIV. Correptio illa peccatorum talium tum universis, tum inprimis Pastori Ecclesiæ, cujus est pro salute Ecclesiæ, omniumque fidelium, & gloria Dei excubare, injungitur.
units.tr: XXIV. That correction of such sins is enjoined on everyone, and above all on the pastor of the Church, whose task it is to keep watch for the salvation of the Church and of all the faithful, and for the glory of God.

units.la: Ubi verò illa & solitaria, & socialis, ex Christi instituto suscepta, nihil proficit, delationem ad Ecclesiam Christus mandat, his verbis: Dic Ecclesiæ. Neque tamen delationem illam ad Ecclesiam semper correptio secretior solitaria & socialis præcedat oportet. Ordinariè quidem & communiter custodiendus hic ordo est; adeóque semper præceptum Christi obligat, sed non, quod ajunt, ad semper, & in quovis casu; sed tum demum, cùm ordo ille correptionis citra periculum peccatoris, Ecclesiæ, Reipublicæ, & proximi offensi teneri potest. In scandalis ergo privatis admonitio privata semper præcedat oportet, quia fratris peccantis existimatio sine gravi necessitate lædi, vel animus ejus irritari, vel scandalum amplificari, vel calumniæ etiam & obtrectationis suspicio temerè & frustra subiri non debet. Indoles enim charitatis & pietatis est, tegere peccata Prov.X.12. XVII.9. Alia ratio est, cùm vel scandalum publicum atque grave est, & in omnium jam notitiam ac offensam incurrit; vel peccatum ejusmodi est, ut propter damnum ex eo ad Rempublicam, Ecclesiam & privatum etiam quemvis redundans, in mora delationis evidens periculum sit. Eos qui peccant, (ita ut peccata eorum, vel post præcedentem correptionem irritam publicari debeant, vel ἐκδηλα[?] manifesta sint per publicum & quotidianum peccandi exercitium ) in conspectu omnium, reprehende, ut & reliqui timorem habeant, I.Tim.V.20. Quorundam hominum peccata manifesta sunt, praecedentia ad judicium, ibid. v.24. Ita S.Paulus Petrum, Gal.II.11. Elymam Magum Act. XIII.7. & Simon Petrus Simonem Magum Act.VIII.20.21. nullo instituto ejusmodi correptionis ordine judicarunt. Et Christus immediatè Judae proditionem, secretam licet adhuc, & sibi soli notam, ob compertum sibi animum ejusdem ἀμεταμέλητον[?] corripuit & damnavit, Joh.XIII.21.&c. Quaelibet enim medicina proportionem ad morbum, cui tollendo inservit, habere debet.
units.tr: Where that private and solitary correction, and the social correction that follows it, undertaken on Christ's institution, achieves nothing, Christ commands that the matter be reported to the Church, in these words: "Tell it to the Church." Yet the report to the Church does not always have to be preceded by the more private solitary and social correction. This order is to be kept ordinarily and generally, and so Christ's precept binds "always," but not, as they say, "for always" and in every case. It applies only when that order of correction can be observed without danger to the sinner, the Church, the commonwealth and the neighbour who has been offended. So in private scandals a private admonition must always come first, because a brother's sinning reputation should not be injured without serious necessity, his mind should not be provoked, the scandal should not be magnified, and the suspicion of calumny and detraction should not be rashly and fruitlessly incurred. For it is the mark of charity and piety to cover sins (Prov. 10.12; 17.9). The case is different when the scandal is public and grave and has already come to the knowledge and offence of all, or when the sin is such that, through the harm it spreads to the commonwealth, the Church and even any private person, there is clear danger in delaying the report. "Those who sin" (so that their sins, even after a previous correction has failed, ought to be made public, or are manifest [ἔκδηλα] through a public and daily practice of sinning) "rebuke in the sight of all, so that the rest also may fear" (1 Tim. 5.20). "The sins of some men are manifest, going before to judgment" (ibid. v. 24). So the apostle Paul judged Peter (Gal. 2.11), and Paul judged Elymas the magician (Acts 13.7), and Simon Peter judged Simon the magician (Acts 8.20-21), without any such fixed order of correction. And Christ himself, though Judas's betrayal was still secret and known to him alone, rebuked and condemned it immediately, because he perceived in Judas a mind that was [ἀμετάμελητον] unrepentant (John 13.21, etc.). For every remedy must be proportioned to the disease it serves to cure.

units.la: XXV. Impiè hic Jesuitae, Sol-ipsi, se ipsos ab ordine illo à Christo instituto eximunt, per regulam suam Antichristianam, quae juri suo, quo ex instituto Christi gaudere debebant, renunciantes, se ipsos obligant ad delationem fratrum immediatam ad Superiorem, sine ulla correptione privata praecedente. Qua de re paulò fusiùs agit Arriaga in 22. q. 33. art. 8. disp. 46. §. 5. nec non Diana Panormitanus P.III.Tract. 2. Resol.37. Hanc verò exemptionem irregularem à Valentia, Torres, Conink, Diana, aliis acriter defensam licet, aperte & fusè oppugnant. Lorca, Philiarcus, Lopez de Texeda, Academia Salmanticensis, ab eodem Diana citata, & paulò timidiùs Bannes, Basseus, qui hanc dubitandi rationem affert, quòd sit inconveniens; nec tamen eam solvit. Sed jugulum ei manifestè petiit tum Christus, immediatam quorumvis delationem ad Superiores prohibens Matth. XVIII. 15. &c. tum S.Paulus juxta Christi institutum Timotheo praecipiens: Contra Seniorem κατηγορίαν accusationem (delationem) ne suscipe, nisi ubi duo vel tres testes fuerint, I.Tim.V.19. Quomodo ergo Jesuitae, λεγόμενον[?] πρεσβύτερον Seniores Societatis, socios suos Presbyteros immediatè deferre ad Superiores, vel Superiores delationem immediatam suscipere possunt?
units.tr: XXV. Here the Jesuits, the Sol-ipsi, impiously exempt themselves from that order instituted by Christ. Through their own Antichristian rule they renounce the right which, by Christ's institution, they ought to enjoy, and bind themselves to report their brethren immediately to the Superior, with no private correction preceding. Arriaga treats this matter rather at length (in 22, q. 33, art. 8, disp. 46, §5), as do Diana of Palermo (P. III, Tract. 2, Resol. 37). Although Valentia, Torres, Coninck, Diana and others have defended this irregular exemption vigorously, Lorca, Philiarchus, Lopez de Texeda, the Salamanca Academy (cited by the same Diana), and, more timidly, Bannes and Basseus, openly and at length oppose it. Basseus brings forward this objection, that it is "inconvenient," but he does not resolve it. But Christ dealt it a mortal blow, forbidding the immediate report of anyone whatever to the superiors (Matt. 18.15, etc.), and Paul likewise, following Christ's institution, instructs Timothy: "Do not receive an accusation [κατηγορίαν] (report) against an elder, unless there are two or three witnesses" (1 Tim. 5.19). How, then, can the Jesuits immediately report their so-called [λεγόμενον] "presbyters," the seniors of the Society, their fellow presbyters, to the superiors, or the superiors receive such an immediate report?

units.la: XXVI. Dignum porrò observatu est, quòd cum & Lex Divina prohibeat suscipere שֵׁם רַע[?] famam incertam, seu delationem quamvis ἄδηλον[?], Exod. XXIII.1. atque ad omne judicium duos vel tres testes requirat, Num. XXXV. 30. Deut.XVII.6. Num.XIX.15. & Christus, juxta eandem Legem, interdixerit delationem quorumvis immediatam ad Ecclesiam, duobus vel tribus testibus destitutam, Matth.XVIII.16; S.Paulus tamen loco citato peculiariter Presbyterorum delationem suscipi, nisi ubi duo vel tres testes fuerint, vetat. Cujus rei causa non ea est, quam Canonistae afferunt, quia lai- ci clericos oderunt. Nam nec de plebejis solis deferentibus Apostolus loquitur: nec Canonistae ipsi admittunt, ut à plebejis Ecclesiastici deferantur: nec plebeji quosvis Ecclesiasticos oderunt, sed eos demum, qui se supra gregem efferentes, spurci, voluptuarii, otiosi, inutiles sunt, & non quae Christi, sed quae sua sunt, quaerunt. Quorum infamia & odium publicum meritissimum testimonium contra ipsos omni exceptione majus est. Sicut etiam Tyri spiritualis (Hierarchiae Romanae) infamia erubescenda indicatur per querelam maris de מעון ים [?] arce maris (illis, qui se pro arce maris gerunt, seu pro Ecclesia illa, cui portae inferorum praevalere nequeant) quod non parturiverint, nec pepererint, nec enutriverint juvenes, nec extulerint virgines, Esaj. XXIII.4. De quibus Deus loquitur: Contra Pastores illos iratus est furor meus, & hircos ipsos visitabo, Zach.X.3. Neque etiam, quod alii interpretes afferunt, ad judicium solum, non ad suscep-tionem delationis, testes duos Lex Divina & Christus: Paulus vero insuper etiam ad suscipiendam delationem. Presbyterorum duos vel tres testes requirit. Manifeste enim Christus correptionem per duos vel tres testes delationi etiam ad Ecclesiam faciendae, & ab eadem suscipiendae praemittit. Quid ergo? Hoc sibi vult S. Paulus, tum ipsos etiam presbyteros deferri & judicari aeque ac coeteros posse, secus quam Papae gnathones nugantur, eum à nemine deferri vel judicari posse: tum delationem eorum ad fidem faciendam ei, qui suscipere debet, prae coeteris niti debere testimonio duorum vel trium (non septuaginta non laicorum, quem numerum ad damnationem Episcopi insolenter Canonistae exigunt) qui considerandi inprimis & examinandi sint, an fide digni & idonei sint, idq; eam ob causam, quia Presbyterorum tanta, & tam probe circumvallata esse existimatio atque authoritas debet, ut non temere adhibenda sit fides iis, qui famam eorum appetunt; atque insuper Sathanas iisdem prae coeteris insidiatur, & impii etiam homines reperiuntur ἀντιλέγοντες [?] correptionis impatientes, & in eos à quibus corripiuntur, canum instar, insurgentes, ut confictis criminibus eorum correptionem obscurant, & corripientium fidem animumque frangant. Corripiens derisorem sibi ipsi accipit igneminiam: & increpans impium accipit sibi maculam. Ne increpes igitur derisorem, ne odio te habeat: sed increpa sapientem, ut diligat te, Prov. IX.7.8.
units.tr: XXVI. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the Divine Law forbids the receiving of an [שֵׁם רַע] "evil report" (that is, an uncertain report, or any report that is [ἄδηλον] obscure), and requires "two or three witnesses" for every judgment (Exod. 23.1; Num. 35.30; Deut. 17.6; Num. 19.15). Christ, following the same Law, forbade the immediate report of anyone to the Church without two or three witnesses (Matt. 18.16). Yet Paul, in the passage cited, specifically forbids the receiving of a report against elders unless there are two or three witnesses. The reason for this is not the one the canonists give, namely "because the laity hate the clergy." For the apostle is not speaking only of reports made by common people, and the canonists themselves do not admit that clergy may be reported by common people. Nor do common people hate every clergyman, but only those who, lifting themselves above the flock, are filthy, pleasure-loving, idle and useless, and who seek not the things of Christ but their own. The infamy and public hatred of such men is the most deserved testimony against them, and greater than any objection. Likewise, the shame of the spiritual Tyre (the Roman hierarchy) is indicated by the complaint of the sea concerning [מעון ים] "the stronghold of the sea" (that is, of those who presume to be the stronghold of the sea, or of that Church against which the gates of hell cannot prevail): "they have not travailed, nor borne, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins" (Isa. 23.4). Concerning these God speaks: "My anger is kindled against the shepherds, and I will punish the he-goats" (Zech. 10.3). Nor is it the case, as other interpreters maintain, that the Divine Law and Christ require two witnesses only for judgment, and not for receiving a report, while Paul requires two or three witnesses for the receiving of a report against presbyters. For Christ plainly places correction before a report even to the Church, and before its acceptance, through two or three witnesses. What then does Paul mean? That presbyters too may be reported and judged just like the rest, contrary to what the Pope's flatterers babble, that he cannot be reported or judged by anyone. And that their report, to bring faith to him who must receive it, must rest on the testimony of two or three witnesses more than on others (not seventy, the number which the canonists insolently demand for the condemnation of a bishop), who are first to be considered and examined as to whether they are trustworthy and fit. This is for the following reason: the reputation and authority of presbyters ought to be so great and so well protected that faith should not be rashly given to those who seek to attack it. Moreover, Satan lays snares for them above others, and wicked men are found who [ἀντιλέγοντας] contradict and cannot endure correction, and who, like dogs, rise up against those by whom they are corrected, so that by fabricated crimes they may obscure the correction and break the trust and courage of those who correct them. "He who corrects a scoffer gets dishonour for himself, and he who rebukes a wicked man gets a stain. So do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you" (Prov. 9.7-8).

units.la: XXVII. Sed & delatio peccatorum ad Ecclesiam instituenda certo ordine progrediatur oportet, ne per saltum nimium delatio statim fiat ad omnes, qui in Ecclesia disciplinæ præsunt. Si enim is, qui deferre debet, sit ipse Ecclesiæ Pastor, mitius utique est, ut uni cuipiam seniori primum peccator denuntietur: sin vel senior, vel privatus quivis alius est, prudentiæ pariter & charitatis est, Pastori prius quam toti consessui eorum, qui Ecclesiæ nomine disciplinam moderantur, delictum indicare. Neque obstant verba Christi: Dic Ecclesiæ. Dici enim aliquid potest vel immediate Ecclesiæ illi particulari, cujus peccator membrum est; vel mediate, per Synedrium, & Synedrio ipsi mediate per Ministrum aut Seniorem, qui Synedrii illius membrum est. Potest autem vel Minister vel Senior delicta, nondum publice nota, & privatim sibi hac vel alia ratione innotescentia tegere, & ad confessum ampliorem non deferre, si vera resipiscentia abrumpantur, in futurum non pendeant, & publico non obsint.
units.tr: XXVII. But the report of sins to the Church must also proceed in a fixed order, so that the report does not leap too far at once to all who preside over discipline in the Church. For if the one who must report is himself the pastor of the Church, it is surely gentler that the sinner first be denounced to a single elder. But if the one reporting is an elder or some other private person, it is equally a mark of prudence and charity to disclose the offence to the pastor before the whole assembly of those who govern discipline in the name of the Church. Nor do Christ's words, "Tell it to the Church," stand in the way. For something may be told either immediately to that particular church of which the sinner is a member, or mediately, through the consistory, and to the consistory itself mediately through the minister or the elder who is a member of that consistory. Moreover, a minister or an elder may conceal offences not yet publicly known, which have come to his private knowledge by this or that means, and not bring them to the wider assembly, provided that they are cut off by true repentance, do not hang over the future, and do no harm to the public.

units.la: XXVIII. Si ad Ecclesiam delatus peccator ferrea fronte ejusdem admonitioni & correptioni obsistat, fraenum mordeat, & spes correctionis animam jam efflaverit, neque agnus lupo eripi ulla arte valeat, Christus peccatorem ejusmodi præfractum pro Ethnico & Publicano, h.e. pro homine enormiter scandaloso, impio, deplorato, & Dei abnegatore, habere jubet. Hic vero Ecclesiarum sententia & praxis nonnihil variat, dum aliæ quidem eos, quos ita pro Ethnicis & Publicanis habent, sic excommunicant, ut ab usu Cœnæ Dominicæ, aliisque Ecclesiæ privilegiis eosdem suspendant, vel, si ita contumaciæ & flagitii ratio postulet, graviori denuntiatione, ab omni communione, quæ Sanctorum propria est, arceant: aliæ vero, missa inprimis solenni illa à S. Cœnæ usu remotione, quam excommunicationem majorem appellant (abstentionem simplicem, siquidem ordine, fiat, non omnino improbantes) eosdem ad Civilem Potestatem, siquidem idem[?] illa consentiens Ecclesiæ & Orthodoxa fuerit, coercendos, & pœnis civilibus, ad pœnitentiam usque salutarem, vel interitum corporis frangendos deferant. Quæ quidem posterior sententia & praxis in Republica patria, à Viris Sanctissimis, Huldrico Zwinglio & Henrico Bullingero introducta, & ad nostra usque tempora producta, etiamnum ita viget, ut peccatore contumaciter Ecclesiam ipsam corripientem spernente, & pro Ethnico & Publicano declarato, Ecclesiastica disciplina tantum non respiret, & locus detur disciplinæ civili, Christianis tamen legibus, non intra civilem duntaxat honestatem, sed evangelii etiam Christi πολιτείαν[?] consistentibus instructæ, per quam pestes & carcinomata ejusmodi carcere, vel exilio ab Ecclesia mulctentur, quinimo, si insanabile vulnus appareat, ne pars sincera trahatur, ense etiam recidantur. Quandiu tamen illa Sathanæ pabula, citra pœnitentiæ testificationem, in Ecclesia tolerantur, juxta eandem sententiam & praxin monentur fideles, ut non tantum lugeant, sed etiam hominum illorum consortium cane pejus & angue vitent, cum operibus eorum infrugiferis commercium nullum habeant, ac ne ave quidem iis dicant, ut ita Salvatoris sententiæ, præcipientis; Sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, amplius satisfiat, quin & ipsi contumaces & enormiter scandalosi, quandiu in peccato persistunt, abstinere ultro à Cœna Domini & Symbolis gratiæ severe jubentur (quæ excommunicationis, sed non violentæ, species quædam est) non neglecta interim, ac ne suspensa quidem admonitione fraterna, cum ex Evangelio constet, nec de Ethnicorum, nec de Publicanorum salute desperandum esse. Ministerium enim Ecclesiasticum ædificium est, quod in perpetuo actu versatur, neque unquam apicem attingit.
units.tr: XXVIII. If a sinner brought before the Church sets his brazen forehead against its admonition and correction, bites the bridle, and hope of correction has already breathed its last, so that no art can snatch the lamb from the wolf, Christ commands that such a stubborn sinner be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector, that is, as a man grossly scandalous, impious, hopeless, and a denier of God. Here, however, the judgment and practice of the Churches vary somewhat. Some indeed excommunicate those whom they thus hold as heathens and tax collectors, suspending them from the use of the Lord's Supper and the other privileges of the Church, or, if the seriousness of the obstinacy and disgrace requires it, excluding them by a more severe proclamation from all communion, which belongs to the saints. Others, above all by that solemn removal from the Lord's Supper which they call the greater excommunication (not wholly disapproving a simple abstention, provided it is done in an orderly way), hand these men over to the civil power, if it agrees with the Church and is orthodox, to be restrained by civil penalties and broken, even to salutary repentance or the destruction of the body. This latter judgment and practice, introduced in our fatherland's commonwealth by the most holy men Huldrych Zwingli and Heinrich Bullinger, and carried down to our own times, still holds such sway that, when a sinner obstinately spurns the Church that rebukes him and has been declared a heathen and tax collector, ecclesiastical discipline scarcely breathes and room is given to civil discipline. That civil discipline, however, is furnished with Christian laws, resting not merely on civil decency but also on the polity [πολιτείαν] of the Gospel of Christ, and by it such pests and cancers are punished with prison or exile from the Church, and moreover, if an incurable wound appears, are cut away even with the sword, lest the sound part be dragged down with it. As long as, however, those fodders of Satan are tolerated in the Church without any testimony of repentance, the faithful are admonished, according to the same judgment and practice, not only to mourn but also to avoid the company of those men worse than a dog or a snake, to have no dealings with their unfruitful works, and not even to bid them hail, so that the saying of the Savior, who commands, "Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector," may be more fully satisfied. Moreover, the obstinate and grossly scandalous themselves, as long as they persist in sin, are severely ordered to abstain of their own accord from the Lord's Supper and the symbols of grace. This is a certain kind of excommunication, though not a violent one. Meanwhile fraternal admonition is not neglected, nor even suspended, since it is clear from the Gospel that there is no reason to despair either of the salvation of heathens or of the salvation of tax collectors. For the ecclesiastical ministry is a building that is in perpetual activity and never reaches its capstone.

units.la: XXIX. Hac equidem de quæstione vexatissima heic contendendi locus non est. Id solum monemus, nec reliquarum Ecclesiarum sententiam & usum à nobis rejici, vel damnari; nec eam nobis animositatem hactenus fuisse, ut famosam illam excommunicationem, quam Majorem vocant, cum violentia quadam conjunctam, in Ecclesiam nostram ἀ[?]ἐ[?]αλέως introduceremus. inprimis cum nobis non liquido appareat, illam à Christo & Apostolis, ut perpetuo, & in qualibet conditione temporum ac status publici Ecclesiæ necessariam, præceptam & commendatam esse; & vetus ac innocentior adhuc Ecclesia, quæ illam exercuit, necessitate quadam compulsa, quia Magistratu plane discorde, & Christianis legibus inviso, vitiosis contra legibus moribusque Rempublicam gubernante, usa est, hunc disciplinæ rigorem adhibuerit. Confessionis Helveticæ hac de re sententiam adscribere lubet. Cum, ita verba ejus Cap. XVII. sonant, omnino oporteat esse in Ecclesia disciplinam, & apud Veteres quondam usitatæ fuerit Excommunicatio, fuerintque judicia Ecclesiastica in populo Dei, in quibus per viros prudentes & pios exercebatur hæc disciplina; Ministrorum quoque fuerit ad ædificationem disciplinam hanc moderari pro conditione temporum, status publici, ac necessitate. Ubi semper tenenda est regula, omnia fieri debere ad ædificationem, decenter, honeste, sine tyrannide & seditione. Apostolus enim testatur, sibi à Deo traditam esse in Ecclesia potestatem ad ædificationem. Nam ipsemet Dominus vetuit, lolium in agro Dominico eradicari, quando periculum sit, ut & triticum evellatur. Non ergo disciplinæ illam ἀποτομίαν [?] quæ in vetustiori Ecclesia ad Excommunicationem majorem & diras usque processit, simpliciter improbat, sed pro conditione temporum, Status publici, & necessitate ita moderari jubet, ut ædificationi, non destructioni inserviat. Cujusmodi moderationem pluribus etiam S. Augustinus lib. III. contra Epist. Parm. cap. 2. commendat, allato eodem argumento, quòd zizanium eradicari non debeat, quando periculum est, ut triticum evellatur.
units.tr: XXIX. Indeed, this most vexed question is not the place to contend about it here. We only remind the reader that neither the judgment nor the practice of the other Churches is rejected or condemned by us, nor has there hitherto been in us such animosity that we would introduce that infamous excommunication, which they call the Greater, joined with a certain violence, rashly into our Church. Above all, since it does not clearly appear to us that it was commanded and recommended by Christ and the Apostles as necessary for all times and every condition of the Church and of the public state, and the older and still more innocent Church, which practised it, was compelled by a certain necessity, because the magistracy was entirely discordant and governed the commonwealth with vicious laws and morals hostile to Christian law, it adopted this rigor of discipline. It pleases us to set down the opinion of the Helvetic Confession on this matter. "Since," so its words in chapter 17 run, "there must necessarily be discipline in the Church, and excommunication was once in use among the ancients, and there were ecclesiastical judgments among the people of God, in which this discipline was exercised by prudent and godly men, it also belongs to the ministers to moderate this discipline for edification, according to the condition of the times, the public state, and necessity. Where the rule must always be held that all things be done for edification, decently, honestly, without tyranny and sedition. For the Apostle testifies that the power given him by God in the Church was for edification. For the Lord himself forbade the tares in the Lord's field to be uprooted, when there is danger that the wheat be pulled up too." Thus it does not simply disapprove that severity [ἀποτομίαν] of discipline which in the more ancient Church went as far as the greater excommunication and the curses, but bids it be moderated "according to the condition of the times, the public state, and necessity," so that it serves edification and not destruction. S. Augustine, too, in book 3 against the Epistle of Parmenian, chapter 2, commends such moderation at some length, adducing the same argument, that the tares ought not to be uprooted when there is danger that the wheat be pulled up with them.

units.la: XXX. Sed habuerunt Ecclesiæ Helveticæ suæ in revocanda disciplina severiori cunctationis & verecundiæ rationes haud pœnitendas, quas inprimis Benedictus Aretius, Bernensis Theologus eximius, Probl. Loc. 112. cumulavit, & quas ex eodem, aliisque etiam, velut per saturam exhibere hoc loco haud pigebit, ut agnoscant etiam exotici, illam, quam in disciplina nostra notant, infirmitatem & labeculam haud temerè & ἀλόγως tolerari. Viderunt ante omnia sanctæ recordationis Antecessores nostri, rem optimam pessimo abusu Pontificio invisam, & pene execrabilem redditam esse. Bannus enim (ita vocari suevit) non aliud quàm arcanum Pontificiæ dominationis & conscientiarum carnificina fuit: & tam invisum jam nomen ejus esse cœpit, quàm est tyrannidis. Tum exigua, vel nulla spes iis affulsit, fore, ut rebus sic, uti erant, & etiamnum sunt, jacentibus obtineatur, atque obtenta retineatur. Non est autem prudentis, rem pene ἀδύνατον conari, inprimis cùm simpliciter necessaria non est. Ad excommunicationem enim Majorem requiruntur tum Pastores cordati, qui præter Deum metuant neminem, & parati sint pro salute Ecclesiæ vitam sanguinémque periclitari: tum populus, & in eodem imperantes æquè atque parentes, qui obedire & pati jugum isthoc velint, & valeant; Verbo, Ambrosii & Theodosii. Ubi verò illi sunt? Et si qui sunt, quàm rari, ut nantes in gurgite vasto? Quàm facilè apud eos, quibus res isthæc committitur, dominandi studium subrepit, ut odia privata, & affectus maligni vincant? Experientia enim testis est, per hanc viam Antichristum ad dominationis suæ arcem enixum esse. Et olim quidem Excommunicatio isthæc non in consistorio vel consessu paucorum, sed in Conventibus Ecclesiasticis, sub conscientia & suffragiis fidelium suscipi consuevit. Hodie quid fiet, ubi vulgus & plebs, in libera inprimis Republica, dissolutiòr, & major saltem pars corruptissima est [?] Peccatori patrocinabitur, palliabit vitia, quæ in sinu suo similia reperit; denique bonam partem suffragiis vincet. Quid porrò fieret majori parti, si χωεὶς πλοπολίσεως [?], & procul omni studio partium, & corvorum jure, atque columbarum injuria, ebrii, lascivi, avari, tyranni, blasphemi, injusti, Magistratus subditis iniqui, & subditi dominantibus obliqui atque immorigeri, hanc aleam subire juberentur? Accedit periculum schismatis, cujus metu tum S. Cyprianus Coëpiscopos suos malos toleravit: tum Irenæus Victorem Episcopum Romanum admonuit, temperaret sibi ab Excommunicatione Orientalium: tum S. Augustinus, diu cum Donatistis, Manichæis, aliisque conflictatus, & in hoc prœlio miles veteranus, loco citato, alibique, Zizania tolerari maluit. Ad Christum & Apostolos ubi deflexerit cogitatio, unicum exemplum occurrit incestuosi, in peccato singulari, enormi, publico, cùm judicem Christianum nullum haberet, Sathanæ traditi, ad interitum carnis. quæ actio potestatis, an charitatis; miraculosa, an communis, imitabilis & omni tempori conveniens fuerit, nondum convenit. Alios certè, qui & ipsi in Corinthiorum Ecclesia alibique gravissimè peccarunt, excommunicatos & Sathanæ traditos reperire non est. Jam & metum ciebant exempla aliarum Ecclesiarum, quibus assumptus ille rigor minùs auspicato cessit. Basileæ Oecolampadius, dissuadente Zuinglio, Schedis ad Templi fores affixis, excommunicare quosdam cœpit. Cœterùm adeò durabilis non fuit illa consuetudo, ut, quod Zuinglius prædixerat, idem Oecolampadius à cœpto desistere, non sine existimationis suæ jactura, necesse habuerit. Argentinæ Bucerus & Capito, Viri pii & docti, dicentes ad Dominum: Vis ibimus, & colligemus Zizania? (Matth. XIII. 28.) nullo cum successu laborarunt. Idem Constantiæ acciderat, Blaurero Consule, & fratre Ambrosio eventum sinistrum augurantibus. Denique carentibus illo rigore Ecclesiis nostris non desunt tamen ἀναθεματίζομενα [?], uti Medici vocare solent. Nam & Ministri Ecclesiæ non tantùm quotidie illam excommunicationis formulam: Qui talia committunt, non habent partem in Regno Cœlorum; graviter intonant: Sed etiam ante Cœnam præfractos & ἀμεταμελήτας [?] peccatores severe objurgant, & iisdem authores, publica etiam obnuntiatione, sunt, ne impœnitentes & imparati manum ad sacra Symbola mittant, mittentibus judicium grave minitantur, & consistoria ac fora tum mere Ecclesiastica, tum mixta[?] adhortationibus, comminationibus, instructionibus ex Dei verbo assiduè calent: & Magistratus pius omnium ordinum homines in officio suo continet, in sceleratos verò gladio, laqueo, carcere, exilio, infamia aliisque modis severè animadvertit; & pii gemunt atque clamant propter cunctas abominationes, quæ in populo fiunt: & Deus ipse, quod caput est, suam quotidie excommunicationem exercens hypocritas prodit, apertè sceleratos malè perdit, solemniterque in extremo judicio à cœtu fidelium separatos declarabit. Huic verò ordini & instituto sic Deus hactenus pro immensa gratia sua benedixit, ut Ecclesiam nostram, quod ἀξιακόντως[?] dixero, non major corruptio in doctrina & moribus, quàm alias, majorem illam disciplinæ austeritatem professas, afflixerit. Sed hæc παρέργως ὁδὸν[?] de incidente hoc argumento, citra ullum φιλονεικίας[?] studium, dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: XXX. But our Helvetic Churches, in reviving the severer discipline, had reasons for caution and restraint that are by no means to be regretted. Benedict Aretius, the outstanding theologian of Bern, gathered these above all in his Loci problemata 112, and it will not irk us to set them out here, as a kind of medley drawn from him and others, so that even foreigners may recognize that the weakness and blemish which they note in our discipline is tolerated not rashly and without reason. Our reverend predecessors saw first of all that an excellent thing had been made hated and nearly execrable by the worst Papist abuse. For the ban (as it was customarily called) was nothing other than the secret instrument of Papal domination and the butcher of consciences, and its name has begun to be as hateful as tyranny itself. Then little or no hope dawned on them that things would be kept as they were, and as they still are, lying prostrate, or that, once obtained, the ban would be retained. It is not the mark of a prudent man, however, to attempt what is almost impossible, especially when it is not simply necessary. For the greater excommunication requires both ministers of sound judgment, who fear no one but God and are ready to risk life and blood for the salvation of the Church, and a people, and rulers who are like parents to them, who are willing and able to bear this yoke; in a word, the Ambroses and Theodosiuses. But where are they? And if there are any, how rare are they, like swimmers in a vast whirlpool? How easily does the desire to dominate creep in among those to whom this business is committed, so that private hatreds and malign passions prevail? Experience is witness that by this road Antichrist strove to the citadel of his domination. And formerly this excommunication was undertaken not in a consistory or the assembly of a few, but in ecclesiastical gatherings, under the conscience and votes of the faithful. What will happen today, when the common crowd and the rabble, especially in a free commonwealth, are looser, and at least the greater part is most corrupt? They will defend the sinner, will cover up the vices they find like their own in their own bosom, and finally will win the greater part of the votes. What, moreover, would happen to the greater part, if, without any civil polity [πολιτείας], and far from all party spirit, with the right of crows and the wrong of doves, drunkards, wanton men, the greedy, tyrants, blasphemers, the unjust, magistrates unfair to their subjects, and subjects unbending and unruly towards their rulers, were ordered to undergo this lottery? To this is added the danger of schism, through fear of which S. Cyprian tolerated his evil fellow bishops; and Irenaeus admonished Victor, bishop of Rome, to refrain from excommunicating the Eastern Churches; and S. Augustine, who had long struggled with the Donatists, Manichaeans, and others, and in this battle was a veteran soldier, preferred, in the passage cited and elsewhere, that the tares be tolerated. When thought turns to Christ and the Apostles, there is one example, that of the incestuous man, who for a singular, enormous, public sin, since there was no Christian judge, was delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. Whether that act was one of power or of love, whether it was miraculous or ordinary, imitable and suitable for every time, is not yet agreed. Certainly one cannot find others who, in the Church of Corinth or elsewhere, sinned most gravely and yet were excommunicated and delivered to Satan. Moreover, the examples of other Churches, where that assumed rigor ended with less favorable results, also aroused fear. At Basel, Oecolampadius, though Zwingli dissuaded him, began to excommunicate certain persons, posting placards on the doors of the church. But that custom was not so lasting that Oecolampadius, as Zwingli had foretold, did not find it necessary to give up what he had begun, not without loss of his reputation. At Strasbourg, Bucer and Capito, pious and learned men, who said to the Lord, "Will you have us go and gather up the tares?" (Matt. 13:28), labored to no effect. The same happened at Constance, when Blaurer was consul and brother Ambrose foretold an unhappy outcome. Finally, although our Churches lack that rigor, there are still [ἀναθεματίζομενα], as physicians are accustomed to call them. For the ministers of the Church not only thunder daily that formula of excommunication, "Those who commit such things have no part in the Kingdom of Heaven," but also before the Lord's Supper severely rebuke sinners who are obstinate and [ἀμεταμελήτας] unrepentant, and by public announcement are the authors that the impenitent and unprepared not put their hands to the sacred Symbols, threatening a heavy judgment on those who do. Consistories and courts, both purely ecclesiastical and mixed, are constantly warm with exhortations, threats, and instructions from God's word. The pious magistrate restrains men of every rank in their duty, and punishes the wicked severely with the sword, the noose, prison, exile, infamy, and other means. The godly groan and cry out because of all the abominations that are done among the people. And God himself, who is the head, exercising his own excommunication daily, exposes hypocrites, plainly ruins the wicked, and will solemnly declare at the last judgment that they are separated from the assembly of the faithful. This order and institution God has hitherto so blessed, by his immense grace, that, to speak worthily, our Church has not been afflicted by greater corruption in doctrine and morals than the others, which professed that greater austerity of discipline. But these things, said in passing [παρέργως] about this incidental subject, and without any spirit of contention [φιλονεικίας], will suffice.

units.la: XXXI. Ex iis verò, quæ dicta sunt, liquere potest, quæ delatio in foro Ecclesiastico locum habere possit. Nam delicta corripienda, & in foro Ecclesiæ discutienda deferri possunt ordine servato, tum à quovis ob proximi peccatum scandalum patiente, ad Pastorem, vel Seniorem, vel immediatè etiam ad Ecclesiam: tum à Pastore vel Seniore ad Ecclesiam seu γερουσίαν, Senatum & Presbyterium Ecclesiæ: tum ab Ecclesia, si peccator callum obduxerit, vel alia ratio ita postulet, ad Magistratum civilem. Prima & Secunda delatio communis est politiæ Ecclesiasticæ in universum omni, utpote quam ordo à Christo ipso institutus postulat. Sicut autem in foro Divino ita in Ecclesiastico etiam Pastor Ecclesiæ delationem sibi factam ad gloriam Dei & salutem proximi equidem suscipere potest: at delatores, & insidiosos quidem, subornare, mercede conducere, aut tanquam munus aliquod prætorium cuiquam imponere non potest; secus quàm fit in Papatu, ubi ad tyrannidis Antichristianæ stabilimentum אנשי דמים viri sanguinolenti (Prov. XXIX. 10.) Inquisitores hæreticæ pravitatis (qui lepores ipsi pulpamentum quærunt) & Confessarii conducta habent mancipia, quorum delatione, seu proditione potius, secretissima quæque penetrant. Tertia verò delationis species politiæ Ecclesiasticæ in Patria nostra receptæ propria est; cùm aliarum Ecclesiarum Presbyteria causas Ecclesiasticas in ipsa Ecclesia terminent, neque ad Civilem potestatem terminandas deferre teneantur. Cautio tamen heic etiam necessaria videtur, ut non tam Pastor Ecclesiæ, quàm Senior quispiam alius Magistratui juratus, totius Presbyterii nomine delatoris munere apud Magistratum fungatur. Neque enim vel dignitas muneris, vel ædificationis Ecclesiæ ratio fert, ut Ecclesiæ Pastores, qui Dei & Ecclesiæ, seu Regni Christi ad salutem animarum, non Magistratus, seu Regni hujus mundi, ad executionem legum civilium, vel moralium, atque temporalium pœnarum inflictionem ministri sunt, delatorum ; exceptis nonnullis casibus, partes obeant. Homines suadeo, an Deum? An quæro hominibus placere? Si enim hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem, Gal. I. 10. Ὑπὲρ Χρισ̄ πρεσβευόμεν[?]. Pro Christo legationis munere fungi-mur,&c. 2.Cor.V.20.
units.tr: XXXI. From what has been said, it can be seen what place delation can have in the ecclesiastical forum. Offences that are to be rebuked and dealt with in the forum of the Church may be reported, in the proper order: first, by anyone who suffers scandal from a neighbour's sin, to the minister or an elder, or directly to the Church; second, by the minister or an elder to the Church, that is, to the gerousia [γερουσίαν], the senate and presbytery of the Church; and third, by the Church, if the sinner has grown hardened or some other reason requires it, to the civil magistrate. The first and second kinds of delation are common to the ecclesiastical polity in general, since the order instituted by Christ himself demands them. However, just as in the divine forum, so in the ecclesiastical forum the minister of the Church may indeed accept a delation made to him for the glory of God and the salvation of his neighbour; but he cannot hire informers, or secretly suborn them, or impose such a task on anyone as if it were some official duty. This is not the case among the Papists, where, to establish the Antichristian tyranny, the men of blood (אנשי דמים; Prov. 29:10) are employed as inquisitors of heretical depravity, who seek out prey for themselves, and confessors keep hired creatures whose informing, or rather betrayal, lays bare all their most private affairs. The third kind of delation, however, is peculiar to the ecclesiastical polity received in our own country, since the presbyteries of the other churches settle ecclesiastical causes within the Church itself and are not bound to refer them to the civil power for settlement. Even so, caution seems necessary here as well: it is not the minister of the Church but some other elder sworn to the magistrate who should discharge the office of informer before the magistrate in the name of the whole presbytery. For neither the dignity of the office nor the edification of the Church requires that the ministers of the Church, who serve God and the Church, that is, the kingdom of Christ, for the salvation of souls, and not the magistrate, that is, the kingdom of this world, for the enforcement of civil and moral laws and the infliction of temporal penalties, should take on the role of informers, except in certain cases. Am I now trying to persuade men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? For if I still pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ, Gal. 1:10. On behalf of Christ we are ambassadors (Ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν), that is, we discharge the office of ambassadors for Christ, etc., 2 Cor. 5:20.

units.la: XXXII. Ad Forum Politicum pergimus.
units.tr: XXXII. We come to the political forum.

units.la: In eo delatio non tantum admittitur, vel suscipitur, sed certis etiam atque fidis hominibus, velut munus quoddam muneri judiciali & censorio cuivis inserviens, jurato etiam imponitur. Interest enim Reipublicæ, ut Jurisconsulti dicunt, ne scelera impunita maneant. Interest etiam pacis publicæ & charitatis, ne quis alteri injuriam faciat, sed ut suum cuique tribuatur. Ut ergo & suum cuique maneat, Deo, quod Dei est, Cæsari, quod Cæsaris est, proximo cuivis, quod proximi est: utque scelera vel delicta contra leges publicas, humanæ societatis nervum, commissa puniri, publicæ securitatis & exempli causa possint, necesse est, ut delicta ad notitiam judicis perveniant. Neque pervenire semper sine opera delatorum possunt. Habet ergo Civilis Potestas, qui ex officio nocentes deferre tenentur, quoties publici boni ratio id postulat. Tales sunt Procuratores fisci, aliisque officiales similes, apud nos in Urbe quidem fori Censorii & Matrimonialis Assessores singuli; in agro Præfecti, Subpræfecti, matrimoniorum custodes, & jurati alii, quibus munus isthoc propter utilitatem publicam legitimè imponitur.
units.tr: Here delation is not only permitted or accepted, but is also imposed, as a kind of duty serving the judicial and censorial office, on certain trustworthy men who have been sworn to it. For it concerns the Commonwealth, as the jurists say, that crimes should not remain unpunished. It also concerns public peace and charity that no one should wrong another, but that each should be given what is his due. So that each keeps what is his, that what belongs to God is rendered to God, what belongs to Caesar to Caesar, and what belongs to one's neighbour to one's neighbour; and so that crimes and offences committed against the public laws, which are the sinews of human society, may be punished for the sake of public safety and as an example, it is necessary that offences come to the knowledge of the judge. And they cannot always come to him without the work of informers. Therefore the civil power has those who are bound by their office to report wrongdoers whenever the public good requires it. Such are the procurators of the treasury and other similar officials: among us, in the city, the individual assessors of the censorial and matrimonial court; in the countryside, the prefects, subprefects, guardians of marriages, and other sworn officers, to whom this duty is lawfully imposed for the public benefit.

units.la: XXXIII. Neque hi duntaxat, sed quilibet cives & privati, nulla speciali vocatione ad id obstricti, neque ad id requisiti, sola charitate proximi, Reipublicæ cumprimis, impellente, deferre apud Magistratum quædam crimina tenentur. illa puta, quæ vel immediatè sive Dei Majestatem & gloriam lædunt, cujusmodi blasphemiæ crimen est; sive humanam societatem infestant, velut crimen perduellionis, conspirationis, peculatus, &c. vel mediatè in publicam perniciem tendunt, cujusmodi sunt crimina quædam atrociora, humanam societatem consequenter vastantia, veluti latrocinia quævis, incestus, adulteria, aliáque [ἀθέσμων?] crimina: vel denique ejusmodi sunt, ut eorum revelatio & delatio ad delinquentium emendationem procurandam,vel continuationem etiam delicti impediendam, omitti non possit. Neque tamen prius instituenda a quovis cive,& privato delatio est, quam conspicuum est, detrimentum ex talibus delictis in societatem publicam, & peccatorem ipsum redundans, alia via, commodiore & molliore averruncari non posse. Quæ ubi nulla apparet,justitia & lex charitatis, qua civitati & fratri ac proximo cuivis devincti sumus, nos obligat, ut ad mala ejusmodi non conniveamus,sed omnem potius operam studiumque eo convertamus, ut delicta ejusmodi, quorum ab aliis patratorum probe conscii sumus, ad notitiam eorum,qui mederi ex officio debent,provehantur. Major enim ratio habenda justitiæ & charitatis boni communis, ac innocentis cujusvis est, quam famæ hominis criminosi, quæ ipsa tamen mere per accidens & ex propria delinquentis culpa lædSitur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Not only these, but also any citizens and private persons, not bound to it by any special calling and not required for it, but moved by love of neighbour and above all by concern for the commonwealth, are bound to report certain crimes to the magistrate. Namely, those which either directly injure the majesty and glory of God, of which blasphemy is such a crime; or threaten human society, like the crime of treason, conspiracy, embezzlement, etc.; or indirectly tend to public ruin, such as certain more atrocious crimes which consequently lay waste human society, for example, all kinds of robbery, incest, adultery, and other [ἀθέσμων] lawless crimes; or finally, are of such a kind that their disclosure and report cannot be omitted if the offender is to be reformed or the continuation of the offence prevented. Yet a private citizen should not initiate a report before it is clear that the harm arising from such offences to public society and to the sinner himself cannot be averted by another, more convenient and gentler way. Where no such way appears, justice and the law of charity, by which we are bound to the state and to our brother and to any neighbour, oblige us not to connive at evils of this kind, but rather to direct all our effort and zeal to bring offences of this kind, of which we are rightly aware as committed by others, to the knowledge of those who ought to remedy them by their office. For a greater account must be taken of justice and of the common good and of any innocent person than of the reputation of a criminal man, which is nonetheless harmed purely by chance and through the wrongdoer's own fault.

units.la: XXXIV. Extra hos casus delicta aliorum occulta, nulla præcedente infamia vel suspicione, temerè a quovis propalari & indicari,inprimis si privata & fraterna correctione delinquens emendari possit, vel spes sit, etiam sine ea sponte emendatum iri; non debent. Ille enim, cujus delictum adhuc occultum est, si de cæterο infamia nulla laboret, habet adhuc jus ad famam suam hactenus conservandam,ne temere manifestum fiat. Neque etiam judicis est, occulta quævis scrutari, quia is,ut publica persona,ex publica aliqua notitia,suspicione, vel infamia procedere debet. Inprimis nemo bonus inquisitoris,delatoris aut denuntiatoris, & quasi prætoris atque apparitoris universalis munus sibi ultro arrogare ; nec ipso facto quodvis cujusvis delictum Ecclesiæ, nedum Magistratui aut judicibus denuntiare debet, ne quadruplatoris, proditoris, sycophantæ συκοφάντης[?] crimen incurrat. Contra talem enim etiam Solomonis illud: הולך רכיל מגלה סוד Obtrectator revelat arcanum, Prov. XI. 13. stringit. Probi autem hominis character ibidem statuitur: Qui fidelis est animo, tegit rem. Quo referendum encomium Josephi, tanquam justi,eò quòd Deiparam,quam prægnantem sciverat, παραδειγματίσαι[?] ostentui facere, & palam deferre reformidaverit. Matth. I. 19.
units.tr: XXXIV. Apart from these cases, the hidden offences of others should not be rashly divulged and disclosed by anyone, where there is no prior infamy or suspicion, especially if the offender can be amended by private and brotherly correction, or if there is hope that he will reform spontaneously even without it. For the one whose offence is still hidden, if he is otherwise free from infamy, still has a right to keep his reputation intact so far, so that it is not rashly made public. Nor is it the judge's business to search out any hidden matters, since he, as a public person, ought to proceed from some public knowledge, suspicion, or infamy. Above all, no good man should arrogate to himself the office of informer, accuser, or denouncer, a sort of universal praetor and apparitor, nor, merely by the fact, should he denounce anyone's offence to the Church, much less to the magistrate or judges, lest he incur the charge of a quadruple-informer, betrayer, or sycophant [συκοφάντης]. For against such a person that saying of Solomon applies: הולך רכיל מגלה סוד, A talebearer reveals secrets, Prov. 11:13. The character of an upright man is stated in the same place: He who is faithful in spirit conceals the matter. To this belongs the praise of Joseph, as a just man, because, although he knew Mary to be pregnant, he shrank from making her an example [παραδειγματίσαι] and from denouncing her openly, Matt. 1:19.

units.la: XXXV. Sed de Pastore Ecclesiæ dubitatio incidit, an & ille ad Magistratum civilem delicta & crimina quævis deferre teneatur? Quæ de re non omnes idem sentiunt. Sunt enim; qui id nefas esse abitrentur, quia Pastoris Ecclesiæ & Potestatis Civilis munera prorsus distincta sunt, adeoque Pastor Dei, Christi & Ecclesiæ, non hominum, non Magistratus Civilis minister est. Constat autem delatoris in Republica munus merè civile esse. cujusmodi munera in Personam Pastoris, Regno Christi amplificando, non seculari potestati exornandæ addicti devotiqúe non cadunt. Alii contrà Pastorem Ecclesiæ, utpote Magistratus subditum, ad delationem eorum, quæ contra leges publicè promulgatas committuntur, obligari posse, æquè ac officiales quosvis alios censent. & parum abest, quin, sepositâ[?] omni veneratione sacri ordinis, ad apparitorum & lictorum subsellia eundem relegent. Nos μέσον τέμνειν[?] hac etiam in re potius ducentes, neutri sententiæ, utpote in extremi vitium impingenti utrique, calculum addimus, adeóque mediam potiùs, nec à munere Pastoris Ecclesiæ alienam, & communi subditorum omnium officio congruentem amplectimur.
units.tr: XXXV. But a doubt arises concerning the minister of the Church: whether he too is bound to report to the civil magistrate any offences and crimes whatever? On this matter not all think alike. For some hold that this would be wrong, because the offices of the minister of the Church and of the civil power are wholly distinct, and so the minister is a servant of God, of Christ, and of the Church, not of men or of the civil magistrate. It is agreed, however, that the office of informer in the commonwealth is purely civil, and such offices do not fall to the person of a minister, who is devoted to extending the kingdom of Christ and not to adorning secular power. Others, on the contrary, judge that the minister of the Church, as a subject of the magistrate, can be bound to report those offences which are committed against publicly promulgated laws, just like any other officials, and they come close to sending him off to the benches of the apparitors and lictors, setting aside all reverence for the sacred order. We, however, preferring to take the middle course [μέσον τέμνειν] in this matter too, add our vote to neither opinion, since each falls into the vice of an extreme; and we embrace the middle view, which does not estrange the minister from his office and yet agrees with the common duty of all subjects.

units.la: XXXVI. Duplex ante omnia via est, per quam delicta atque crimina in Pastoris notitiam venire possunt; alia communis, per revelationem aliorum, vel notitiam propriam: alia singularis, per confessionem vel revelationem privatam ipsius delinquentis, qui peccati commissi conscientia anxius institutionem & consolationem quærit. Quod ad peccata, quæ communi via ad notitiam Pastoris veniunt, οἰκεῖον[?] & proprium Pastoris, quâ talis, munus est, non illa ad Magistratum, civili pœnâ coërcenda, deferre, sed suo potiùs foro Divino Ministeriali, vel Ecclesiastico, prout ratio delicti fert, subjicere. Est enim Minister reconciliationis cum Deo, atque in id potissimùm incumbere debet, ut peccator in peccati sui agnitionem & detestationem perduci, & ad ejusdem per fidem veram in Christum, atque pœnitentiam salutarem, gratuitam condonationem, conscientiæ tranquillitatem, & Divinæ gratiæ sensum pertingere valeat. Quo officio proprio neglecto, qui ad delationem & seculi brachium præcipitat, næ is, non Pastor est, sed prævaricator & proditor, ovem suam lupo mactat, & securus atque otiosus interitum ejusdem quo ad animam & corpus intuetur. qua equidem impietate nulla alia major esse potest. Estque haud postremum Sathanæ, qui, ceu indefessus insidiator, & veterator maximus, dolos suos astu colit, stratagema, quo is Ecclesiæ Pastoribus, ut cum ovium sibi commissarum præsentissimo exitio licet, tempus suum in otio, ἀσελγείᾳ[?] & carnali securitate consumere & comburere valeant, persuadet, belle eos officio suo defunctos esse, dummodo oves suas seculari brachio immolent, & civilibus pœnis, quæ non tam ad salutarem cordis compunctionem, quàm loculorum subinde emunctionem valent, objiciant. Sic enim tum peccator ipse in peccato suo manet, neque ad regenerationem salutarem ullatenus promovetur: tum Pastor & ovi suæ terribilis atque invisus evadit, & ipse tandem, neglectæ salutis ovium suarum damnas, esurienti Sathanæ in victimam opimam cedit.
units.tr: XXXVI. First of all, there is a twofold way by which offences and crimes can come to the minister's notice: one common, through the disclosure of others or his own knowledge; the other particular, through the confession or private disclosure of the offender himself, who, anxious in his awareness of the sin he has committed, seeks instruction and comfort. As for sins which come to the minister's notice by the common way, it is the proper [οἰκεῖον] and peculiar function of the minister, as such, not to report them to the magistrate for civil punishment, but rather to submit them to his own ministerial or ecclesiastical forum, as the nature of the offence requires. For he is a minister of reconciliation with God, and he ought above all to labour so that the sinner may be brought to acknowledge and detest his sin, and may attain, through true faith in Christ and saving repentance, free forgiveness, tranquillity of conscience, and a sense of divine grace. If he neglects this proper office and rushes instead to delation and the arm of the secular power, then he is not a minister but a prevaricator and traitor; he sacrifices his sheep to the wolf and, secure and idle, looks on at their destruction in soul and body. No impiety can be greater than this. And it is no small stratagem of Satan, who, like a tireless ambusher and most experienced old campaigner, cultivates his wiles with cunning, to persuade the ministers of the Church that, while their sheep committed to them are in the greatest danger of perishing, they may spend and waste their time in idleness, wantonness [ἀσελγείᾳ], and carnal security, provided they sacrifice their sheep to the secular arm and expose them to civil penalties, which serve less for the salutary contrition of the heart than for the repeated emptying of purses. For in this way the sinner himself remains in his sin and is in no way advanced to salutary regeneration; and the minister becomes terrible and hateful to his own sheep, and at last, having neglected the salvation of his sheep, he yields himself as a rich victim to the hungry Satan.

units.la: XXXVII. Illud vero animo nostro alte infixum sit oportet, disparatas plane Ecclesiastici & Politici muneris partes esse. Magistratus enim cum circa externam in Ecclesia disciplinam versetur, politicum eatenus & externum officium exercet, ut justus & legitimus ordo in humana societate instituatur & conservetur, Ministerium contra circa conscientias potissimum, & illa, quæ ad animarum & conscientiarum sanctificationem requiruntur, versatur, adeoque Legis & Evangelii prædicatio & applicatione ad conscientias hominem totum æternum salvare nititur. Cum ergo in sanctis, dum peregrinantur a Domino, duplex homo fit, exterior & interior, politica administratio circa exteriorem, Ecclesiastica circa interiorem potissimum occupata est. Tum leges, quarum custos & exactor Ecclesiæ Pastor est, Dei & Christi leges sunt, sublimes in primis & spirituales. Magistratus vero leges ab hominibus sancitæ, societati externæ in officio continendæ providen t. Aliæ certe Christi, aliæ Cæsaris leges sunt: aliter Paulus, aliter Papinianus loquitur: ac longe plura in Cœlestis, quam in terrenæ civitatis cive requiruntur. Sed & præmia legum observantibus, atque pœnæ immorigeris, decretæ plurimum discrepant. Pastor Ecclesiæ pœnitentibus, & in viis Dei ambulantibus interna, spiritualia, & æterna bona promittit, tanquam spiritus & reconciliationis Minister; incredulis vero & impœnitentibus per fulmineos terrores & comminationes legis, gravissimè imminet, & spiritus gladium adversus eosdem strenuè vibrat. Magistratus contra obedientiam & fidelitatem muneribus, dignitatibus, locupletationibus, aliisque corporalibus præmiis remuneratur, & in contumaces atque immorigeros corporali gladio animadvertit, ultor ad malum ei, qui malum patraverit: ac ne pœnitentibus quidem parcit, vel indulget, sed pro delicti ratione pœnam ἀπαρακλήτως exigit, ut universus populus audiat & timeat, nec addat facere aliquid simile rei pessimæ, Num.XXXV.31. Deut.XIII.8.11. XIX.13. In disciplinæ quoque praxi & exercitio eatenus differunt, quòd Pastor Ecclesiæ externa obedientia & gubernatione locomotivæ, quam Magistratus urget, neutiquam contentus, conscientiis homihominum, regenerationi, verae pietatis exercitiis, & internis cordis motibus insistit, omnium primo & potissimum, quod intra poculum & patinam est, purgari per Dei gratiam curat; lapsos quoscunque haud temere differt, traducit, Magistratui, ut facultatum, existimationis aut vitae jacturam faciant, prodit, sed, quantum fieri potest, ac debet, delicta illorum occultat, lapsorum resipiscentiae per continuas admonitiones, correptiones, consolationes, quanto potest studio intentus, & ejusdem peractae manifestos in gratiam recipit: atque hoc fere modo Ministerii sui partes implet. Magistratus contra, si quid scelerum in subditis subodoretur, sine praeviis praemonitionibus reum χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν[?] adoritur, neque resipiscentiae lapsorum rationem ullam habet, scelera propalat, leges suas quocunque vult, rigore exercet. Ita quem resipiscentem latronem in gratiam suam Christus in cruce recepit, juste tamen judex Politicus crucifigere perrexit, Luc.XXIII. 40. Quin & cessante politico judicio, non illico Ecclesiasticum cessat, si qui poenas dedit, resipuisse nondum videatur. Praeterea qui in civilibus, & sacrorum externo ordine Ecclesiae praeest, & dominatur Magistratus, idem in spiritualibus verbo, quod Pastor Ecclesiae in ore fert, & ex revelatione Divina profert, in conscientia subjicitur. Neque enim Ministerium Ecclesiasticum Magistratui civili ita subalternum & ὑπηρετικὸν[?] est, ut in officii sui administratione ab hoc pendeat, aut ab eo vim & authoritatem sui muneris habeat, quae a solo Christo, cui omnis in Coelo & terra potestas data est, dependet. Est sane Magistratus non tranquillitatis tantum publicae in rebus corporalibus, sed pietatis etiam in spiritualibus in Ecclesia custos; sed custos tantum, non dominus; qui praescriptas habet hujus custodiae metas, cancellos & limites. De quo alibi fusius.
units.tr: XXXVII. It must be firmly fixed in our minds that the parts of the ecclesiastical office and the political office are clearly distinct. The magistrate, since he is concerned with external discipline in the Church, exercises a political and external office, so far as a just and lawful order is established and maintained in human society. The ministry, on the other hand, is concerned chiefly with consciences and with what is required for the sanctification of souls and consciences, and so by the preaching of Law and Gospel and their application to consciences it strives to save the whole man eternally. Therefore, since in the saints, while they are sojourning away from the Lord, the man becomes twofold, outward and inward, political administration is occupied chiefly with the outward, and ecclesiastical administration chiefly with the inward. The laws whose guardian and enforcer the minister of the Church is are the laws of God and Christ, sublime above all and spiritual. The laws enacted by men, which the magistrate provides, serve to keep external society in its duty. Certainly some laws are Christ's and others are Caesar's: Paul speaks one way, Papinian another; and far more is required of a citizen of the heavenly city than of an earthly one. Also, the rewards decreed for those who observe the laws and the penalties for the disobedient differ greatly. The minister of the Church, as minister of the Spirit and of reconciliation, promises the penitent and those who walk in the ways of God inward, spiritual and eternal goods; but to unbelievers and the impenitent he threatens most severely through the thunderbolts of terror and the threats of the Law, and vigorously brandishes the sword of the Spirit against them. The magistrate, on the contrary, rewards obedience and fidelity with offices, dignities, enrichments and other bodily rewards, and punishes the stubborn and disobedient with the bodily sword, being an avenger to bring wrath upon him who does evil. Nor does he spare or indulge even the penitent, but exacts punishment for the offence according to its nature without consolation [ἀπαρακλήτως], so that the whole people may hear and fear, and not add to do any such wicked thing, Num. 35.31; Deut. 13.8, 11; 19.13. The practice and exercise of discipline also differ in this respect: the minister of the Church, not content with external obedience and the outward governance that the magistrate enforces, attends to consciences, regeneration, the exercises of true piety and the inward movements of the heart. First and above all he takes care, by the grace of God, that what is within the cup and dish be cleansed. He does not lightly hand over or betray the fallen to the magistrate, to their loss of property, reputation or life; as far as can and should be done, he conceals their offences. Intent with all the zeal he can muster, he works for the repentance of the fallen through continual admonitions, rebukes and consolations, and when that repentance is evident he receives them back into grace. In this way he generally fulfils the parts of his ministry. The magistrate, on the contrary, if he suspects any crimes in his subjects, attacks the accused without prior warning and without mercy [χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν], takes no account at all of the repentance of the fallen, publicises the crimes and enforces his laws with rigour as he pleases. Thus the political judge, though Christ received the repentant thief into his grace on the cross, went on to crucify him, Luke 23.40 (as printed). Moreover, when the political judgment ceases, the ecclesiastical judgment does not cease at once, if one who has paid the penalty does not yet appear to have repented. Furthermore, the magistrate who presides and rules in civil matters and in the external order of sacred things in the Church is himself subject in conscience, in spiritual matters, to the word that the minister of the Church bears in his mouth and utters from divine revelation. The ecclesiastical ministry is not so subordinate and subservient [ὑπηρετικόν] to the civil magistrate that in the administration of its office it depends on him or has from him the force and authority of its function. That depends on Christ alone, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given. The magistrate is indeed a guardian in the Church not only of public tranquillity in bodily matters but also of piety in spiritual matters; yet he is only a guardian, not a lord, and he has prescribed limits, bars and boundaries for this guardianship. Of this more fully elsewhere.

units.la: XXXVIII. Hæc vero cum ita sint, manifestum est, Pastorem Ecclesiae adeo eximium & proprium habere munus, ut civili administrationi implicari non possit, nec, quod imperiosi quidam Politici pertendere solent, eundem cum juratis, aut specialiter vocatis Magistratus ministris funem ducere debeat. Aliena proin ab ejusdem munere est delatio civilis, qua delicta quaevis adversus publicas leges admissa ad judicem civilem, ex imposito peculiari officio deferuntur, utpote quae executioni legum civilium directe inservit. Et perinde est in hoc foro delatoris partes ex speciali vocatione obire, ac fisci procurationem suscipere, Praefecti, Subpraefecti, aliorúmque ejusmodi officialium munere defungi. Quod equidem tam alienum esse à Ministro Ecclesiæ debet, quàm alienum à suo munere esse judicavit Christus, Dominus ipse, qui mulierem in adulterio deprehensam non tantùm non judicavit, sed ne detulit quidem, satis habens, his verbis suadere pœnitentiam: Vade, & amplius non pecca. Joh. VIII.11.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Since these things are so, it is plain that the minister of the Church has an office so distinguished and proper to himself that it cannot be entangled in civil administration, nor ought he to draw a line with sworn or specially called ministers of the magistrate, as certain domineering politicians are accustomed to demand. Civil informing, by which any offences committed against public laws are reported to the civil judge by a specially imposed duty, is therefore foreign to his office, since it serves directly the execution of the civil laws. And in this forum it is just the same for the informer to discharge the duties of a special calling, as for a man to take on the office of the treasury or to perform the functions of a prefect, sub-prefect or other officials of that kind. This ought to be as foreign to the minister of the Church as it was judged foreign to his office by Christ the Lord himself, who did not merely refrain from condemning the woman taken in adultery, but did not even report her, being content to urge repentance with these words: Go, and sin no more. John 8.11.

units.la: Sed & Ecclesiæ & fidelium ædificationi, atque saluti plurimùm oberit, si Ecclesiæ Pastor huic officio se patiatur obstringi, tum quia ignavi Pastores, neglectis muneris proprii partibus præcipuis, delatione ad alios facta, molestiam homines per spiritualia remedia corrigendi, & regenerationem salutaribus remediis promovendi, facilè deponent, omnémque curam in sæculare brachium, cujus pœnæ quamvis atroces parùm ad conversionem salutarem valent, devolvent: tum quia Pastores optimi etiam, si deferendi ossicium in se susceperint, ovibus suis plerisque adeò exosos & contemptibiles se reddere poterunt, ut spiritualis animarum negotiatio præsens detrimentum patiatur: tum quia Pastoribus mercenariis isthoc munere ad turpem quæstum, & commodorum atque incommodorum suorum supputationes abuti, proclivè erit. Ne dicam, hac etiam ratione fieri posse, ut politicorum delatorum, à Magistratu institutorum, in munere eo obeundo fides & industria vehementer languescat, dum à ministris illis meticulosis, negligentibus vel perfidis in Pastoris humeros totum isthoc negotium devolvitur; tandemque stertentibus, dormitantibus, & alia omnia agentibus illis, quorum hæ præcipuæ & propriæ partes erant, universalis morum corruptio Ecclesiæ Pastoribus solis, non sine eorundem infamia, Ecclesiæ ludibrio & nequitiæ vel prævaricationis Ministrorum Politicorum, qui amant [illegible, ~10 letters], & subinde etiam Pastoribus populi invidiam & odium concire, fraudulenta occultatione, imputetur. Denique nihil propius est, quàm ut munus isthoc deferendi diversi adeò generis hominibus impositum in universum negligatur, atque civilis disciplina frigescat plané, & tantùm non intermoriatur. Dum enim certamen hoc inter diversi ordinis homines gliscit, neutri officio suo bona fide defunguntur, & neglecti officii culpam alii aliis impingunt, non sine disciplinæ publicæ certissima clade. Experientia enim omni testatum habemus, periclitari & dispergi gregem, cùm plurium, nedum diversorum custodum cura regitur.
units.tr: But it would also greatly harm the building up and the salvation of the Church and the faithful if the minister of the Church allowed himself to be bound to this office. For, first, idle ministers, neglecting the chief parts of their own office and handing the matter over to others by informing, will readily give up the trouble of correcting men by spiritual remedies and of promoting regeneration by salutary remedies, and will roll all their care onto the secular arm, whose punishments, however atrocious, are of little use for salutary conversion. Second, even the best ministers, if they take upon themselves the duty of informing, could make themselves so hateful and contemptible to most of their sheep that the spiritual business of souls would suffer present loss. Third, it would be easy for mercenary ministers to abuse this office for base gain and for calculations of their own advantage and disadvantage. Not to mention that by this arrangement it could happen that the faithfulness and diligence of political informers appointed by the magistrate grow very slack in performing that office, while the whole matter is rolled onto the shoulders of the minister by those timid, negligent or faithless officials; and at last, while those whose chief and proper duties these were are snoring, dozing and doing everything else, universal moral corruption is imputed to the ministers of the Church alone, not without their infamy, to the mockery of the Church, and by a fraudulent concealment to the wickedness or prevarication of the political ministers, who love [illegible] and sometimes also stir up popular envy and hatred against the ministers. Finally, nothing is nearer than that this duty of informing, laid upon men of such different kinds, should be utterly neglected in general, and civil discipline should grow completely cold and all but die out. For while this contest between men of different orders grows hot, neither side discharges its duty in good faith, and each lays the blame for neglected duty on the other, not without the most certain ruin of public discipline. Experience has taught us all that the flock is endangered and scattered when it is ruled by the care of many guardians, let alone of different ones.

units.la: XXXIX. Neque obstat, quòd leges quædam publicæ, in executione earundem promovenda, Pastores Ecclesiae cum civilibus Ministris & delatoribus conjungunt.
