Id enim, ne cum iis, quae hactenus diximus, pugnet & confusionem apertam munerum inducat, cum grano salis accipi debet, ut sensus sit, in ἀγωγῇ[?] seu executione legum civilium suas etiam partes Ecclesiae Pastores habere, ut & publicè & privatim populo obedientiam erga Magistratum & leges ejusdem, quatenus pietati & honestati non repugnant, serio atque assiduè commendent; & praefractos atque immorigeros, qui obdurata in impudentiam fronte peccant, Ecclesiae foro, & clavium sibi commissarum potestati subjiciant, quin & pro re nata, eo quem supra indigetavimus, ordine ad Magistratum deferant. Qua in re plurimùm delatorum Politicorum & Pastorum Ecclesiae delationes differunt. Illis enim ex officio, quod illis impositum est, singula delicta, in leges publicas quascunque arietantia, manifesta & occulta, immediate & sine admonitione praevia ad Magistratum deferre incumbit: hi nec manifesta ex officio speciali sine praemonitione immediatè, nec occulta, quorum etiam extra confessionem conscientiam habent, quaevis, inprimis si de resipiscentia seria peccatoris constet, Ecclesiae, nedum Magistratui denuntiare tenentur, usque dum peccator obstinatione sua ansam dederit propalandi, & ordine justo ad Magistratus conscientiam perducendi, quae hactenus occultata in Pastoris Divino Ministeriali, & Ecclesiastico foro & sinu delituerant.
units.tr: XXXIX. Nor does it stand in the way that certain public laws join the ministers of the Church with civil officials and informers in promoting their execution. For this, lest it conflict with what we have said so far and introduce a plain confusion of offices, must be understood with a grain of salt, to mean that the ministers of the Church also have their own part in the conduct or execution of the civil laws: that they earnestly and constantly commend obedience to the magistrate and his laws to the people, both publicly and privately, so far as these do not conflict with piety and honesty; and that they subject the stubborn and disobedient, who sin with a brow hardened into impudence, to the forum of the Church and to the power of the keys committed to them, and indeed, as the occasion arises, report them to the magistrate in the order indicated above. In this matter the reports of political informers and those of the ministers of the Church differ greatly. For political informers are bound by the duty imposed on them to report to the magistrate, immediately and without prior admonition, each single offence against any public laws, both manifest and hidden. The ministers, however, are not bound to report to the Church, let alone to the magistrate, what is manifest by special office immediately and without prior admonition, nor what is hidden, of which they have knowledge even apart from confession, especially if the serious repentance of the sinner is clear; they are bound only until the sinner, by his obstinacy, gives occasion for it to be disclosed, and in due order brings it to the knowledge of the magistrate. Until then these things, hidden in the Divine ministerial and ecclesiastical forum and bosom of the minister, had lain concealed.

units.la: XL. Atque haec causa est, quòd Ampl. Magistratus nostri leges publicae, die 25. Junii A. MDCXXXVI. rogatae, & typis publicis exscriptae, Pastoribus quidem Ecclesiae aequè ac aliis officialibus iniungunt, ut in crimine adulterii & scortationis fideli & diligenti observatione defungantur (ihr getreu fleissigs aufsehen habind) ut quotquot criminum illorum manifesti sunt, locis convenientibus deferantur (an gebührenden orten gemeldet und geleidet werdind) cùm locus Pastoris delationi conveniens sit Consistorium, seu Confessus Ecclesiae, ex quo ulterior delatio pro re nata per Magistratus officiales institui debet: sub finem tamen delationum promiscuum, & ex officio nonnisi Politicos[?] (ein jeder under uns bey seinen Regi- mentspflichten) & specialiter in Urbe octo Ephoris, qui foro censorio praesunt, in agro Praefectis, Subpraefectis & reliquis officialibus (Nachgesetzten) injungunt. Neque etiam aliter interpretari fas est ea, quae Epitome & declaratio Magni, uti vocatur, Mandati, die 17. Nov.A. MDCLXXX. conclusa,& typis vulgata,sub finem,de Ministrorum Ecclesiæ debita delatione (verpflichteter leidung) habet. Debita enim Pastorum Ecclesiæ delatio ea demum intelligitur, quæ muneri eorum Ecclesiastico convenit; quam ab ea, quæ officialibus Magistratus convenit, haud parum discrepare, liquidò constat.
units.tr: XL. This is why our honourable Magistrate's public laws, drawn up and printed on 25 June 1636, charge the ministers of the Church, like the other officials, to carry out their duty with faithful and diligent watch (<bl>ihr getreu fleissigs aufsehen habind</bl>) over adultery and fornication, so that all such crimes that become known are reported in the proper places (<bl>an gebührenden orten gemeldet und geleidet werdind</bl>). The proper place for a minister's report is the Consistory, or the assembly of the Church, from which further reporting is to be made by the magistrate's officials as the case requires. Toward the end, however, the laws impose the general and ex officio reporting of such matters on the political officials (<bl>ein jeder under uns bey seinen Regimentspflichten</bl>), and specifically in the city on the eight Ephors who preside over the censorial court, and in the countryside on the Prefects, Subprefects and other lower officials (<bl>Nachgesetzten</bl>). Nor can the phrase "due reporting" (<bl>verpflichteter leidung</bl>) in the Epitome and Declaration of the so-called Great Mandate, concluded and printed on 17 November 1680, be read otherwise. For the "due reporting" by the Church's ministers is rightly understood only as that which suits their ecclesiastical office, and it is plain that this differs considerably from the reporting that suits the magistrate's officials.

units.la: XLI. Tametsi verò speciale & proprium munus delationis delinquentium ad forum politicum, Pastorum Ecclesiæ humeris malè sedet; non ideo tamen iis assentimur, qui quadam ἀμελεία[?] τῆς ἀνθολκῆς peccantes, nullam omnino delationem Pastoribus Ecclesiæ convenire pertendunt. Etenim primò Pastorum Ecclesiæ est tum in Synodis, tum extra eas, quoties necessitas & usus postulat, generales saltem delationes & querimonias ad Magistratum instituere de peccatis & scandalis publicè in populo grassantibus, tum ut eum ad officium resistendi peccatis atque scandalis, & leges suas severius exercendi, vel earum rigorem, crescentibus delictis, intendendi, excitent: tum ut in certis casibus ejusdem consilio & auxilio utantur. Sunt nempe duæ hæ administrationes, Politica & Ecclesiastica, distinctæ licet, quodammodo tamen etiam ἀντίστροφοι[?], & variis modis circa eadem objecta versantes, auxiliares sibi manus porrigunt, consiliorúmque adeò & operarum conjunctionem postulant, Hinc Deus Mosen & Aharonem,& post hunc,Eleazarum filium conjunxit, vel conjunctim cum iis, in rebus Ecclesiam & Politicam spestantibus, locutus est, Exod.XII 1. Levit. IX. 1, XI. 1. XIII.1. XV.1o[?] Num.II.1. IV.1, XIX.1. XX.23. XXVI.1. Atque hi etiam sua conjunctim sæpe tractarunt, mutuasque sibi operas præstiterunt & tradiderunt, uti ex Exod. V. 1. Num. I. 17. XIV. 5. Num. XXVII. 2, XXXII.2. aliisque locis liquet. Secundo Ecclesiæ Pastorem haud omnino decet delatio delinquentium mediata illa, quam juxta disciplinæ apud nos receptæ praxin, post adhibitos ejusdem gradus, Ecclesiam apud Magistratum instituere,supra § XXXI. diximus. Delationem verò Pastoris mediatam dixi, quia non ipse Pastor, sed juratus quispiam nomine Pastoris & Consistorii eadem defungi tenetur, juxta tenorem etiam legis nostræ Consistorialis decimæ septimæ, qua officium illud delinquentes nomine Consistorii Ecclesiastici diserte Subpraefectis, Praetoribus & Juratis ( den Untervögten / Weibel und Geschwornen ) demandat. Tertio Pastores Ecclesiæ ad eam etiam delationem sive mediatam, sive, si necessitas exigat, immediatam obligantur, ad quam quoslibet cives & privatos, nulla speciali vocatione ad id obstrictos, obligari, § XXXVII. [?] diximus. Neque enim profundo silentio premere potest עונות פלילים [?] pravitates judiciales (Job.XXXI.11.28.) hoc est, delicta quaedam, quae vel patrata jam, vel patranda noscuntur, & quae juxta leges non humanas duntaxat, sed Divinas etiam severè propter publicam utilitatem vindicari patrata, & patranda impediri debent, cujusmodi sunt illa, quae vel immediatè sive Dei Majestatem & gloriam laedunt, sive humanam Majestatem & Societatem vastant, vel mediatè in publicam perniciem tendunt, vel graviter innocentem quemvis laedunt. Communia enim charitatis erga Rempublicam, Ecclesiam, proximum quemvis officia aequè Pastorem Ecclesiae, ac quemvis civem & privatum obligant; si non magis, cùm in omnibus typus gregis esse debeat.
units.tr: XLI. Although the special and proper duty of reporting offenders to the political court sits badly on the shoulders of the Church's ministers, we nevertheless do not agree with those who, through a certain negligence [ἀμελεία] of the counter-hauling [ἀνθολκῆς], contend that no reporting at all belongs to the ministers of the Church. For, first, it is the duty of the Church's ministers, both within and outside the Synods, whenever necessity and custom require, to bring before the Magistrate at least general reports and complaints about sins and scandals rife among the people in public. They do this so that the Magistrate may be stirred to resist sins and scandals, to exercise his laws more severely, or to tighten their rigour as crimes multiply, and so that the ministers may in certain cases use his counsel and help. These two administrations, the political and the ecclesiastical, are indeed distinct, yet in a way also reciprocal [ἀντίστροφοι], and, working on the same objects in various ways, they stretch out helping hands to one another and require a joining of counsel and labour. Hence God joined Moses and Aaron, and after him Eleazar the son of Aaron, or spoke to them jointly in matters concerning both Church and polity (Exod. 12:1; Lev. 9:1; 11:1; 13:1; 15:1; Num. 2:1; 4:1; 19:1; 20:23; 26:1). These men also often handled their business together and rendered and gave each other mutual service, as is clear from Exod. 5:1; Num. 1:17; 14:5; Num. 27:2; 32:2, and other places. Secondly, it is not wholly fitting for a minister of the Church to report offenders in that mediated way which, according to the practice of discipline received among us, the Church is to carry out before the Magistrate after the steps of that discipline have been taken, as we said above in §31. We call the minister's report "mediated" because the minister himself is not the one to perform it, but some sworn person is bound to do so in the name of the minister and the Consistory, in keeping with the terms of our Consistorial law of the seventeenth chapter, which expressly assigns this duty of reporting offenders in the name of the Ecclesiastical Consistory to the Subprefects, Praetors and sworn men (<bl>den Untervögten / Weibel und Geschwornen</bl>). Thirdly, the Church's ministers are bound to that reporting, whether mediated, or, if necessity demands, immediate, to which we said in §37 that any citizens and private persons, not bound to it by any special calling, are obliged. For the "judicial iniquities" [עונות פלילים] (Job 31:11, 28), that is, certain offences already committed or known to be about to be committed, cannot be passed over in deep silence. By laws not merely human but also Divine, these must be severely punished for the public good once committed, and prevented while still in prospect. Such are those offences which either directly wound the majesty and glory of God, or lay waste human majesty and society, or tend indirectly to public ruin, or gravely injure any innocent person. For the common duties of love toward the commonwealth, the Church and any neighbour bind the minister of the Church equally with any citizen and private person, if not more so, since in all things the minister ought to be a pattern for the flock.

units.la: Quaecunque ergo non delata publicum exitium post se trahunt, vel propter singularem atrocitatem criminis in Dei gloriam & Societatis humanae detrimentum incurrunt; cujusmodi sunt blasphemiae horrendae, crimina atrociora, à quibus natura ipsa abhorret; perduellionis, proditionis, conspirationis adversus Magistratum legitimum nefas, patrata vel patranda caedes proximi, aliáque ejusmodi, quae & quatenus ad judicem deferri punienda vel impedienda gloriae Dei, Reipublicae, & ipsius delinquentis interest, eorum denuntiatio à Pastore aeque ac quovis alio salva conscientia omitti non potest, & omissa ignis instar est, qui in sinum assumi, & in eodem retineri illaesis vestimentis nequit, Prov.VI.27. Quod ipsum etiam leges nostrae Patriae adversus Pensionarios, uti vocantur, Reipublicae pestes, sancitae his verbis sciscunt: So aber jemand der sachen (daß jemand pensionen nähme) allein wüssen hätte/und das einem Burgermeister/bynend/ wie er zuthun schuldig/nit läidete/und fürbrachte/der sol seiner ehren entsetzt/&c. hoc est, Si quis (nullo ordinis & status discrimine) solus conscius fuerit (hunc vel illum pensiones admisisse) atque id ad Consulem sub juramento, quo ei tenetur, non detulerit, dignitate sua omni abdicabitur, & centum florenorum multam dabit. Sic tamen crimina ejusmodi Pastor judici denuntiabit, ut ipse interim conversionis criminosi curam neutiquam abdicet, sed primore velut loco, ceu sibi eximiam, occupet.
units.tr: Therefore, whatever crimes do not bring public ruin upon themselves but nonetheless incur danger to God's glory and to the detriment of human society because of their singular atrocity, such as horrible blasphemies and the most heinous crimes, at which nature itself shudders; treason, betrayal, and conspiracy against the lawful magistrate; a murder of a neighbour that has been committed or is being planned; and other crimes of this kind, which, insofar as it serves the glory of God, the Commonwealth, and the offender himself that they be reported to the judge so that they may be punished or prevented, cannot with a clear conscience be left unreported by a minister any more than by anyone else. If they are left unreported, such silence is like fire, which cannot be taken into the bosom and kept there without the clothes being burned, Prov. 6.27. Our own country's laws likewise decree this very thing against the Pensionaries, as they are called, the plagues of the Commonwealth, in these words: "But if anyone who knows of the matter (that someone took pensions) alone, and does not report it and bring it to a burgomaster, as he is bound to do, shall be deprived of his honour, etc." That is: If anyone (without distinction of rank or station) alone is aware (that this or that man has admitted pensions), and does not report it to the Consul under the oath by which he is bound, he shall be stripped of all his dignity and shall pay a fine of one hundred florins. In this way, however, the minister shall report such crimes to the judge, yet meanwhile he shall by no means give up the care of the offender's conversion, but shall take it up first and foremost, as something especially his own.

units.la: XLII. Quantum vero ad delicta occulta, graviora etiam, sive jam patrata, sive patranda, quae soli Pastori, vel paucis, non ex ipso reo, sed aliunde cognita Dei gloriam & Rempublicam enormiter non laedunt, ad illa deferenda & temere propalanda Pastor Ecclesiae non magis, quàm quivis privatus alius, obligatur. De quo §. XXXIV. dicta huc revocanda sunt. Propalatio occultorum scandalum parit. Illud vero, ceu Ecclesiæ noxium, vitari, quantum fieri potest, debet, adhibitis gradibus, quos Christus ipse Matth.XVIII.15. &c. præscripsit. Eodem faciunt argumenta, quibus delationis ossicium à Pastore supra removimus.
units.tr: XLII. As for secret offences, even grave ones, whether already committed or about to be committed, which are known only to the minister or to a few, and known not from the offender himself but from elsewhere, and which do not enormously injure God's glory or the commonwealth, the Church's minister is no more bound to report and rashly disclose these than any other private person. On this, what was said in §34 must be recalled here. The disclosure of secrets gives rise to scandal, and that, as harmful to the Church, must be avoided as far as possible, by observing the steps which Christ himself prescribed in Matt. 18:15 ff. The same arguments by which we removed the duty of reporting from the minister above apply here.

units.la: XLIII. Providè igitur Serenissimi Electoris Brandenburgici Friderici Wilhelmi, Seculi nostri Herculis, Constitutiones Ecclesiasticæ Marcanæ & Clivenses, sic § 136. sanciunt: Die jenige betreffend/ welche in lehr oder leben irren / und unrichtig wandlen / deren sünde und fehler doch noch zur zeit verborgen wären/sollen die Prediger auch verborgen seyn lassen/ihnen aber ihre sünden vorhalten/und davon abzustehen sie fleissig in aller stille vermahnen; hoc est, Quantum ad illos, qui in doctrina vel vita errant, & inordinate ambulant, quorum peccata tamen & errores occulti adhuc sunt, eorum (peccata & errores) Pastores Ecclesiæ in occulto latere sinant, ita tamen, ut eadem peccata illis exprobrent, & eosdem, ut iis abstineant, diligenter magnoque cum silentio admoneant. Cui Sanctioni conformis est Ampl. Magistratus nostri lex Consistorialis vicesima secunda, qua Pastori Ecclesiæ potestas conceditur, peccatores sibi singulariter notos vel indicatos seorsim accersendi, & eosdem salutari admonitione corrigendi (durch die Oberfeitliche Still stands-ordnung sol einem Pfarzer nicht benommen seyn / die jenige/ so ihm sonderbar bekannt sind / oder gemacht worden / sonderbar zubeschicken /und mit heilsamem zusprechen zuverbesserẽ.) Estque hæc, nisi fallor Ecclesiarum Protestantium constans & perpetua praxis, adeò ut ne Gallicanæ quidem Ecclesiæ,cùm imperio heterodoxo & tyrannico adhuc obnoxiæ fuissent, ad occulta ejusmodi, quatenus statum publicum non feriebant,reseranda obstrictæ fuerint.
units.tr: XLIII. Therefore the Ecclesiastical Ordinances of the Most Serene Elector of Brandenburg, Frederick William, the Hercules of our age, for the Marks and Cleves, providently decree in §136: "As for those who err in doctrine or life and walk amiss, whose sins and faults are still hidden for the time being, the preachers shall also let them remain hidden, but shall set their sins before them and diligently admonish them in quiet to abstain from these." That is: As for those who err in doctrine or life and walk inordinately, whose sins and errors are as yet hidden, the ministers of the Church shall let them lie hidden in secret, yet in such a way that they reproach them for those same sins and diligently and with great quietness admonish them to abstain from them. The law of our most illustrious Magistrate, the twenty-second Consistorial law, conforms to this sanction, by which the power is granted to a minister of the Church to summon privately those sinners who are singularly known to him or pointed out to him, and to correct them with wholesome admonition. (Under the official ordinance of silence, a pastor shall not be forbidden to summon privately those who are particularly known to him or have been pointed out to him, and to correct them with wholesome exhortation.) And this, unless I am mistaken, is the constant and perpetual practice of the Protestant Churches, so much so that not even the Gallican Churches, while they were still subject to a heterodox and tyrannical government, were bound to disclose such hidden matters, insofar as they did not strike at the public state.

units.la: XLIV. Sed fortè Pastor Ecclesiæ officii sui in corripiendis pro suggestu etiam peccatoribus & scandalis, tum à populo, tum à Magistratu ipso manantibus, palàm pulsandis & corrigendis partes obire non poterit, nisi scandalorum illorum authores σημειῶν notare, & ad Magistratum etiam deferre velit & possit. Hoc scilicet illud est,quod à Pastoribus exigere quandóque audent illi, qui correptionis impatientes, ægrè ferunt, imò ringuntur, cùm in publica scandala,perjuria inprimis,dorophagiam,nefarias artes, capitalem injustitiam,aliáque ejusmodi palam & impunè grassantia, Ecclesiæ Ministri pro suggestu detonant. Nos quidem probare non possumus Ministros illos [?], suae & alienæ salutis prodigos, qui monitionibus, correptionibus, & obtestationibus privatis & secretis, per quas quorumvis hominum, adeóque potentum etiam conscientiae & saluti, imò publicae etiam incolumitati haud parùm equidem consuli potest, ob metum hominum, vel socordiam etiam supinam neglectis, ad [illegible, ~9 letters] & Philippicas publicas coram toto populo audacter prosiliunt, & cum Chamo parentum etiam verenda impiè exponunt & prostituunt. Si tamen nil privatae commonefactiones & correptiones profecerint, & scandala insuper publica fuerint, atque ex peccantium etiam audacia & multitudine vires & incrementa sumpserint, ut jam de salute Ecclesiae & Reipublicae conclamari incipiat; illa pro suggestu produci, notari, populo lugenda & detestanda proponi, nulla praevia, vel subsequente etiam peccantium personarum ad Magistratum delatione, debere, nulli profecto dubitamus. Aliud enim est accusatio civilis, quae de sententia Ciceronis etiam crimen desiderat, rem, ut definiat, hominem, ut notet, argumento probet, teste confirmet: aliud Ecclesiastica correptio. Illa sontis poenam & satisfactionem cum intendat atque postulet, à personae definitione abstinere non potest. Haec quia peccatoris pudorem, compunctionem & salutem, scandali publici reparationem, Reipublicae & Ecclesiae incolumitatem unicè quaerit, atque in Ecclesiastico insuper, non civili foro versatur, locum, non designatis, nedum ad Magistratum delatis peccatoribus, habere potest. Nam & peccator, de cujus correctione publica agitur, licet non notatus, vel delatus à Pastore, peccati admissi sibi conscius, ad poenitentiam sic adduci: & Ecclesia, quae si non personarum peccantium, at detrimenti publici, quod ex peccatis ejusmodi patitur, conscientiam habet, lugere, ad Deum suspirare, & à scandalo sanari, nec notato, nec delato pariter peccatore, potest. Atque sic absque delatione etiam tali Ecclesiastica correptio finem suum assequitur. Praeterea Ecclesiae Pastores [Hebrew, ~1 word: צֹפִים[?]] speculatores Ezech. III. 17[?]. cluent. Atqui speculatores (ita similitudinem istam quondam Ecclesiae cujuspiam Helvetiae [illegible, ~7 letters] gravissimus, mihique, dum viveret, longè amicissimus, apud Ampl. Magistratum suum ore & scripto sapientissimè praefuit) incendio oborto, signum ejusdem dant, conclamant, populum excitant: at incendiarii nomen edere, vel eum deferre haud tenentur. Constat enim non illos, utpote in edita turri excubantes, nec incendiarium observare valentes; sed vigiliarum praefectos, & quotquot armati per compita urbis incedunt, & civium excubias agunt, requiri & interrogari, num quid incendiarios & nebulones ejusmodi alios obvios habuerint? Ad hoc enim munus conducti illi, officii sui partes neutiquam implebunt, si contra tristem illum conspectum publicum desides incendium obortum inficiari, & ignorantiam perpetuam obtendere ausi fuerint. Ita planè speculatores spirituales mala gliscentia & grassantia ordine suo proclamare: at in eorum authorem Magistratus per Ministros suos inquirere tenetur.
units.tr: XLIV. But perhaps a minister of the Church cannot fulfil his duty of rebuking sinners and scandals from the pulpit, whether they arise from the people or from the magistrate himself, and of openly attacking and correcting them, unless he is willing and able to mark [σημειῶν] the authors of those scandals and also to denounce them to the magistrate. This, surely, is what some people, impatient of correction and bearing it badly, sometimes dare to demand of ministers. Indeed they rage when ministers of the Church thunder from the pulpit against public scandals, especially perjuries, gluttony, wicked arts, capital injustice, and other such things that flourish openly and with impunity. We certainly cannot approve of those ministers [?], who, squandering their own and others' salvation, neglect private admonitions, corrections and entreaties, secret ones, through which the conscience and salvation of any men, even of the powerful, and indeed the public safety, can be not a little cared for. Out of fear of men, or from a lazy indolence, they neglect these and boldly rush forth to public harangues and Philippics before the whole people, and impiously expose and prostitute the private parts of parents, like Ham. Yet if private reminders and corrections have achieved nothing, and the scandals have become public, and have gathered strength and growth even from the boldness and number of the sinners, so that the cry about the salvation of the Church and commonwealth begins to go up, we do not doubt at all that such things should be brought forward from the pulpit, marked out, and set before the people to be lamented and detested, without any prior or subsequent denunciation of the sinning persons to the magistrate. For civil accusation is one thing, which, in Cicero's view, even requires a crime, to define the thing, to name the man, to prove by argument, to confirm by witness; ecclesiastical correction is another. The former, since it aims at and demands punishment and satisfaction for the guilty, cannot refrain from defining the person. The latter, because it seeks solely the shame, contrition and salvation of the sinner, the repair of public scandal, and the safety of the commonwealth and Church, and moreover works in the ecclesiastical, not the civil, forum, can have its place without the sinners being marked out, much less denounced to the magistrate. For the sinner whose public correction is in question, even if he is neither marked nor denounced by the minister, being conscious of the sin he has committed, can thus be brought to repentance. And the Church, which, if not conscious of the persons of the sinners, at least is conscious of the public harm it suffers from such sins, can mourn, sigh to God, and be healed of the scandal, without the sinner being marked or likewise denounced. And so, without denunciation, such ecclesiastical correction attains its end. Moreover, the ministers of the Church are watchmen [צֹפִים?], watchmen (Ezek. III. 17?). Now watchmen (I use that simile of a certain Church in Helvetia, whose most grave man, and to me, while he lived, by far the most dear friend, presided over his honourable magistrate most wisely both by voice and by writing), when a fire breaks out, give the signal, raise the cry, and rouse the people. But they are not bound to name the arsonist or to denounce him. For it is clear that they, keeping watch on a raised tower, cannot observe the incendiary. Rather, the prefects of the night watch, and all who go armed through the crossroads of the city and keep the citizens' watch, are asked and questioned whether they have encountered any incendiaries or such rogues. For those hired for this duty will by no means fulfil the parts of their office if, in the face of that dismal public sight, they slothfully dare to deny the fire that has broken out and feign perpetual ignorance. Thus, in the same way, spiritual watchmen must proclaim, each in their own order, the evils that are growing and raging; but the magistrate is bound to inquire through his own ministers after their author.

units.la: XLV. Atque sic etiam via patefacta est ad decisionem casus: An Pastor Ecclesiae peccata sibi ab afflictis, institutionis & consolationis percipiendae gratiâ, revelata, confessa & credita ad Magistratum deferre teneatur? Nostris quidem Ecclesiis jam pridem abominationi fuit Confessio auricularis Pontificia, ab Innocentio III. primò introducta, utpote quae conscientiarum carnificina atque μελέτη ἀναισχυντίας [?] exercitatio impudentiae (1. Tim. III. 6.) est, & inter dominationis Papalis arcana & sacerrima stratagemata merito censetur. Ne-que etiam usque quaque probamus sententiam Ecclesiarum quarundam, quae sublatis Confessionis secretae abusibus nonnullis, necessitatem tamen ejusdem, velut Divinitus praeceptae, morosè nimis urgent, & absolutionem ipsam quaestui habent. quod ipsum tamen aliis ejusdem communionis moderationibus non omnino probatur. Nam ex pietate quaestum facere cui non sordeat? Ac necessitatem etiam privatae confessionis non agnovit Lutherus ipse, qui, uti Franzius Disput. I. super XI. Art. Aug. Conf. th. 156. loquitur, æque ac fidelissimi ejusdem parasitæ [?] & sectatores omnes, eam ut liberam retinuerunt, non ut necessariam conscientiis imposuerunt, neque singulos & universos ad usum illius rigidissimè & strictissimè astrinxerunt. Non enim, uti etiam Sigwartus lib.III. Contra Iren. Par. cap.3. arguit, a Christo, nec ab Apostolis est mandata, vel exemplo commendata, sed Ecclesiastico instituto ab Episcopis aliquando recepta & dissimiliter observata. Ejus verò loco Ecclesiae nostrae pro ea libertate, quam in adiaphoris verbum Dei permisit, visitationes familiarum, & in iis infirmiorum inprimis, institutiones rudiorum, examina eorum, qui primùm ad sacram Synaxin aspirant, substituerunt.
units.tr: XLV. And so the way is also opened to deciding the case: Is a minister of the Church bound to denounce to the magistrate sins revealed to him by the afflicted, confessed and entrusted to him in order to receive instruction and consolation? In our Churches the Papal auricular confession, first introduced by Innocent III, has long been an abomination, since it is a torture of consciences and a practice of shamelessness [μελέτη ἀναισχυντίας], an exercise of impudence (1 Tim. III. 6.), and is rightly counted among the secret and most sacred stratagems of papal domination. Nor do we altogether approve the opinion of certain Churches, which, having removed some abuses of secret confession, nonetheless urge its necessity, as if divinely commanded, rather too harshly, and make absolution itself a source of gain. Other moderates of the same communion do not wholly approve this either. For who would not be tainted by making gain out of piety? Luther himself did not recognise the necessity of private confession, who, as Franzius says in Disput. I. super XI. Art. Aug. Conf. th. 156., like all his most faithful parasites and followers, retained it as free, and did not impose it as necessary on consciences, nor bound each and all to its use most rigidly and strictly. For it was not, as Sigwart also argues in lib. III Contra Iren. Par. cap. 3, commanded by Christ or by the Apostles, nor recommended by example, but at some time received by ecclesiastical institution from the bishops and observed in various ways. In its place our Churches, using the liberty which the Word of God has allowed in things indifferent, have substituted visitations of families, and especially of the weaker members within them, instruction of the ignorant, and examinations of those who first aspire to the holy Synaxis.

units.la: XLVI. Si tamen etiam privata confessio libera, nec pretio addicta relinquatur, & conscientiis importunè non obtrudatur; illam Ecclesiae nostrae non aspernantur. Ita enim Confessio Helvetica Cap.14. declarat quidem, Confessionem ingenuam, quae soli Deo fit, vel privatim inter Deum & peccatorem, vel palam in Templo, ubi generalis illa peccatorum Confessio recitatur, sufficere, nec necessarium esse ad remissionem peccatorum consequendam, ut quis peccata sua Sacerdoti confiteatur. Nihilominus paulò post subjicit: Si quis vero peccatorum mole, & tentationibus perpetuis oppressus velit Consilium, institutionem & consolationem privatim vel à Ministro Ecclesiæ, aut alio aliquo fratre, in lege Dei docto, petere, non improbamus. Quæ tamen; uti scitè Ven. Bullingerus noster Decad. IV. Serm. I. & ante ipsum Zwinglius Explanat. art.52. monent, non tam Consessio, quàm Consultatio est, ad quam nemo cogi potest. Articulus XI. Conventus Marpurgensis consentit: Confessionem seu petitionem Consilii à suo Pastore vel proximo liberam quidem, neque extortam esse debere, admodum tamen utilem esse afflictis conscientiis, quæ tentationibus, aut peccatorum mole, aut errorum laqueis gravantur, maximè verò propter absolutionem & consolationem Evangelii, quod vera absolutio est. Fusè etiam & facundè eandem rem Calvinus Instit. lib.III.4-12. sic explicat. Ergo id officii sui unus quisque fidelium esse meminerit, si ita privatim angitur & afflictatur peccatorum sensu, ut se explicare, nisi alieno adjutorio, nequeat, non negligere, quod illi à Domino offertur, remedium, nempe ut ad se sublevandum privata confessione apud suum Pastorem utatur, ac ad solatia sibi adhibenda privatam ejus operam implorét, cujus officium est, & publicè & privatim populum Dei Evangelica doctrina consolari. Verùm ea moderatione semper utendum est, ne, ubi Deus nihil certum præscribit, conscientiæ certo jugo alligentur. Hinc sequitur, ejusmodi Confessionem liberam esse oportere, ut non ab omnibus exigatur, sed iis tantùm commendetur, qui ea se habere opus intelligent. Deinde, ne hi ipsi, qui ea utuntur pro sua necessitate, ad enumeranda omnia peccata vel præcepto aliquo cogantur, vel arte inducantur, sed quo ad interesse sua putabunt, ut solidum[?] consolationis fructum referant.
units.tr: XLVI. If, however, private confession is left free, not bound to payment, and not importunately thrust upon consciences, our Churches do not reject it. For the Helvetic Confession, chapter 14, indeed declares that the sincere confession which is made to God alone, either privately between God and the sinner, or openly in the temple, where that general confession of sins is recited, suffices, and it is not necessary for the obtaining of remission of sins that anyone confess his sins to a priest. Nevertheless, shortly afterwards it adds: If anyone, however, oppressed by the weight of sins and perpetual temptations, wishes to seek counsel, instruction and consolation privately from a minister of the Church, or from some other brother learned in the law of God, we do not disapprove. Which, however, as our venerable Bullinger wisely observes in Decad. IV, Serm. I, and before him Zwingli in Explanat. art. 52, is not so much a confession as a consultation, to which no one can be compelled. Article XI of the Marburg Conference agrees: confession or request for counsel from one's pastor or neighbour should indeed be free and not extorted, yet very useful to afflicted consciences, which are weighed down by temptations, or by the mass of sins, or by the snares of errors, and most of all for the absolution and consolation of the Gospel, which is true absolution. Calvin also explains the same matter at length and eloquently: Instit. lib. III, 4-12. Therefore each of the faithful should remember that it is his duty, if he is so privately troubled and afflicted by a sense of sins that he cannot explain himself without another's help, not to neglect the remedy the Lord offers, namely to use private confession to his pastor for his own relief, and to implore his private help in finding consolation, whose office it is to console the people of God both publicly and privately by the Evangelical doctrine. But this moderation must always be used, lest, where God prescribes nothing certain, consciences be bound by a certain yoke. Hence it follows that such confession ought to be free, so that it is not demanded of all, but commended only to those who understand that they have need of it. Next, that those who use it for their need should not be compelled, either by some precept or led on by craft, to enumerate all their sins, but to do so as far as they think it serves their interest, so that they may bring back the solid fruit of consolation.

units.la: XLVII. Duo vero casus sunt, in quibus fideles Pastorum Ecclesiæ, qui ceu Patres spirituales, in Christo Jesu per Evangelium eos gignunt, 1.Cor. IV.15. & ὠδίνωσι[?] parturiunt, donec Christus in iis formetur, Gal.IV.19. consilium & auxilium negligere non possunt. Prior est, cùm dubitatio incidit, an hoc vel illud peccatum sit, nec ne. Multa enim speciem virtutis & boni facti habent, quæ nisi ab oculatioribus & perspicacioribus dignosci facilè nequeunt. Vicissim etiam non nulla observatu vel factu indifferentia & libera à simplicioribus pro illicitis fœdisque factu censeri possunt. Qua in fluctuatione omnino consulendi sunt Ecclesiæ Pastores, quorum labia custodire debent scientiam, & ex quorum ore lex requiri debet, quia sunt Legati Jehovæ Exercituum. Mal II.6. Posterior est, cùm peccator conscientiam peccato enormi & gravi sauciatam componere & tranquillare nullo modo potis ipse est, Tum enim ad sacram Pastoris Ecclesiæ anchoram confugere pium, cōnsultum, imò necessarium est. Cum redargutus fuerit peccator in cubili suo, & in multitudine ossium ejus ingens dolor est, & secerit ipsum anima ejus nauseare ad panem, & vita ejus ad cibum delicatum. Consumpta quin etiam anima ejus fuerit a visu, & confringentur ossa ejus non visa, atque adeo appropinquaverit anima ejus ad occidentes (Diabolum). Tum verò, si est apud ipsum מלאך מליץ אחד מני אלף[?] Angelus Adroctatus[?] unus inter mille (is Angelus foederis, Christus est, princeps & praecipuus inter mille Angelos & intercessores, ac ministros etiam reconciliationis) ad indicandum homini rectitudinem ejus; & gratia illum complectatur ac dicat: Redime ipsum, ne descendat in foveam, inveni Lytrum, Revirescens augescit caro ejus prae pueritia, redit ad dies adolescentiae suae. Supplicat Deo, & gratum ipsum habet, & videt faciem ejus cum jubilo, & reddit homini justitiam suam, &c Job. XXXIII. 19–27. Etenim si morbo corporis gravi & sontico laborantes nec judicio nostro, nec obvio cuivis medicastro confidimus: & in causa difficili coram judice disceptaturi, optimi & pertissimi cujusque consilium avidè imploramus: quid non in periculoso animae morbo tentandum nobis videbitur? Inprimis ubi diu cum conscientiae terroribus luctatis, & coram gratiae Divinae tribunali prostratis, ad tranquillitatem & pacati Numinis sensum difficulter vel plane non eniti & eluctari datur. Hic nuncii pacis, ministri reconciliationis, malo pudore omni posito, adiri, iisque incurata ulcera fidenter detegi debent, inprimis cum constet, non solum iis consolationum ex limpidis Israelis fontibus malagmata suppetere, sed potestatem etiam peccata remittendi, Joh.XX.23. hoc est, remissionem peccatorum in Evangelio credentibus & resipiscentibus promissam, efficaciter, & jure commissae legationis, longè potentiùs, quàm a quoquam alio clavium potestate destituto fieri possit, applicandi, competere. Si plus paterna benedictio, nulla licet speciali promissione Divina freta, quàm communis alia quaevis operatur, potentior etiam longè erit, non tam precaria, quàm ex Divina promissione & speciali potestate profecta benedictio & absolutio Pastoris, quàm promiscua alterius cujusvis. Sicut ergo graviter peccant, qui sacrificulos, ceu idola quaedam, cernui adorant, & dictis eorum perinde atque Divinis Oraculis assurgunt: ita haud levius peccant, qui conclamatis fere rebus Pastorum consilia, dicta & auxilia spernunt, &, ut olim Megarenses Oraculum, ἐν ᾠδεῖ ἀριθμῷ[?] nullo numero, ceu vacuas cifras habent.
units.tr: XLVII. There are two cases in which the faithful cannot neglect the counsel and help of the Church's ministers, who as spiritual fathers beget them in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, 1 Cor. 4:15, and labour in birth until Christ is formed in them, Gal. 4:19. The first is when doubt arises whether this or that is a sin or not. For many things have the appearance of virtue and of good deeds, and can hardly be distinguished except by the more discerning and perceptive. Conversely, some things that are indifferent to observe or do, and free, may be judged by simpler people to be unlawful and shameful. In such wavering the ministers of the Church must certainly be consulted, for their lips should keep knowledge, and from their mouth the law should be sought, because they are the messengers of the LORD of hosts, Mal. 2:7. The second is when a sinner, his conscience wounded by an enormous and grave sin, is in no way able to settle and quiet it himself. Then it is pious, advisable, indeed necessary, to flee to the holy anchor of the Church's minister. When the sinner has been rebuked on his bed, and there is great pain in the multitude of his bones, and his soul makes him loathe bread and his life dainty food; yea, his soul is consumed from sight, and his bones that were not seen are broken, so that his soul draws near to the destroyers (the Devil). Then indeed, if there is with him a messenger, an interpreter, one among a thousand [Hebrew: mal'akh melits echad mini elef] (that angel of the covenant is Christ, the prince and chief of the thousand angels and intercessors, and also the ministers of reconciliation) to declare to man his uprightness; and grace embraces him and says: Redeem him, lest he go down into the pit, I have found a ransom. His flesh grows fresh again from childhood, he returns to the days of his youth. He prays to God, and God is gracious to him, and he sees his face with joy, and he restores to man his righteousness, etc., Job 33:19–27. For if we, suffering from a grave and dangerous bodily disease, trust neither our own judgment nor any quack who happens by, and when about to plead a difficult case before a judge we eagerly seek the counsel of the best and most expert, what should we not think must be tried in the perilous disease of the soul? Especially when, after long struggling with the terrors of conscience and lying prostrate before the tribunal of divine grace, a person can hardly or not at all strive and struggle towards tranquillity and a sense of a reconciled God. Here the messengers of peace and ministers of reconciliation must be approached, with all wrong shame set aside, and the incurable ulcers boldly laid open to them. This is especially so since it is established that they have at hand not only the balms of consolation from the clear fountains of Israel, but also, by the right of the commission entrusted to them, the power of the keys, John 20:23, that is, to apply effectively, and far more powerfully than anyone else destitute of that power could do, the remission of sins promised in the Gospel to those who believe and repent. If a fatherly blessing, though relying on no special divine promise, works more than any other common blessing, then the blessing and absolution of the minister, which rests on a divine promise and special authority, will be far more powerful, and not so precarious, than that of any other person whatever. Just as those sin grievously who fall prostrate before priests as before idols, and rise at their words as at divine oracles, so those sin no less who, when matters are almost despaired of, spurn the counsels, words and help of the ministers, and, as the Megarians once treated an oracle, hold them as empty ciphers, [Greek: ἐν ᾠδεῖ ἀριθμῷ] in no number.

units.la: XLVIII. In tractandis porrò peccatis occultis, gravissimis etiam & capitalibus, quæ conscientia pavidi delinquentes Pastori clanculum, & remotis arbitris omnibus, confitentur & committunt, hæc omnino Pastori eidem circumspectio adhibenda est, ne vel nulla, vel omnia prodenda & ad Magistratum deferenda putet. Si enim peccata confessa & credita ejusmodi sunt, ut non prodita vel delata in gloriæ Divinæ detrimentum notorium, & Reipublicæ, vel cujusvis innocentis præsentissimam perniciem immediate redundent, omne intempestivum, irreligiosum & impium silentium est. Neque de non deferendis ejusmodi delictis vel fides cuiquam obligari potest, vel obligata servari, sed potius conscio etiam confitente, rescindi debet. Major enim ratio habenda est unitatis, quàm unius: communitatis, quàm singulorum. Salus patriæ suprema lex est, & charitas erga Rempublicam antiquissima.
units.tr: XLVIII. Furthermore, in dealing with secret sins, even the gravest and capital ones, which fearful offenders confess and commit to the minister privately, with all witnesses removed, the minister must exercise the greatest caution, so that he neither thinks that nothing should be disclosed and reported to the magistrate, nor that everything should be. For if the sins confessed and entrusted to him are of such a kind that, if not revealed and reported, they would immediately bring notorious harm to the glory of God, and most imminent ruin to the commonwealth or to any innocent person, then silence is untimely, irreligious and impious. Nor can anyone be bound by faith not to report such offences, nor should a binding faith be kept. Rather, even with the sinner's consent, it ought to be annulled. For the consideration of unity must count for more than that of one person, and that of the community for more than that of individuals. The safety of the fatherland is the supreme law, and love towards the commonwealth is the oldest.

units.la: XLIX. Sed necessaria tamen hic est delinquentis & delicti discretio. Si enim ita in perniciem publicam delictum tendit, ut, nisi detecto etiam delinquente, malum præsens vel futurum à Republica averruncari nequeat, delinquens confessor monendus est, ut Deo det gloriam, & judici, in primis si in crimen illud inquirat, ipsemet arcanum resignet, atque sic temporalis vitæ vel commodi jactura animæ suæ saluti consulat. Si monitis hisce vacivas aures substringere renuerit, à Pastore ordinaria via ad judicem deferri haud dubie debet. Sin delictum ejusmodi est, ut ejus in Rempublicam perniciosa operatio vel transierit, atque infecta reddi nequeat, vel pendeat in præsens & futurum, ita tamen, ut non revelato delinquente damnum Reipublicæ inferendum alia ratione præcaveri, sufflaminari & penitus averti possit, delictum quidem ipsum omnino revelandum est; quoad delinquentem vero prudentiæ & charitatis Pastoris erit, eum vel deferre, si pœnitentiæ signa evidentia non appareant, & ab ejusmodi delinquente Reipublicæ in futurum etiam metuendum videatur: vel, ad explorandum delinquentem, delationem suspendere: vel omnino non deferre, si certa exemplaris pœnitentiæ indicia se exeruerint, nec quicquam amplius à delinquente metuendum sit. Ubi enim publicæ saluti satis provisum & consultum est, atque fratrem peccantem lucratus Pastor fuerit, silentium tutò præstari potest. Ita si peccans Pastori hæreticorum conventicula, veneni in puteum injectionem, ignis in domum vel civitatem immissionem, de prodenda civitate vel principe conspirationem, atque id genus alia confessus fuerit, cùm periculo non careat silentium, res seu delictum ipsum deferri & detegi poterit, personâ, quae scelus id fassa, & ingenti cum dolore. ac poenitentia detestata est, non delatâ, vel detectâ, dummodo non delatâ vel detectâ illâ, malum pendens à patria averti possit, nec de delinquente quicquam amplius metuendum videatur. Non mediocri tamen heic prudentia, quae ἐν τοῖς καθ' ἕκαστα [?], & in singularibus circumstantiis occupatur, opus est, ne vel pietas erga patriam, Rempublicam, innocentesque alios, vel fides & charitas erga peccatorem poenitentem jure desiderari possit. Et juvabit etiam heic non absolutum silentium confessuro stipulari, sed certa lege, si praestari illud sine gloriae Dei & Reipublicae detrimento posse putetur. Quod si silentium praestari non poterit, cavendum nihilominus confitentis saluti etiam temporali est, quantum conscientia, & prudentiae arbitrium permittit.
units.tr: XLIX. Here, however, a distinction must be made between the offender and the offence. If an offence tends so to the public ruin that the present or future evil cannot be averted from the commonwealth unless the offender too is revealed, then the confessor who committed the crime must be admonished to give glory to God, and to the judge, especially if he is inquiring into that crime, to reveal the secret himself; and so, by the loss of temporal life or advantage, he will provide for the salvation of his soul. If he refuses to bind his empty ears to these admonitions, the minister must undoubtedly report him to the judge by the ordinary way. But if the offence is of such a kind that its destructive operation against the commonwealth has either already passed and cannot be undone, or hangs over the present and future, yet in such a way that, without revealing the offender, the harm to the commonwealth can be guarded against by some other means, checked and wholly averted, then the offence itself must indeed be revealed in full. As for the offender, however, it will be for the prudence and charity of the minister either to report him, if clear signs of repentance do not appear and it seems that the commonwealth has reason to fear him in future; or to suspend the report in order to test the offender; or to refrain altogether from reporting him, if clear and exemplary signs of repentance have shown themselves and nothing more is to be feared from the offender. For when the public safety has been sufficiently provided for and the sinning brother has been gained by the minister, silence can be kept safely. Thus, if a sinner has confessed to the minister the meetings of heretics, the throwing of poison into a well, the setting of fire to a house or city, a conspiracy to betray a city or a prince, and other things of that kind, then, since silence is not free from danger, the matter or offence itself may be reported and disclosed, but the person who confessed the crime, and detested it with great grief and repentance, need not be reported or disclosed, provided that, without reporting or disclosing him, the threatening evil can be averted from the fatherland, and nothing more is to be feared from the offender. Yet here no small prudence is needed, which is exercised in particular and in individual circumstances, lest either piety towards the fatherland, the commonwealth and other innocent people, or faith and charity towards the penitent sinner, be rightly neglected. And it will also help here to demand of the one confessing not an absolute silence, but silence under a fixed condition, if it can be thought that it may be kept without detriment to the glory of God and the commonwealth. But if silence cannot be kept, care must nevertheless be taken for the salvation of the confessor, even temporal salvation, so far as conscience and the judgment of prudence allow.

units.la: L. Adeò detestamur Cleri Pontificii, Jesuitarum cumprimis, insignitam perfidiam, cum Suarezio de Poenit. diff. 33.§.1.n.2. diserte asserentium; in nullo casu, & propter nullum finem, etiam pro tota Republica ab ingenti malo temporali & spirituali tuenda, violari sigillum Confessionis posse. Idem affirmat Emanuel Sa Jesuita, Aphorismis, verbo Confessor.
units.tr: L. So greatly do we detest the notorious perfidy of the Papist clergy, especially of the Jesuits, who, with Suárez, De Poenit. disp. 33, §1, n. 2, plainly assert: in no case, and for no end, not even for protecting the whole commonwealth from a great temporal and spiritual evil, can the seal of confession be violated. Emanuel Sá, a Jesuit, affirms the same in his Aphorismi, under the word Confessor.

units.la: Ubi ergo agitur non tantum de praecavendo proximi cujusvis periculo, sed etiam de ipsorum Regum & Principum vita, à conjurationibus sicariorum vindicanda, solenne illis est excipere notitiam, quam Sacerdos ex audita in Confessione auriculari conjuratione hausit. Cujus obtentu negant, se teneri vel monere Principem, caveat sibi à periculo, si metuendum sit, ne velit scisscitari causas, & exigere ea, quae sub Confessionis sigillo sibi commissa sunt. Hoc fundamentum fuit martyrii nebulonum in Anglia, Garneti & complicum, qui pulverariam conspirationem adversus Regem & supremas Curias, in Confessione sibi revelatam, velut nondum executioni datam, sed demum exequendam, ad Regem deferri potuisse negarunt, atque propter omissam delationem justissimas poenas dantes, martyrum laureolam sibi vendicarunt, latronum & parricidarum certissimi complices. Horrendam profecto doctrinam, quae Confessionis auricularis Antichristianum inventum ejusmodi sigillo munit, ut cuilibet perduelli, sicario & parricidae impune conscientiam suam, etiam dum consilium petit, nec eum suscepti criminis poenitentem aperire & exonerare liceat, cum tamen juxta Jesuitas eosdem Sacramentum Poenitentiae, cujus Confessionem partem faciunt, tantum in gratiam poenitentis, quâ poenitens est, & cujus semper vox esse debet, peccavi, poenitet, non peccabo amplius; institutum fuerit. Confessio enim praeterita tantùm peccata detegit & deplorat, non futura prositetur. Illa contriti animi, hæc obstinati & impœnitentis index est. Sigillum autem Sacramenti ipso Sacramento latius esse, aut ultra Sacramenti rationem extendi non potest. Si igitur tale omnino sigillum esset, ut nunquam illud referare liceret; non obligaret tamen confessorem ad facinus futurum non revelandum, pro aliquorum temporali vel spirituali salute, maximè ubi ipsa confitentis anima tali silentio Sathanæ magis magisque mancipatur. Sed hoc de iniquitatis mysterio Doctissimus Casaubonus Epistola ad Frontonem Ducæum pluscula dixit, testatus inter alia, sibi à Jesuita Bineto dictum; præstare omnes Reges occidi, quàm vel semel Confessionis sigillum revelari. Cui consentientia dixere alii. Dominicus Soto in 4. Sent. dist. 18. q. 4. art. 5. Licet, inquit, Sacerdos videat personam innocentissimam, dignitate & authoritate maximam, in supplicium capitis rapi, sitque certissimus per sontis Confessionem, illum esse innocentem, posseque eum facilimè, detecta Consessione, liberare, neutiquam illi fas est. Henricus Henriquez in summa de Pœnit. lib. III. 16. 3. Ob nullam causam confessa revelari possunt, quamvis esset totius orbis salus, aut ipsius pœnitentis utilitas, nec pro vitando ullo damno gravissimo innocentis, aut quòd esset totius Orbis conflagratio, aut perversio religionis, & omnium Sacramentorum intentata demolitio. Sed & Casaubono Epist. ad Front. Ducæum, & responsad Perron. teste, Jesuita Gallus os suum in blasphema hæc verba resolvit: Si Dominus noster Jesus Christus in terra versaretur morti obnoxius, & aliquis sibi in Confessione dixisset, velle se illum occidere; priusquam Confessionem revelaret, passurum se, ut Christus occidatur. Nequissimus fit oportet sacrificuli confessoris sinus, in quo parricidæ, Christicidæ, sicarii, proditores omnes tutum receptum habent: ipse verò Christus, Salvator noster, Religio universa, Respublica, Reges, Principes innocentissimi, quin & reliquus totus orbis præsidii & solatii nihil.
units.tr: Where the question concerns not only guarding against some danger to any neighbour but also defending the very lives of kings and princes against plots of assassins, these men habitually claim knowledge that a priest has gained from a conspiracy heard in private confession. On this pretext they deny that they are bound to warn the prince, or to advise him to beware of danger if danger is to be feared, lest he should wish to ask the causes and demand what has been entrusted to them under the seal of confession. This was the foundation of the martyrdom of the scoundrels in England, Garnet and his accomplices, who denied that they could have reported to the King the gunpowder conspiracy against the King and the highest courts, which had been revealed to them in confession as not yet carried out but still to be carried out. On account of their failure to report it, they received their most just punishments, and claimed for themselves the laurel of martyrs, though they were certainly accomplices of robbers and parricides. This is a truly horrible doctrine, which fortifies with the seal of confession that Antichristian invention, the auricular confession, so that any traitor, assassin or parricide may, with impunity, keep his conscience to himself, even when he seeks counsel, and is not allowed to open it up and unburden it as one repenting of the crime he has undertaken. Yet, according to these same Jesuits, of whose confession this doctrine forms part, the Sacrament of Repentance was instituted only for the benefit of the penitent, insofar as he is penitent, and its voice must always be: I have sinned, I repent, I will sin no more. For confession discloses and laments only past sins; it does not profess future ones. The former is a sign of a contrite spirit, the latter of an obstinate and impenitent one. Moreover, the seal of the sacrament cannot be wider than the sacrament itself, nor be extended beyond the reason of the sacrament. So even if the seal were of such a kind that it could never be broken, it would still not bind the confessor not to disclose a crime yet to come, for the temporal or spiritual salvation of some people, especially where the penitent's own soul is delivered more and more into Satan's hands by such silence. But the most learned Casaubon, in his letter to Fronto Ducaeus, said a good deal more about this mystery of iniquity, testifying among other things that a Jesuit, Binet, had told him: It is better that all kings be killed than that the seal of confession be revealed even once. Others have agreed with this. Dominic Soto, in 4 Sent. dist. 18, q. 4, art. 5: "It is permitted," he says, "for a priest to see a most innocent person, very great in dignity and authority, being dragged off to capital punishment, and to be most certain through the guilty man's confession that he is innocent, and to be able most easily to free him once the confession was disclosed; yet it is by no means lawful for him to do so." Henry Henriquez, in Summa de Poenitentia, lib. III, 16, 3: "For no cause may confessed matters be revealed, even if the salvation of the whole world, or the advantage of the penitent himself, were at stake; nor to avert any most grave harm to an innocent person, nor if the whole world were to be set on fire, or religion overturned, and the destruction of all the sacraments were threatened." Moreover, according to Casaubon, in his letter to Ducaeus and his reply to Perron, a French Jesuit opened his mouth to utter these blasphemous words: "If our Lord Jesus Christ were living on earth and subject to death, and someone had said to him in confession that he wished to kill him, the priest would, before revealing the confession, permit Christ to be killed." Surely the bosom of that wicked little confessor must be most wicked, in which parricides, Christ-killers, assassins and traitors all have a safe refuge; while Christ our Saviour, the whole religion, the commonwealth, kings and innocent princes, and indeed the whole rest of the world, have no protection or comfort at all.

units.la: LI. Alia verò ratio est delictorum etiam gravissimorum, quæ in sinum Pastoris clanculum à peccatore, conscientiæ stimulis compuncto, depositá in Reipublicæ & proximi innocentis damnum nullatenus vergunt. quæ deferre ad judicem civilem, vel revelare aliis Pastor pius, & illibatæ conscientiæ nullo modo ausit. Meminisse enim eum oportet, quòd in hoc negotio Legati Dei & Christi vicem sustineat. Sicut Pater me misit, ita ego mitto vos, &c. Joh. XX.21. &c. Pro Christo legatione fungimur, &c.2. Cor. V.20. Cùm ergo Deus & Christus peccata etiam gravissima hominis, peccata sua ingenuè confitentis, & ex animo detestantis, non revelet ad ulteriorem poenam (uti vel solius adulterae à Christo non delatae, sed dimissae exemplum Joh. VIII. 11. fidem facit) sed potius tegat, Rom. IV. 7. 8. deleat, Esaj. XLIV. 22. longissime ab homine removeat, Psal. CIII. 12. imo in profundum maris projiciat, & demergat, Mich. VII. 9. atque hanc ipsam clementem suam erga poenitentes μετανοίαν[?] per hosce legatos & praecones publicos praedicari jubeat: quomodo animum inducent hi Dei & Christi Legati, ut, quae tegi, deleri, abjici, in profundum maris demergi dominus & legatarius vult, & se velle per eosdem significat, illi detegant, aperiant, & in conspectum & notitiam hominum punienda producant? Fateor equidem, distincta esse Divinum & Politicum forum, ut, quod in illo remittitur, in hoc puniri possit, ut supra diximus.
units.tr: LI. But the case is different for crimes, even most grave ones, which a sinner, pricked by the goads of conscience, has secretly deposited in a minister's bosom, and which in no way tend to the harm of the commonwealth or of an innocent neighbour. A devout minister, whose conscience is unstained, must not dare in any way to report these to the civil judge or disclose them to others. For he ought to remember that in this business he stands in the place of God's and Christ's ambassador: As the Father sent me, so I send you, etc., John 20:21, etc. We are ambassadors for Christ, etc., 2 Cor. 5:20. Since therefore God and Christ do not disclose even the gravest sins of a man who openly confesses them and detests them from the heart, for further punishment (as the example of the adulteress, not reported but dismissed by Christ, John 8:11, bears witness), but rather cover them (Rom. 4:7, 8), blot them out (Isa. 44:22), remove them far from man (Ps. 103:12), indeed cast them into the depths of the sea and sink them (Mic. 7:19), and command that this very merciful disposition of theirs towards penitents be proclaimed through these ambassadors and public heralds, how will these ambassadors of God and Christ bring themselves to disclose, open up and bring into the sight and knowledge of men, for punishment, those things which their Lord and principal wishes to be covered, blotted out, cast away and sunk in the depths of the sea, and which he signifies through the same men that he wishes? I admit indeed that the divine and the political courts are distinct, so that what is remitted in the one may be punished in the other, as we said above.

units.la: Coeterum peccatores delictorum conscientia aegri Pastores adeunt, non ut ministros fori Politici, sed Divini. Cum peccatore igitur confitente, vel consilium implorante agendum ipsis est, pro ratione fori illius, cui ministrant, non pro ratione fori heterogenei. In hac enim consultatione Dei, Christi, non Magistratus personam agunt. Neque enim in hoc negotio inquisitio arcanorum judicialis instituitur, sed conscientiis perturbatis, afflictis & tabescentibus consulitur. Tum Minister verba omnia, dicta & facta sua ad aedificationem, non ad destructionem fidelium referre debet. Potestatem mihi dedit Dominus εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν ad aedificationem & non ad destructionem, 2.Cor.XIII.10. Atqui potestate & severitate sua Ministri Verbi Dei ad destructionem, non ad aedificationem uterentur, si miserorum & poenitentium anxietatem & occulta proderent, tum quia peccatoribus peccata sua ingenuè confitentibus praesentissimum periculum crearent, ipsiusque etiam poenitendi tempus praecederent, atque sic panem consolationis petenti lapidem, piscis spiritualem escam appetenti serpentem, denique ovum desideranti scorpionem porrigerent; quod ab omnium patrum carnalium, nedum spiritualium affectu & ingenio abhorrere satis Christus Matth. VII. 9. Luc. XI. 11. 12. innuit: tum quia innumeri peccata & ulcera sua Pastori consolationis gratiâ nudare parati, proditionis, & atrocis in primis poenae metu id omne negligent, atque sic conscientiam criminibus implicatam exsolvere ipsi non valentes, Pastores ejusmodi & ἀνυπερ[illegible, ~3 letters]ς reformidantes, ad desperationis barathrum praecipites ruent. Talisne vero fuit spiritus, tale φρόνημα Christi, cujus in reconciliationem[?] ciliatione hominum cum Deo ministros se profitentur? Atqui ille venit,non ut perdat ampliùs,sed ut salvet,quod perierat, Matth.XVIII.11. Ecce servus ille meus,quem elegi,dilectus ille meus, in quo acquiescit anima mea. Ponam spiritum meum super ipsum,& judicium gentibus annuntiabit. Non litigabit, neque clamabit, neque audiet quisquam in plateis vocem ejus. Arundinem quassatam non confringet, linum fumigans non extinguet, usque dum protulerit ad victoriam judicium, Matth.XII.18.19.20. Faciunt huc dicta Solomonis: Qui obtrectat, revelat secretum, & qui fidelis est anima, tegit rem, Prov. XI.13. Qui revelat arcanum obtrectator est, ibid.XX.19. Cúmque in consultatione hac semper promissio de celando delicto ejus, qui consultatur, vel expressa, vel tacita, quae ex modo dicendi ac recipiendi, & ex verbis confidentiam significantibus & suadentibus colligitur, intercedat, manifestum est, hanc secreti revelationem cum veracitate & fidelitate, quam jure naturali observare tenemur, quin & cum ipsa societate civili, cujus ex istiusmodi secretorum detectione perturbatio oritur, pugnare. Si porrò juxta illud S.Petri, Charitas multitudinem peccatorum operit, 1.Pet.IV.8. & illa Solomonis: Odium excitat lites, & omnia delicta tegit dilectio, Prov.X.12. Tegit delictum, qui quaerit charitatem, Cap. XVII.9. maxima porrò Pastoris erga oviculas Christi poenitentes charitas esse debet, non utique multitudinem delictorum is aperire, sed operire debet. Accedit, quòd consentiente omnium fere Juris peritorum calculo, gravis etiam sceleris sibi conscius se ipsum deferre ad judicem non tenetur, quia non aliis praeter ipsum scelus innotuit. Pari ergo ratione qui solus ex rei libera confessione scelus aliquod compertum habet, ad revelandum illud non tenetur. Cur enim teneretur magis, quàm reus ipse? Denique haec infida secretorum proditio non caret periculo. Quid enim si, qui arcanum in Pastoris sinum necessitates suas deposituit, proditus, poenae sibi imminentis metu, spontaneam confessionem, delictorum inprimis atrocium prius factam revocet, & in revocatione illa adigentibus tormentis perstet, qua ratione Pastor fidem suam ita liberabit, ut vel detractor, vel crudelis, qui tormentorum causa oviculis suis extiterit, vel Sinoniis artibus deditus, hoc est, astutus & fallax proditor non habeatur, & muneri suo labem nullam aspergat? Hinc adeò Christus non ad judicium duntaxat, sed ad delationem etiam eorum, qui occultis peccatis admissis corrigi se ab uno vel duobus non patitur, testimonium duorum vel trium exigit. Si non audiverit te, assume unum vel alterum, ut in ore duorum vel trium testium veritas consistat. Si net his obediverit, dic (stipatus testibus illis) Ecclesia, Matth.XVIII.17.18. Et contra seniorem (atque ἀναλόγως[?] quemvis alium) accusationem nisi duobus vel tribus testibus stipati suscipi S. Paulus 1. Tim. V.19. vetat; cum tamen ordinarie ad delationem qualicunque notitia sufficiat, neque testimonia requirantur. Sed aliud videlicet est notitia ex confessione delinquentis petita: aliud notitia aliis argumentis freta. Illa testibus indiget: haec non item.
units.tr: Moreover, sinners sick with a consciousness of their crimes approach their ministers not as ministers of the political court but of the divine one. Therefore, when a sinner confesses or seeks counsel, they must act according to the nature of that court to which they minister, not according to the nature of a foreign court. For in this consultation they act the part of God and Christ, not of the magistrate. Indeed, in this business no judicial inquiry into secrets is instituted; rather, counsel is given to troubled, afflicted and wasting consciences. Then the minister ought to refer all his words, sayings and deeds to the building up of the faithful, not to their destruction: The Lord has given me authority for building up and not for pulling down [εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν], 2 Cor. 10:8 (the text says 13:10). But ministers of the Word of God would use their power and severity for destruction, not for building up, if they disclosed the anxieties and hidden matters of the wretched and penitent. This would be so, first, because they would create a most immediate danger for sinners who candidly confess their sins, and would even anticipate the time of repentance itself, thus offering a stone to one who asks for bread, a serpent to one who seeks a fish, and finally a scorpion to one who desires an egg. Christ indicates (Matt. 7:9; Luke 11:11, 12) that such an attitude is far from the feeling and disposition not only of all carnal fathers but of spiritual ones. Second, because countless people, ready to lay bare their sins and sores to the minister for the sake of comfort, would, out of fear of betrayal and especially of atrocious punishment, neglect all of this; and so, being unable to free their conscience entangled in crimes, they would, while the ministers dread such a reputation, fall headlong into the abyss of despair. But was this the spirit, this the mind [φρόνημα] of Christ, into whose reconciliation of men with God these ministers profess themselves servants? Yet he came not to destroy any more, but to save what had perished, Matt. 18:11. Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he shall declare judgement to the Gentiles. He shall not strive nor cry aloud, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench, until he brings forth judgement to victory, Matt. 12:18–20. The sayings of Solomon agree with this: He who slanders reveals a secret, but he who is faithful in spirit covers a matter, Prov. 11:13. He who reveals a secret is a slanderer, ibid. 20:19. And since in this consultation there is always, either express or tacit, a promise to conceal the offence of the one who consults, which is gathered from the manner of speaking and receiving, and from words that signify and persuade confidence, it is plain that this disclosure of a secret would clash with the truthfulness and faithfulness which we are bound to observe by natural law, and indeed with civil society itself, in which disturbance arises from the disclosure of such secrets. Furthermore, according to the saying of St Peter, charity covers a multitude of sins, 1 Pet. 4:8, and that of Solomon, hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offences, Prov. 10:12, he who seeks love covers an offence, ch. 17:9, the greatest charity of a minister towards the penitent little sheep of Christ must surely be this: he ought not to disclose the multitude of their offences, but to cover them. Moreover, by the almost unanimous verdict of the experts in law, a man conscious of a grave crime is not bound to denounce himself to the judge, because the crime is known to no one but himself. By the same reasoning, one who alone has learned of some crime from the free confession of the guilty party is not bound to reveal it. For why should he be bound more than the accused himself? Lastly, this faithless betrayal of secrets is not free from danger. For what if the one who has deposited his needs as a secret in the minister's bosom, once betrayed, and out of fear of the punishment hanging over him, retracts his voluntary confession, especially of the more atrocious crimes, and persists in the retraction under the compulsion of torments? By what means would the minister then free his faith so that he is not regarded as a betrayer of his flock, a cruel man who became the cause of torments for his little sheep, or as a man given over to Sinonian arts, that is, a crafty and deceitful informer, and so not stain his office with any disgrace? Hence Christ also demands witnesses, not only for judgement but for the reporting even of those who, having committed hidden sins, do not allow themselves to be corrected by one or two. If he will not hear you, take with you one or two more, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses the truth may stand. If he will not obey even them, say (supported by those witnesses) to the Church, Matt. 18:17, 18. And St Paul forbids that an accusation be received against an elder (and [ἀναλόγως] any other) unless supported by two or three witnesses, 1 Tim. 5:19; yet ordinarily some knowledge of any kind suffices for a report, and witnesses are not required. But clearly knowledge sought from the confession of an offender is one thing, and knowledge founded on other arguments is another. The former needs witnesses; the latter does not.

units.la: LII. Neque haec priva & singularis sententia est unius vel paucorum, quanquam satis est, eam firmissimarum rationum tibicine niti, ut hominum consensus exigi non debeat. Sed novitatis tamen & ἰδιογνωμοσύνης suspicionem satis illud depellit, quòd & Ecclesiae patriae antecessores, & Theologi exotici, quotquot in hoc argumentum inciderunt, se paria sentire testati sunt. Inclytae memoriae ille Papalis stabuli expurgator, Hercules, Huldricus Zwinglius, Explanat.art. § 2. in confessione auriculari Pontificia hoc inter alia vitium notat, quòd Sacerdotes quidam male taciti sint, qui omnia effutiant, pleni rimarum, ut pertusa dolia. Subjicit: Factum est aliquando, ut non raro confitentes in capitis discrimen hoc pacto venerint. quod detestanti similis narrat. Ludovicus Lavaterus, magni nominis quondam Ecclesiae nostrae Antistes Comment.in Prov. XXV.9. Arcana, inquit, non sunt temere divulganda. Nam si deposita sunt custodienda, etiam arcana, quae nobis commissa sunt. Paulo post: Concionatores illa, quae eis committuntur ab afflictis hominibus, ne effutiant; Hoc enim non est bonorum virorum. Synopsis Theologica à Ven. Ecclesiae nostrae Antistite, Jacobo Breitingero, qui, ob sapientiam rarum, Platonis Christiani nomen meruit, composita, & à Theologo solidissimo, Praeceptore nostro meritissimo, Rodolpho Stuckio, scholiis aucta, sic lib. IV. 3. eandem in rem sic loquitur: Confessio à peccatore postulanda est dexterrime & prudentissime, partim, ne illam non exigendo peccatorem dimittas faucium: partim, ne confiteri adhuc reluctantem instantius urgendo peccatorem ipse saucies, & vim afferas innatae verecundiae: Scholion sic haec declarat. Jubet Apostolus Gal. VI.1 praeoccupatum peccato καταρτίζετε ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος[?] instruere cum spiritu mansuetudinis, vel reconcinnare, ac supplere in eo, quod deest. v. 2. Alios enim aliorum onera portare, & ita complere legem Christi oportet. Peccatorem irae Divinae motu consternatum erigere & sublevare, prudentiae & charitatis est. Sic cum illo agere oportet, ut conscientiae suae vulnus tibi aperiat. Quod ut lubens faciat, (NB) promittendum illi silentium, ut honori ipsius consulas: solatium, ut saluti. Ex innata autem verecundia confitari reluctanti, temporis non nihil concedendum est, donec de charitate & dexteritate tua certior conscientiam suam peccatis sauciam ultro tibi detegat, & consolationem appetat. Tunc illum, ut Apostolus monet, καταρτίζειν[?], id est, spiritu lenitatis, argumentis ex Verbo Dei petitis instaurare & curare oportet: sicut medici luxata membra componere, & vulnera sedare solent. Deum imprimis ora, ut ipse proximi tui infirmitatem spiritu suo sublevet. Difficilius hoc fit negotium, si ex peccato pluribus noto ignominiosae alicujus poenae metus impendet. Nihil profecto ad salutem peccatoris sobrium magis & sapientius praescribi poterat; ad quam consequendam multum conducere manifestum omnino est, ut haud multis peccatum, quod conscientiam vastavit, innotescat, quod si innotuerit, difficilior cura spiritualis evadet. Denique cursus Theologicus, ex Theologi consummatissimi, Henrici Altingii scriptis à Celeb. Hottingero in usum Scholae nostrae collectus, Loc. XVIII, 12. Lit. C. p. 806. ita confessionem apud homines arbitrariam commendat, ut confitentibus simili modo caveat. Ministrorum, inquit, cumprimis & Presbyterorum hic commendari debet opera: qui tamen facinus aliquod occultum sibi ab homine conscientiae angustia presso revelatum, nisi publicae tranquillitatis & salutis ratio id requirat, evulgare non debent, ne consolationis Ecclesiae occasio aliis praecidatur.
units.tr: LII. Nor is this a private and singular opinion of one person or a few, though it is enough that it rests on the support of very firm reasons, so that the agreement of men need not be required. Yet the suspicion of novelty and of a peculiar opinion [ἰδιογνωμοσύνης] is sufficiently removed by the fact that both the earlier teachers of our own homeland's Church and the foreign theologians, as many as have taken up this question, have testified that they hold the same view. That man of illustrious memory, the Hercules who cleansed the Papal stable, Huldrych Zwingli, in Explanatio articulorum, §2, notes among other faults of the Papists' auricular confession that some priests are badly silent, who blab everything, full of cracks, like leaking casks. He adds: It has happened at times that many who confessed came into mortal danger in this way, which he relates as one who detests it. Ludwig Lavater, once chief minister (Antistes) of our Church and of great name, in his Commentary on Proverbs 25:9: Secrets, he says, are not to be divulged rashly. For if deposits are to be guarded, then so too are the secrets that have been entrusted to us. A little later: Preachers should not blab those things which distressed people entrust to them; for this is not the mark of good men. The Synopsis Theologica, composed by the venerable chief minister of our Church, Jakob Breitinger, who earned the name of the "Christian Plato" for his rare wisdom, and enlarged with scholia by the most solid theologian and our most deserving teacher, Rudolf Stuck, speaks thus to the same point in book IV, 3: Confession is to be sought from the sinner most skilfully and most prudently, partly so that by not seeking it you do not let the sinner slip from your jaws, and partly so that by urging more insistently a sinner who still shrinks from confessing you do not wound him yourself and do violence to his innate shame. The scholion explains this as follows: The Apostle orders in Gal. 6:1 that the one overtaken by a sin be restored [καταρτίζετε ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος], that is, instructed in a spirit of meekness, or put back together and made whole in what is lacking. v. 2: For they ought to bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. To raise up and relieve a sinner terrified by the stirring of divine wrath belongs to prudence and charity. So you must deal with him in such a way that he opens to you the wound of his conscience. That he may do so gladly, (NB) silence must be promised to him, so that you may look after his honour; comfort, so that you may look after his salvation. But when someone reluctant to confess does so out of innate shame, some time must be granted to him, until, becoming more certain of your charity and skill, his conscience wounded by sins discloses itself to you of its own accord and seeks consolation. Then you must, as the Apostle advises, restore him [καταρτίζειν], that is, with a spirit of gentleness, repair and heal him with arguments drawn from the Word of God, just as physicians are accustomed to set dislocated limbs and calm wounds. Above all, pray to God that he may himself relieve your neighbour's weakness by his Spirit. This business is more difficult if fear of some shameful punishment hangs over him for a sin known to many. Nothing more sober or wiser could have been prescribed for the salvation of the sinner; and that it greatly helps toward this end that the sin which has wounded the conscience be known to as few people as possible is entirely plain, and if it becomes known, the spiritual cure will become more difficult. Finally, the theological course, collected for the use of our school from the writings of the most accomplished theologian Henry Alting by the celebrated Hottinger (Loc. XVIII, 12, Lit. C, p. 806), so commends confession made to men in confidence that it guards against those who confess in a similar manner: Here, he says, the work of ministers and especially of elders ought to be commended: yet those who have had some hidden crime revealed to them by a man pressed by anguish of conscience ought not to make it public, unless the reason of public peace and safety requires it, lest the occasion of the Church's consolation be cut off from others.
