units.la: LIII. Exoticorum testium nubem colligere proclive foret. Pleni eam in rem sunt canones Juris Canonici ita dicti. quanquam illis inniti nihil attinet. Pleni libri Theologorum Augustanorum, qui dicta quaedam magni cœterum Lutheri ostentant paulo crudiora, quibus ille confessionem non Sacerdoti, sed Christo factam, adeoque à Sacerdote, ut pote inscio, neutiquam producendam, pertendit. Verba ejus Colloq. Mensal. cap. 14. ejusmodi sunt, ut repetere verecunder. Ordinatio Ecclesiastica Electoris Saxonica art.gener.7 §.ult. gravi sub poena sancit, ut Minister Ecclesiae crimina sibi confessa nemini, quisquis ille sit, (niemand / wer der auch seyn möchte) revelet. Unde JCtus celebris Carpzovius lib.III. Jurispr. Consistor.Tit.II. def.25. infert. Quòd si ergo nemini prorsus Minister Ecclesiae confessionem aperire debet, non certè judex Ministrum Ecclesiae ad testimonii depositionem compellens exceptus erit.
units.tr: LIII. It would be easy to gather a crowd of foreign witnesses. The so-called canons of Canon Law are full of this, though there is no need to rest on them. The books of the Augsburg theologians are full of certain rather harsh sayings of the great Luther, by which he insists that confession is made not to a priest but to Christ, and therefore by no means to be brought forward by a priest, as one who is ignorant of it. His words in the Colloquia Mensalia, ch. 14, are of such a kind that I blush to repeat them. The Ecclesiastical Ordinance of the Elector of Saxony, general article 7, last §, under heavy penalty forbids a minister of the Church to reveal crimes confessed to him to no one, whoever he may be (niemand / wer der auch seyn möchte). Whence the celebrated jurist Carpzov, Jurisprudentia Consistorialis, book III, title II, def. 25, infers: But if a minister of the Church must in no way disclose a confession to anyone, then certainly a judge who compels a minister of the Church to give evidence as a witness will not be exempted.

units.la: LIV. Sed missis his, Theologi Reformati exotici haud ima ex cera produci plures possent. Paucos & celebriores Ecclesiasticae Politices & Casuum Scriptores adducere haud pigebit. Guilielmus Perkinsus Anglo-Britannus, doctrina, candore, judicio praestantissimus Theologus, Caf. Consc. lib. I. cap. I. circa privatam confessionem cautiones edisserens, quartam & postremam his verbis explicat: Is, coram quo confitendum, & in cujus sinum conscientiae onus deponendum, bonae fidei & magna taciturnitatis esse debet, qui potest & velit confessa silere, & in oblivionis quasi sepulchro recondere. Charitas enim juxta illud Petri, operit multitudinem peccatorum. Josephus Hallus, Episcopus Norvicensis, Anglus, pietatis & eruditionis rarae decantatus Theologus, Consil. Consc. q. 7. graviter sic consulit: Si quis conscientiae angustiis pressus peccatum occultum antehac patratum, desiderio consilii vel consolationis a te percipiendae tibi revelaverit, potius animam a corpore tuo dividi, quam committere, ut arcana ista labiis tuis excidant, patieris. Facit huc inprimis Ecclesiae Gallicanae olim sub Imperio heterodoxo & infenso licet, Editorum sacro-sanctorum vi, florentis adhuc, Disciplina, cujus articulus 30. sic habet: Quod crimina spectat, quae Ministri illi detexerunt, qui consilium & solatium quaesiverunt, omnibus Ministris illorum revelatio, seu delatio ad Magistratum interdicta est, ne Ministerium reprehensionem incurrat, & peccatores a poenitentia, & libera delictorum confessione absterreantur. Id quod in omnibus criminibus confessis, solo laesae Majestatis excepto, obtinebit. Et tantum sanctionis illius rigor fuit, ut non tantum art. 28. severe cautum fuerit, ne vel consistoria, vel membra consistorii scripto vel alio modo cuiquam detegant confessionem resipiscentium eorum, qui vel sponte sua, vel aliorum hortatu delicta sua ipsis confessi fuerint, solo laesae Majestatis excepto: sed etiam art. 29. constitutum sit, ut censura Ecclesiastica, usque ad excommunicationem, in eos stringatur, qui Pastores & Seniores, vel integrum consistorium ad tribunal Magistratus vocant, quo testentur contra delinquentes, qui lapsus suos coram iis confessi fuerint. Henricus Alstedius, πολυμαθέστατ[?]ος ille, Theol. Cas. cap. 2. Pastor ille, inquit, qui audit confessionem, non debet divulgare peccatum, sed illud omni studio secretum habere, nisi gloria Dei, & salus tum Ecclesiae, tum Reip. tum ipsius peccatoris contrarium suadeat. Guilielmus Zepperus, prudentissimus ille Politices Ecclesiasticae consultus. Polit. Eccl. lib. I. 19. Quodsi, inquit, Seniorem quispiam (quos inter etiam Pastores refert) ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ sceleris solus quendam deprehenderit, aut reus peccatum in unius Presbyteri aurem retexerit, ad Presbyterium rem non deferet, neque ad alios divulgabit, sed secreto illum ad resipiscentiam exhortabitur. Si enim is forte scelus admissum neget, Presbyter testibus destitutus, Penelopes telam texet. Deinde Presbyteria, tanquam ad artes Sinonias comparata, traducentur, vilescent, & nullis non suspecta reddentur. Alii etiam absterrebuntur, quo minus conscientiae scrupulos in sinum Ministrorum aut Presbyterorum exonerent, aut Ecclesiae consolationem quaerant, adeoque nimia tristitia absorpti, & a Sathana praeoccupati salutis jacturam facient. Denique si factum suum, aut confessionem inficiaretur reus, omnia in incerto essent, neque proficeretur quicquam, &c. Hac enim tota disciplinae ratio & administratio non est Politica, sed Ecclesiastica & Spiritualis, adeóque conscientiae coram Deo spectat, & non fori, sed Poli judicium est. Quare hic confusio graduum, seu Ordinis Ecclesiastici & Politici probe cavenda est. Ubi regula tenenda, quod in sceleribus publicis poena publica Magistratus, disciplinam vel censuram Ecclesiasticam non tollunt, & vicissim. Versantur enim hic Magistratus & ministerium circa idem objectum quidem, verum dissimili ratione, & distincta jurisdictione, potestate & gladio.
units.tr: LIV. But setting these aside, foreign Reformed theologians could be brought forward in no small number. I will not be sorry to cite a few of the more celebrated writers on Ecclesiastical Polity and cases of conscience. William Perkins, the English-British theologian, most outstanding in learning, candour and judgement, in Cases of Conscience, book I, ch. 1, setting out the cautions concerning private confession, explains the fourth and last in these words: He before whom one confesses, and into whose bosom the burden of conscience is laid down, ought to be a man of good faith and great discretion, who is able and willing to keep silent about what has been confessed, and to bury it, as it were, in the grave of forgetfulness. For charity, according to the saying of Peter, covers a multitude of sins. Joseph Hall, Bishop of Norwich, an Englishman, a theologian celebrated for rare piety and learning, in Resolutions of Conscience, q. 7, gravely advises: If someone, pressed by anguish of conscience, has revealed to you a hidden sin committed earlier, out of desire for counsel or for the consolation to be received from you, you would rather suffer your soul to be separated from your body than allow those secrets to slip from your lips. Here above all belongs the discipline of the French Church, which, though once under a heterodox and hostile empire, still flourished by the force of the sacred Edicts, whose 30th article reads: As for the crimes which those ministers have disclosed who sought counsel and comfort, the revelation or denunciation of them to the magistrate is forbidden to all their ministers, lest the ministry incur reproach and sinners be frightened away from repentance and free confession of their offences. This shall hold in all confessed crimes, the sole exception being treason. And so strict was the rigour of that sanction that not only was it severely provided in art. 28 that neither the consistories nor the members of a consistory should disclose by writing or in any other way to anyone the confession of those who repent, who have confessed their offences to them either of their own accord or at the urging of others, the sole exception being treason; but also in art. 29 it was established that ecclesiastical censure, up to excommunication, should be applied to those who summon the ministers and elders, or the whole consistory, to the tribunal of the magistrate, in order to testify against offenders who have confessed their lapses before them. Henry Alstedius, that most learned man, in Theological Cases, ch. 2: The minister who hears a confession, he says, ought not to divulge the sin, but ought to keep it secret with every care, unless the glory of God and the salvation of the Church, the commonwealth and the sinner himself advise otherwise. William Zepper, that most prudent counsellor on ecclesiastical polity, in Politia Ecclesiastica, book I, 19: But if someone alone has caught an elder (among whom he also counts ministers) in the very act [ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ] of a crime, or if a guilty person has confided a sin into the ear of a single elder, he will not refer the matter to the presbytery, nor make it known to others, but will privately exhort him to repentance. For if perhaps he denies that the wicked deed was done, the elder, lacking witnesses, will weave Penelope's web. Then the presbyteries, as if they were prepared for Sinonian tricks, would be dragged through the mud, would become cheap, and would be made suspect to everyone. Others too would be frightened away from unburdening the scruples of their conscience into the bosom of ministers or elders, or from seeking the consolation of the Church; and so, swallowed up by excessive sadness and forestalled by Satan, they would suffer the loss of their salvation. Finally, if the accused were to deny his deed or his confession, everything would be left in doubt and nothing would be accomplished, etc. For this whole rationale and administration of discipline is not political but ecclesiastical and spiritual, and so it concerns conscience before God, and its judgement belongs not to the forum but to heaven. Therefore the confusion of the degrees, that is, of the ecclesiastical and political order, must be carefully avoided here. The rule to be held is that public punishment by the magistrate does not abolish ecclesiastical discipline or censure for public crimes, and conversely. For the magistracy and the ministry are concerned with the same object indeed, but in a different way, and with distinct jurisdiction, power and sword.

units.la: LV. Cœterum grave nonnullis videtur, à Pastore & quovis alio occultari, & non deferri ad judicem peccata in sinum sibi deposita, quae iterari possunt, atque iterari ad judicem delata, & ab eodem punita non potuissent. Verum isthæc ratiocinatio viro prudente indigna est. Primò enim non stringit nisi in criminibus atrocioribus & capitalibus, quae vita erepta iterari non possunt. Sunt verò alia etiam delicta non capitalia, quae Pastori revelata, & ab eodem ad judicem delata, & secundum leges punita, nihilo secius iterari possunt. Secundò peccata atrociora Pastori revelata, ab eodem occultantur non temerè, sed graves, quas supra attulimus, ob causas. Facta autem & consilia humana ratione librari & institui[?], non ex eventu, qui ut plurimùm incertus, nulla providentia avertitur, dijudicari debent. ——Careat successibus opto, Quisquis ab eventu facta notanda putat.
units.tr: LV. Moreover, some think it a serious matter that sins entrusted to the minister or to anyone else in confidence should be concealed and not reported to the magistrate. They fear that such sins may be repeated, and that if they had been reported to the magistrate and punished by him they could not have been repeated. But this reasoning is unworthy of a prudent man. First, it applies only to the more atrocious and capital crimes, which cannot be repeated once life has been taken away. There are, however, other offences that are not capital, which, though revealed to the minister and reported by him to the judge and punished according to the laws, can nonetheless be repeated. Second, the more atrocious sins revealed to the minister are concealed by him not rashly but for the serious reasons we have already given. Human deeds and plans must be weighed and judged by human reason, not by their outcome, which is for the most part uncertain and not turned aside by any foresight. ——Let him be without success who thinks deeds should be judged by their outcome.

units.la: Tertiò peccata quaevis Pastori revelata ab eodem occultantur, non ut fomentis adhibitis ab eo alantur, sed potiùs, ut vera & salutari poenitentia, cui longior vitae tractus & Pastoris consilia inservire possunt, expiantur[?], melioribusque adeò, non paribus, vel deterioribus etiam factis in posterum compensentur. Nam qui ejusmodi delicta in Pastoris sinum deponit, non tantùm praesumitur urente & mordente conscientia, adeóque totus in poenitentiam gestiens, & à peccato iterando abhorrens, ita facere, (quotus quisque enim sine gravissima & inevitabili causa ulcera sua nudaverit?) sed etiam à Pastore gravissimis consiliis, admonitionibus, obtestationibus, irae Divinae adversus contumacem denuntiatione, & remissionis peccati erga credentem, poenitentem, & à peccato abstinentem, ex Dei verbo declaratione atque promissione ad poenitentiam ἀνυπόκριτον acriter stimulat; neque semel ita stimulasse contentus, deinceps etiam ejusdem vitae assiduè, & longè, quàm incognito ejus delicto & statu facturus fuerat, diligentius invigilat & imminet, atque plus etiam ab eo, quàm à quovis alio exigit. Quò plura enim & majora peccata remittuntur, hoc ardentior & vehementior Dei dilectio, atque juxta eandem à peccatis quibusvis, gravioribus inprimis, abstinentia requiritur. Multa peccata ei (mulieri poenitenti) remissa sunt, quia multum dilexit. Cui vero parum remittitur, is parum diligit, Luc. VII. 47. Quòd si res ifthaec tota fallit, & eventum contrarium sortitur (quamvis in peccatum idem ex humana infirmitate regenitus etiam incidere potest, atque incidens non ideo statim de statu gratiae, in quem prior illa poenitentia peccatorem confitentem asseruit, ita excidit, ut à Pastore solo relapsus conscio sine ulla delicti & delinquentis discretione ad judicem deferri debeat, quod ex Matth. XVIII. 21. 22. dijudicandum,) jam Pastori accidit, quod medico, qui salutaribus remediis adhibitis alios quidem restituit, alios verò, validiore morbo, sibi relinquit.
units.tr: Third, any sins revealed to the minister are concealed by him not so that they may be nourished by him with encouragement, but rather so that they may be atoned for by true and salutary repentance, to which a longer span of life and the minister's counsel can contribute, and so that they may be made up for in the future by better deeds, not equal or worse ones. For the one who lays such offences in the minister's bosom is presumed not only to be stung and gnawed by conscience, and so eager for repentance and abhorrent of repeating the sin (for who, unless driven by the most serious and unavoidable cause, would bare his sores?), but the minister also urges him sharply to repentance that is unfeigned [ἀνυπόκριτον] by the most serious counsels, admonitions and entreaties, by the proclamation of God's wrath against the stubborn, and by the declaration and promise from God's Word of forgiveness of sin toward the believer who repents and refrains from sin. Nor, having urged him this once, is he content; from then on he watches over and presses upon his life continually and far more diligently than he would have done had the offence and his state remained unknown, and he demands more from him than from anyone else. For the more and greater the sins that are forgiven, the warmer and stronger the love of God, and along with it abstinence from every sin, especially the grave ones, is required. To her (the penitent woman) many sins were forgiven, because she loved much; but to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little, Luke 7:47. But if the whole matter turns out otherwise and has the opposite outcome (although a man reborn may also fall into the same sin through human weakness, and by falling he is not at once cast out of the state of grace into which that earlier repentance placed the confessing sinner, so that a relapsed penitent known to the minister alone, without any distinction of the offence or the offender, must be reported to the judge; this is to be decided from Matthew 18:21-22), then what happens to the minister is what happens to a physician who, having applied wholesome remedies, restores some patients but leaves others to a more stubborn disease.

units.la: Non est in medico semper relevetur ut ager,Interdum docta plus valet arte malum.
units.tr: The physician cannot always relieve the sick as the field is relieved; sometimes skill in the art prevails over the disease.

units.la: Nemo tamen unquam propterea corporali medico succensuit, vel vulnera ei non aperienda insanivit. Cur ergo spirituali medico, cujus omnis operatio à supernaturali Dei gratia unicè dependet, infelix ille successus exprobrari, vel secretior ejusdem cura in universum damnari debeat? Quarto denique scrupulus iste etiam civilem judicem urgebit, ut ei poenam capitalem suspendere, mitigare, imò in solidum etiam condonare integrum futurum nunquam sit. Constat tamen in perduellione, cui magna peccantium turba implicita est, à judice probo & tyrannidi non assueto exemplum poenae ad paucos, terrorem ad omnes dirigi: Ubi locum habet illud Symnachi Epist. lib. I. 30. Moribus saevis familiare est atque cognatum exarmare spiritus impunitatu exemplo. Quando etiam spes est, ut qui deliquit, se ipsum corrigat citra poenam; aut jactura dignitatis, in quem peccatum est, metuenda non est; aut meritum, spes magna in posterum, vel aliud quid delinquentem commendat; aut peccatum ex ignorantia vel infirmitate animi difficulter superabili processit; aut peccatum tale non est, ut ejus poena exemplari publico necessariò consulendum sit; judex civilis se dispensare, vel poenam prorsus remittere posse arbitratur. Quid ergo, si post dispensationem & condonationem poenae à judice factam, peccator delictum suum iteraverit, & ad vomitum redierit? An in se hujus relapsus culpam haerere, judex agnoscet? Par, imo melior causa erit Pastoris, qui peccatorem occultum in sinum suum confugientem ad poenitentiam ducens, facit, quod partium ipsius est, nec de jure suo quicquam remittit.
units.tr: Yet no one has ever been angry with a physician of the body for this, or blamed him for not opening the wounds. Why then should that unhappy outcome be thrown in the face of the spiritual physician, whose whole work depends solely on the supernatural grace of God, or his more secret care be condemned altogether? Fourth, finally, this scruple will also press upon the civil judge, so that it will never be right for him to suspend, mitigate, or indeed wholly pardon a capital penalty. Yet it is established that in treason, in which a great crowd of offenders is involved, an upright judge who is not accustomed to tyranny directs the example of punishment to a few and the fear of it to all. Here applies that saying of Symmachus, Letters, book 1, no. 30: It is characteristic and akin to cruel manners to unnerve spirits by an example of impunity. Also, when there is hope that the offender will correct himself without punishment; or when the loss of dignity in which the offence was committed is not to be feared; or when merit, a great hope for the future, or something else commends the offender; or when the offence arose from ignorance or from a weakness of mind that is hard to overcome; or when the offence is not of such a kind that its punishment must necessarily be set before the public as an example; the civil judge thinks he may dispense with it or remit the penalty altogether. What then, if after the penalty has been dispensed with and pardoned by the judge, the offender repeats his offence and returns to his vomit? Will the judge acknowledge that the guilt of this relapse clings to himself? The minister's cause is equal, or rather better, when he leads the hidden sinner who has fled to his bosom to repentance; he does what is his part and gives up nothing of his right.

units.la: LVI. Superest Forum Privatum. Licet enim proprie privatus judiciale & coactivum, uti appellant, forum nullum habeat, jus tamen habet, offensas & injurias sibi ab aliis factas per implorata judicis sententiam persequendi, & liquidi juris sui restitutionem exigendi. Ad eum proin offensae & injuriae sibi illatae cognitio, & satisfactionis requirendae potestas pertinet. Qua in re fori quaedam ratio & similitudo est. Hinc S. Jacobus hortatur: Confitemini alii aliis peccata, & orate pro vobis invicem, ut sanemini, Jac. V.26. ubi peccatum tum scandalum ex peccato, proximum quemque ad ruinam aedificans, tum injuriam & offensam proximo illatam significat, quae ita proximo confitendae sunt, ut de jure ei restituendo cum eodem amice transigatur.
units.tr: LVI. There remains the Private forum. For although a private person strictly has no judicial and coercive forum, as they call it, he does have the right to pursue offences and injuries done to him by others by seeking a judge's sentence, and to demand restitution of his clear right. Therefore the knowledge of the offence and injury done to him, and the power of requiring satisfaction, belong to him. In this matter there is a certain likeness and resemblance to a court. Hence St James exhorts: Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed, James 5:16, where "sin" means both the scandal arising from sin, which builds each neighbour toward ruin, and the injury and offence done to the neighbour, which must be confessed to him in such a way that concerning restitution of right to him one comes to a friendly settlement with him.

units.la: LVII. In hoc etiam foro delatio quaedam locum habet. Charitas enim, qua proximo cuivis, aeque ac nobis ipsis, devincti sumus, ut ejusdem honori, fortunis & vitae conservandae & vindicandae enixe studeamus; neque adeo de fratre, tribuli, cive interrogati, nobiscum cogitemus: השמר אחי אנכי[?] Num quid custos ego sum fratris mei? Gen. IV.9. Imo Deus & fratri, & civi custodes nos constituit, quem diligere aeque ac nos ipsos debemus. Quos non servasti, perdidisti. Quod si ergo proximi cujusvis innocentis honorem, fortunas & vitam in praesens discrimen ab hominibus improbis adduci videmus, & certo novimus, si aliter periculum ab ejus capite propulsari non posse appareat, cuilibet, non qua is in hoc vel illo statu locatus, sed qua homo, Christianus inprimis est, incumbit, ut improborum machinationes adversus innocentes, vel injurias iisdem illatas, quatenus illas resarciri adhuc posse constat, ad eundem, non malivolentiae, vindictae, vel alio quovis atrae loliginis succo imbutus, & ad prodendum delinquentem concitus, sed solo purae charitatis erga proximum studio inflammatus, deferat. Quae res cum nullam dubitationem habeat, ampliorem etiam tractationem nullam postulare videtur.
units.tr: LVII. In this forum too a certain kind of reporting has its place. For the charity by which we are bound to every neighbour, just as to ourselves, obliges us to strive earnestly to preserve and defend his honour, property and life; nor, when asked about a brother, a fellow-tribesman or a fellow-citizen, should we think: "השמר אחי אנכי" [Am I my brother's keeper?], Gen. 4:9. Indeed God makes us keepers both of brother and of fellow-citizen, whom we ought to love just as we love ourselves. Those whom you did not keep, you destroyed. If therefore we see the honour, property and life of any innocent neighbour brought into present danger by wicked men, and we know for certain that, unless it appears that danger cannot otherwise be averted from his head, it falls to anyone, not as he is placed in this or that state but as a man and above all as a Christian, to report the plots of the wicked against the innocent, or the injuries done to them, insofar as it is established that these can still be repaired, to the proper authority; and let him do so not stirred by ill will, desire for revenge, or any other black juice of the cuttlefish, but inflamed solely by the zeal of pure charity toward his neighbour, and prompted not to betray the offender. Since this matter raises no doubt, it seems to require no longer treatment.

units.la: LVIII. Sed hactenus dicta, coronodis loco, in pauca contrahere, & simul Regulas certas & fixas, juxta quas delatio delinquentium omnis recte & pie dirigi, & instituri valeat, statuere lubet. Pri-mo igitur Delatio delinquentium quaedam, puta in causa honesta, ex authoritate legitima, fine honesto, qui est intentio abrumpendi peccatum proximi, & periculum ingens avertendi ; per media convenientia instituta ipsa quoque honesta, legitima, necessaria est. His vero conditionibus destituta obtrectatio potius, & improba digiti extensio, quam honesta delatio est. Secundò nec quivis delator admitti debet, nec semper, nec in quovis negotio, nec contra quosvis, nec admisso semel temerè & sine inquisitione ulteriore temerè fides adhiberi debet. Tertiò, se ipsum deferre nemo tenetur, etiam anquisitus à judice, si de coetero infamia nulla laboraverit. Quartò, conscientiae tamen stimulis adactus se ipsum ultro apud judicem deferre potest, si conscientiam perturbatam, absque satisfactione eidem debita & oblata tranquillare non potest. Quintò, in foro Divino Ministerali peccator sua, & quivis aliorum etiam gravia delicta, ubi praesens animae periculum id exigit, ad Pastorem deferre, consilii & opis ex Dei verbo impetrandae gratia, potest & debet. Sextò, in Ecclesia fidelis quivis peccato proximi offensus, offendentem, si contumacem se adversus corripientes duos vel tres gesserit, ad Ecclesiam ordine suo deferre tenetur. Septimò, Ecclesia peccatorem praefractum [?] & incorrigibilem ita habere pro Ethnico & Publicano debet, ut vel eum etiam invitum, atque reluctantem sacrorum communione moveat, ubi id sine majori incommodo fieri potest: vel ubi id Ecclesiae & disciplinae ratio singularis non permittit, saltem severe & publice jubeat sacris symbolis ad judicium suum non abuti, atque de coetero eum non immediate, sed per officiales consistorio praesentes ad Magistratum corrigendum deferat. Octavò, in foro Politico delatoris officium sua sponte nemo occupare debet. Vocatus tamen a Magistratu officium illud suscipere & legitime obire potest. Nonò, quilibet tamen privati etiam, ad id specialiter non vocati, sola charitate jubente, ad Magistratum deferre delicta quaedam tenentur, illa puta, quae vel immediate Dei Majestatem, & humanam societatem infestant, vel mediate in publicam perniciem tendunt, vel ejusmodi sunt, ut eorum delatio ad delinquentium emendationem procurandam, & delicti iterationem impediendam omitti non possit, nisi forte detrimentum ex talibus delictis in Dei gloriam, societatem humanam publicam, & delinquentem ipsum alia via molliori averruncari possit. Decimò, Pastor Ecclesiae delatoris ad judicem civilem speciale munus suscipere nullo modo potest. Undecimò, potest tamen & debet Pastor tum Ecclesiae nomine incorrigibiles; tum non à peccatore confitente, sed aliunde sibi nota ejusmodi delicta, quae à quovis privato & cive deferri debere regula nona diximus, ad Magistratum deferre, vel mediate per officiales Magistratus, vel, si hi officio suo defungi neglexerint, immediate etiam. Duodecimò, Pastor Ecclesiae delicta atrocia & capitalia, sibi à delinquentibus, quos ad id conscientiae angores stimulant, consilii & consolationis percipiendae gratia, revelata & confessa, quatenus citra gloriae Dei, Reipublicae, Ecclesiae, & innocentis cujusvis detrimentum notorium vel delinquentes ipsi, vel delicta, vel ambo occultari possunt, religiose occultare tenetur, neque unquam ad judicem deferre potest.
units.tr: LVIII. But, by way of a conclusion, I wish to gather the things said so far into a few words, and at the same time to set down certain and fixed rules by which all reporting of offenders may be rightly and piously directed and carried out. First, therefore, the reporting of offenders, for example in an honourable cause, by lawful authority, for an honourable end, which is the intention of cutting off a neighbour's sin and averting a great danger, and by fitting means that are themselves honourable, lawful and necessary, is right. But a report that lacks these conditions is rather slander and a wicked pointing of the finger than an honourable reporting. Second, no informer should be admitted, neither always nor in every matter, nor against everyone; and once admitted, his word should not be trusted rashly and without further inquiry. Third, no one is bound to report himself, even when questioned by a judge, if he has never laboured under any infamy. Fourth, however, driven by the goads of conscience, he may of his own accord report himself to the judge, if he cannot quiet his troubled conscience without the satisfaction owed to it being offered. Fifth, in the divine forum of the ministry a sinner may and should report his own grave offences, and anyone else's too, to the minister, where the present danger to the soul requires it, in order to obtain counsel and help from God's Word. Sixth, in the Church, any believer who has been offended by his neighbour's sin is bound to report the offender to the Church in its proper order, if the offender has shown himself stubborn against two or three who have rebuked him. Seventh, the Church ought to treat a stubborn and incorrigible sinner as a heathen and a tax-collector, so that either it removes him from communion in the sacred things even against his will and while he resists, where this can be done without greater inconvenience; or, where the particular circumstances of the Church and its discipline do not allow this, at least it orders him severely and publicly not to abuse the sacred symbols for his own judgment, and from then on it reports him to the magistrate for correction, not directly but through its officials present at the consistory. Eighth, in the civil forum no one should take upon himself the office of informer of his own accord. Yet when called by the magistrate he may accept that office and discharge it lawfully. Ninth, nevertheless, even private persons who have not been specially called to it are bound, by charity alone commanding, to report certain offences to the magistrate: namely those which either assail the majesty of God and human society directly, or tend indirectly to public ruin, or are of such a kind that their reporting cannot be omitted if the amendment of the offender and the prevention of a repeated offence are to be secured, unless perhaps the harm that comes from such offences to the glory of God, to public human society, and to the offender himself can be averted by another, gentler way. Tenth, a minister of the Church can in no way undertake the special office of informer to the civil judge. Eleventh, nevertheless, a minister may and should report to the magistrate those who are incorrigible in the name of the Church, and also such offences as he knows from some source other than a confessing sinner, which, as we said in the ninth rule, ought to be reported by any private person and citizen; he may report them either indirectly through the officials of the magistrate, or, if these have neglected to discharge their duty, directly as well. Twelfth, a minister of the Church who has been told and has heard confessed atrocious and capital offences, by offenders whom the anguish of conscience has urged to seek counsel and consolation, is bound to keep those offences religiously secret, so far as without notorious detriment to the glory of God, the commonwealth, the Church, and any innocent person, either the offenders themselves, or the offences, or both can be concealed; and he can never report them to the judge.

units.la: SOLI DEO GLORIA,
units.tr: TO GOD ALONE BE THE GLORY,
